title: Emergent Chromatin Nanodomain Topology: Integrating Hi-C, Super-Resolution Imaging, and Epigenomics to Explain Cell-Type-Specific Gene Regulation
author: gpt-5.2
abstract_original:
Chromatin forms mesoscale nanodomains (50–300 nm) whose collective folding and compartmentalization produce emergent regulatory behaviors—enhancer–promoter communication, insulation, and transcriptional bursting—that cannot be inferred from individual nucleosome modifications. This project will synthesize 3D genome conformation and imaging data to test whether a small set of mesoscale topological motifs explains cell-type-specific gene regulation across mammals.

We will integrate publicly available datasets: (i) population and single-cell Hi-C / Micro-C maps (4D Nucleome, GEO, ENCODE), (ii) super-resolution and multiplexed DNA FISH imaging of chromatin domains (4DN data portal, BioImage Archive; Oligopaint datasets), (iii) epigenomic marks and accessibility (ENCODE ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq; Roadmap Epigenomics), (iv) transcriptional outputs (single-cell RNA-seq from Human Cell Atlas; nascent transcription where available), and (v) structural constraints from nucleosome and chromatin fiber models (PDB where relevant; polymer simulation benchmarks).

Methodologically, we will create a joint inference framework that maps between contact matrices and physical 3D domain geometries. We will (1) infer nanodomain boundaries and interaction strengths from Hi-C/Micro-C using multi-resolution community detection; (2) calibrate polymer models with imaging-derived distance distributions to resolve degeneracies in contact-based reconstructions; (3) learn a “motif dictionary” of recurrent mesoscale folding patterns (e.g., loop clusters, rosettes, compartment microdomains) using unsupervised representation learning that ingests both contact and imaging features; and (4) link motif occupancy to emergent regulatory phenotypes—bursting parameters, enhancer responsiveness, and lineage stability—using hierarchical models across cell types.

The hypothesis is that despite molecular diversity, chromatin nanodomain topology falls into a limited set of mesoscale motifs whose combinations predict regulatory capacity and noise. We will test whether developmental transitions correspond to motif switching, and whether disease-associated noncoding variants preferentially disrupt specific motifs rather than individual loops.

Expected outputs include: a cross-cell-type atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs, quantitative relationships between motif composition and transcriptional variability, and open tools for jointly analyzing Hi-C and imaging. This synthesis requires collaboration among genome informaticians, polymer physicists, microscopy experts, and statistical modelers; no single lab typically has access to and expertise across these modalities. NCEMS working group support is essential for harmonizing standards, building reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to bridge 3D genomics and quantitative imaging under open-science practices.

Title: Emergent Chromatin Nanodomain Topology: Integrating Hi-C, Super-Resolution Imaging, and Epigenomics to Explain Cell-Type-Specific Gene Regulation

Abstract: Chromatin forms mesoscale nanodomains (50–300 nm) whose collective folding and compartmentalization produce emergent regulatory behaviors—enhancer–promoter communication, insulation, and transcriptional bursting—that cannot be inferred from individual nucleosome modifications. This project will synthesize 3D genome conformation and imaging data to test whether a small set of mesoscale topological motifs explains cell-type-specific gene regulation across mammals.

We will integrate publicly available datasets: (i) population and single-cell Hi-C / Micro-C maps (4D Nucleome, GEO, ENCODE), (ii) super-resolution and multiplexed DNA FISH imaging of chromatin domains (4DN data portal, BioImage Archive; Oligopaint datasets), (iii) epigenomic marks and accessibility (ENCODE ChIP-seq, ATAC-seq; Roadmap Epigenomics), (iv) transcriptional outputs (single-cell RNA-seq from Human Cell Atlas; nascent transcription where available), and (v) structural constraints from nucleosome and chromatin fiber models (PDB where relevant; polymer simulation benchmarks).

Methodologically, we will create a joint inference framework that maps between contact matrices and physical 3D domain geometries. We will (1) infer nanodomain boundaries and interaction strengths from Hi-C/Micro-C using multi-resolution community detection; (2) calibrate polymer models with imaging-derived distance distributions to resolve degeneracies in contact-based reconstructions; (3) learn a “motif dictionary” of recurrent mesoscale folding patterns (e.g., loop clusters, rosettes, compartment microdomains) using unsupervised representation learning that ingests both contact and imaging features; and (4) link motif occupancy to emergent regulatory phenotypes—bursting parameters, enhancer responsiveness, and lineage stability—using hierarchical models across cell types.

The hypothesis is that despite molecular diversity, chromatin nanodomain topology falls into a limited set of mesoscale motifs whose combinations predict regulatory capacity and noise. We will test whether developmental transitions correspond to motif switching, and whether disease-associated noncoding variants preferentially disrupt specific motifs rather than individual loops.

Expected outputs include: a cross-cell-type atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs, quantitative relationships between motif composition and transcriptional variability, and open tools for jointly analyzing Hi-C and imaging. This synthesis requires collaboration among genome informaticians, polymer physicists, microscopy experts, and statistical modelers; no single lab typically has access to and expertise across these modalities. NCEMS working group support is essential for harmonizing standards, building reproducible pipelines, and training trainees to bridge 3D genomics and quantitative imaging under open-science practices.

Background: Chromatin organization is a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon: it emerges from molecular interactions among nucleosomes, DNA-binding proteins, and transcriptional machinery, yet manifests as higher-order spatial domains that are tens to hundreds of nanometers in size—larger than single nucleosomes but smaller than whole chromosomes or nuclei. At this mesoscale (roughly 50–300 nm), chromatin exhibits “nanodomains” and microcompartments whose collective topology influences gene regulation in ways not reducible to any single molecular mark. These emergent behaviors include probabilistic enhancer–promoter communication, insulation between regulatory neighborhoods, and transcriptional bursting kinetics. Understanding how such behaviors arise requires synthesis across modalities that each capture only partial projections of the underlying 3D polymer state.

Over the past decade, chromosome conformation capture assays (Hi-C, Micro-C, and related methods) have produced extensive public maps of genome-wide contact frequencies across cell types and species. The 4D Nucleome (4DN) Data Portal, Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO), ENCODE, and other repositories host hundreds of high-depth bulk Hi-C maps and growing collections of single-cell Hi-C and Micro-C datasets. These data revealed canonical organizational features—A/B compartments, topologically associating domains (TADs), and loops—while also highlighting that fine-scale contact patterns vary strongly by cell type, differentiation state, and perturbations. Micro-C, with nucleosome-scale resolution, further suggests that contact maps contain rich mesoscale structure beyond classical TAD boundaries, including nested communities and microcompartmentalization.

In parallel, advances in super-resolution and multiplexed imaging have made it possible to directly measure spatial distances and domain shapes in single cells. Public resources such as the 4DN Data Portal, the BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI), and community-shared Oligopaint and multiplexed DNA FISH datasets provide imaging of chromatin loci, domain boundaries, and nuclear landmarks at tens-of-nanometers precision. Unlike contact maps, which are ensemble-averaged and indirect, imaging provides geometric constraints (distance distributions, radius of gyration, anisotropy, and spatial co-localization) that can disambiguate multiple 3D conformations consistent with the same contact matrix.

Epigenomic maps add a third key axis. ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics provide thousands of ChIP-seq profiles for histone modifications and architectural proteins, along with ATAC-seq and DNase-seq accessibility maps. These data connect chromatin state to physical organization: active and inactive marks correlate with compartment identity; CTCF/cohesin occupancy correlates with loop anchors; and enhancer states correlate with dynamic regulatory potential. Finally, transcriptional outputs are richly represented in the Human Cell Atlas and other single-cell RNA-seq collections, as well as publicly available nascent transcription datasets (e.g., GRO-seq/PRO-seq in GEO/ENCODE for select cell types). Together, these resources enable a synthesis-driven approach to link mesoscale topology to emergent gene expression phenotypes such as cell-type-specific expression programs and transcriptional noise.

Despite this abundance, a major gap remains: we lack a unified, quantitative mapping between (i) contact-based representations of chromatin organization and (ii) physical, nanoscale domain geometries observed by imaging, and we do not know whether diverse cell types share a limited “vocabulary” of mesoscale topological motifs. Current analyses often focus on individual features (e.g., a specific loop, a single TAD boundary, or a single histone mark) and then infer regulatory outcomes. Yet emergent regulatory behavior likely depends on combinations of mesoscale structures: clustered loops may create rosette-like hubs, microcompartments may generate local phase-separated neighborhoods, and boundary strength may modulate enhancer reach and bursting probability. These multi-feature combinations are difficult to infer from any single data type.

Synthesis research is uniquely positioned to resolve this gap by integrating heterogeneous public datasets at scale and extracting generalizable motifs across cell types and mammals. First, contact maps alone are degenerate: many 3D polymer conformations can produce similar contact frequencies. Imaging-derived distance distributions can serve as orthogonal constraints to calibrate and select among candidate polymer models, thereby converting ambiguous contact patterns into interpretable 3D nanodomain geometries. Second, epigenomic annotations can be used to interpret motif composition (e.g., whether a motif preferentially occurs in H3K27ac-rich regions or Polycomb-associated domains) and to test whether motif boundaries align with chromatin state transitions. Third, transcriptional data allow evaluation of emergent outcomes: if mesoscale motifs are mechanistically meaningful, their occupancy should predict not only mean expression but also variability and bursting-related proxies across cell types.

The mesoscale focus aligns with NCEMS’s vision: nanodomain topology sits between molecular interactions (nucleosome modifications, binding factors) and higher-order cellular outcomes (lineage commitment, disease states). Emergence is central here: regulatory behaviors arise from collective folding patterns, not from any single molecular component. By synthesizing publicly available Hi-C/Micro-C, super-resolution imaging, epigenomics, and transcriptomics—without generating new data—this project aims to identify a compact set of mesoscale topological motifs and quantify how motif combinations produce cell-type-specific gene regulation. The availability of community-scale datasets across multiple repositories now makes it feasible to test these ideas rigorously and comparatively across mammals, developmental transitions, and disease-associated variant contexts, but doing so requires coordinated, transdisciplinary expertise and shared standards that exceed the capabilities of any single laboratory.

Research Questions: This working group will address a central question in mesoscale genome biology: do chromatin nanodomains organize into a limited set of recurrent topological motifs whose combinations generate emergent, cell-type-specific regulatory behaviors? We focus on motifs at the 50–300 nm scale—larger than nucleosome-level features but smaller than whole-chromosome compartments—because this is the scale at which enhancer–promoter communication, insulation, and transcriptional bursting are thought to be tuned by collective folding.

Research Question 1 (RQ1): What is the minimal “motif dictionary” of chromatin nanodomain topologies that recurs across mammalian cell types?
Hypothesis 1 (H1): Across diverse mammalian cell types and tissues, mesoscale chromatin can be represented by a small number of motifs (e.g., loop clusters/rosettes, boundary-insulated domains, microcompartment patches, and hub-like interaction communities) that recur with conserved geometric signatures.
Measurable predictions: (i) Unsupervised joint embeddings of contact-map features (from Hi-C/Micro-C) and imaging-derived geometric features will cluster into a limited number of stable motif classes; (ii) motif classes will be reproducible across independent datasets and platforms (e.g., different Hi-C protocols, different imaging studies) after harmonization; (iii) motif frequency distributions will differ by cell type, but motif definitions (feature centroids) will remain conserved.
Validation using existing data: We will test motif stability via cross-study replication (train motif models on 4DN Hi-C + BioImage Archive imaging from one set of cell types, validate on ENCODE/GEO and independent imaging datasets). We will quantify reproducibility using adjusted mutual information between motif assignments and evaluate whether motifs persist under downsampling of contact depth and imaging cell counts.

Research Question 2 (RQ2): How do motif combinations and transitions relate to emergent regulatory phenotypes such as transcriptional variability and enhancer responsiveness?
Hypothesis 2 (H2): Motif composition at gene regulatory neighborhoods predicts emergent transcriptional outcomes—particularly variability proxies—better than individual molecular marks or single loops.
Measurable predictions: (i) For matched cell types, motif occupancy around genes (e.g., within 1–2 Mb windows or within inferred nanodomains) will explain significant variance in gene expression dispersion (from Human Cell Atlas scRNA-seq) beyond what is explained by promoter accessibility and histone marks alone; (ii) genes in motifs characterized by strong insulation and limited cross-boundary contacts will show reduced enhancer-linked coexpression and lower expression noise; (iii) motifs with clustered enhancer–promoter contacts (hub/rosette-like) will associate with higher burst frequency proxies and stronger enhancer-dependent expression.
Validation using existing data: We will use hierarchical models that incorporate covariates from ENCODE/Roadmap (ATAC-seq, H3K27ac, H3K4me3, CTCF/cohesin where available) and compare predictive performance with and without motif features using cross-validation across cell types and donors. Where nascent transcription datasets exist in GEO/ENCODE for specific cell lines, we will test whether motif classes correlate with polymerase density and transcriptional initiation proxies.

Research Question 3 (RQ3): Can imaging constraints resolve degeneracies in contact-based reconstructions sufficiently to infer physically meaningful nanodomain geometries?
Hypothesis 3 (H3): Joint inference that explicitly fits both contact frequencies and imaging distance distributions will produce a constrained ensemble of 3D conformations whose inferred geometric parameters (domain radius, compaction, inter-domain separation) are consistent across datasets and predictive of regulatory outcomes.
Measurable predictions: (i) Polymer model ensembles calibrated with imaging will show reduced uncertainty (narrower posterior distributions) in geometric parameters compared with contact-only models; (ii) calibrated models will better reproduce independent imaging metrics not used in fitting (e.g., distance quantiles for held-out locus pairs); (iii) geometric parameters derived from calibrated ensembles will correlate with motif classes and explain additional variance in transcriptional outcomes.
Validation using existing data: We will perform hold-out tests where imaging distance distributions from a subset of locus pairs are withheld during calibration and then predicted. We will also compare calibrated polymer ensembles to existing published polymer simulation benchmarks and constraints (e.g., nucleosome/chromatin fiber parameters drawn from literature and structural models in the Protein Data Bank when relevant to coarse-graining).

Research Question 4 (RQ4): Do developmental transitions and disease-associated noncoding variants preferentially correspond to motif switching rather than isolated loop disruptions?
Hypothesis 4 (H4): Changes in cell identity and regulatory dysfunction are often mediated by shifts among mesoscale motifs (e.g., from insulated to hub-like motifs or from active microcompartments to repressed compact domains), and disease-associated noncoding variants are enriched in genomic contexts where motif switching occurs.
Measurable predictions: (i) Across developmental trajectories represented in public scRNA-seq atlases and matched epigenomes, motif transitions inferred from available Hi-C/Micro-C datasets will align with lineage bifurcations and changes in expression variance; (ii) GWAS Catalog variants and ClinVar noncoding variants will be enriched at motif boundaries or within motifs characterized by high regulatory sensitivity (e.g., hub-like motifs), compared with matched control variants.
Validation using existing data: We will perform enrichment analyses using GWAS Catalog and ClinVar coordinates, controlling for mappability, GC content, and chromatin accessibility. For developmental contexts, we will leverage publicly available multi-omic references where cell types overlap across 4DN/ENCODE and Human Cell Atlas, and use statistical matching rather than new data generation.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses aim to deliver mechanistic insight into how mesoscale chromatin topology—captured as a small motif vocabulary and its combinations—produces emergent regulatory behaviors across mammalian cell types. The emphasis is on testable, quantitative predictions validated entirely through synthesis of existing public datasets, with rigorous cross-dataset replication as the primary standard of evidence.

Methods: Overview and synthesis strategy
This project is a community-scale synthesis effort integrating orthogonal public data modalities to infer mesoscale chromatin nanodomain motifs and link them to emergent regulatory phenotypes. We will not generate any new experimental data. Instead, we will build harmonized, reproducible pipelines to (i) extract nanodomain-scale features from Hi-C/Micro-C, (ii) extract geometric constraints from super-resolution/multiplexed DNA FISH imaging, (iii) align these with epigenomic annotations and transcriptional outputs, and (iv) jointly infer a motif dictionary and motif–phenotype relationships.

Specific data sources (public repositories)
1) 3D genome contact maps:
- 4D Nucleome (4DN) Data Portal: bulk Hi-C, single-cell Hi-C, Micro-C for key human and mouse cell lines and primary cells.
- ENCODE Portal: Hi-C/Micro-C where available, plus extensive metadata and processing standards.
- NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) / SRA: additional Hi-C/Micro-C datasets, including developmental and disease contexts.
2) Imaging of chromatin organization:
- 4DN Data Portal imaging datasets (DNA FISH, multiplexed FISH, super-resolution imaging where deposited).
- BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI): curated raw and processed microscopy datasets.
- Public Oligopaint/multiplexed DNA FISH datasets released with publications (accessed via linked repositories such as Zenodo/Figshare when applicable and permissive).
3) Epigenomics and accessibility:
- ENCODE: ChIP-seq (H3K27ac, H3K4me3, H3K27me3, CTCF, RAD21/SMC1A where available), ATAC-seq/DNase-seq.
- Roadmap Epigenomics: reference histone marks and chromatin state segmentations for primary tissues.
4) Transcriptional outputs:
- Human Cell Atlas (HCA) scRNA-seq: cell-type-resolved expression distributions.
- GEO/ENCODE: scRNA-seq for specific cell lines/tissues; GRO-seq/PRO-seq/NET-seq where available for nascent transcription proxies.
5) Structural constraints and benchmarks:
- Protein Data Bank (PDB): structural information relevant to nucleosome and chromatin fiber coarse-graining (used as literature-constrained priors, not for new modeling beyond synthesis).
- Published polymer simulation benchmarks and open datasets (e.g., from prior 4DN challenges) to compare reconstruction performance.

Data harmonization and linkage across modalities
- Genome builds and coordinates: standardize to hg38 (human) and mm10 (mouse), with liftOver where needed; store all intervals in BED format with provenance.
- Cell type matching: define a “cell-type concordance table” using ontology terms (Cell Ontology IDs) and repository metadata; prioritize cell types with at least two modalities available (contacts + epigenomics; contacts + imaging; ideally all three plus scRNA-seq).
- Resolution harmonization: represent contact maps at multiple resolutions (e.g., 1 kb–100 kb) and focus motif inference on scales corresponding to 50–300 nm, operationalized via genomic scales inferred from imaging distance–genomic distance calibration and polymer scaling (e.g., tens to hundreds of kb depending on compaction).
- Batch effects: apply modality-specific normalization (ICE/KR balancing for Hi-C; intensity/segmentation QC for imaging; standard ENCODE processing for ChIP/ATAC) and then use cross-study calibration (ComBat-like adjustments for derived features; domain-adversarial learning for embeddings where appropriate).

Aim 1: Infer nanodomain boundaries and interaction communities from Hi-C/Micro-C
- Feature extraction: compute insulation score, directionality index, and multi-scale contact decay features; detect loops (e.g., HiCCUPS-like peaks where available from processed calls) but treat loops as features rather than primary units.
- Multi-resolution community detection: apply graph-based community detection on contact graphs (nodes=bins; edges=normalized contacts) using multi-resolution modularity optimization and/or stochastic block models to identify nested domains and microcommunities.
- Single-cell integration: for scHi-C, use latent embedding methods (e.g., topic models or variational autoencoders designed for sparse contact matrices) to infer cell-to-cell variability in motif occupancy and to estimate uncertainty.
Deliverable: a standardized “nanodomain feature table” per cell type with boundaries, community assignments, and uncertainty estimates.

Aim 2: Extract geometric constraints from imaging and calibrate polymer models
- Imaging processing (existing images only): use published segmentations when available; otherwise apply reproducible, containerized pipelines for spot calling and distance extraction (for FISH) or domain segmentation (for labeled chromatin regions) using established open-source tools.
- Geometric summaries: distance distributions for locus pairs; radius of gyration for labeled regions; domain volume/compactness proxies; spatial co-localization frequencies.
- Polymer modeling: use coarse-grained polymer simulations (e.g., strings-and-binders or loop-extrusion-informed polymer priors) to generate ensembles consistent with contact features. Calibration will be performed by Bayesian or approximate Bayesian computation (ABC) approaches that fit both contact-derived constraints and imaging distance distributions.
- Degeneracy reduction: compare posterior uncertainty for geometric parameters in contact-only vs joint (contact+imaging) inference; quantify improvement via held-out imaging prediction.
Deliverable: calibrated mapping functions between contact features and physical geometry, plus a library of inferred geometric parameters per nanodomain.

Aim 3: Learn a joint motif dictionary from contacts + imaging + epigenomic features
- Representation learning: construct a multimodal feature vector per genomic region/nanodomain including contact-community metrics, imaging-derived geometry, and epigenomic state summaries (e.g., ChromHMM states from Roadmap/ENCODE where available).
- Unsupervised motif discovery: apply mixture models and deep clustering (e.g., variational mixture of autoencoders) to learn discrete motif classes with interpretable feature loadings. Motif number will be selected by stability criteria (bootstrapped clustering stability, held-out likelihood) rather than arbitrary choice.
- Cross-species mapping: map syntenic regions (human–mouse) using chain files and test whether motif classes transfer, allowing for species-specific frequency shifts.
Deliverable: an “Atlas of Chromatin Nanodomain Motifs” with motif definitions, representative examples, and per-cell-type motif occupancy tracks.

Aim 4: Link motif occupancy to emergent regulatory phenotypes
- Outcome variables: gene expression mean and dispersion (from HCA scRNA-seq), coexpression modules, and where available nascent transcription proxies.
- Modeling: hierarchical Bayesian regression or generalized linear mixed models with random effects for cell type/study; predictors include motif occupancy near genes, motif transition scores across regions, and covariates (promoter accessibility, enhancer marks, gene length, GC content).
- Variant enrichment: test enrichment of GWAS Catalog and ClinVar noncoding variants in motif boundaries and motif classes, using matched controls and logistic regression controlling for confounders.
- Positive controls: known locus archetypes (e.g., Hox clusters, globin loci, immunoglobulin loci) with extensive public 3D genome and epigenomic characterization will be used as interpretability anchors; we will also validate that known compartment shifts correspond to motif composition changes.
Deliverable: quantitative motif–phenotype maps and statistical evidence for emergent regulatory roles.

Validation (no experiments)
- Cross-dataset replication: train motif models on one subset of studies and test on independent studies within 4DN/ENCODE/GEO.
- Cross-modality prediction: predict imaging distances from contact-derived motifs and evaluate against held-out imaging datasets; predict transcriptional dispersion from motifs and evaluate against held-out cell types.
- Sensitivity analyses: downsample contacts and imaging to assess robustness; evaluate alternative normalizations and domain-calling methods.

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6: Working group kickoff; finalize cell-type concordance table; build ingestion pipelines; release v0 data inventory and metadata schema.
Months 7–12: Generate nanodomain feature tables from Hi-C/Micro-C; implement imaging distance extraction; first joint calibration prototypes; release v1 reproducible pipelines.
Months 13–18: Complete joint contact+imaging calibration; perform motif discovery; release v1 motif dictionary and initial atlas tracks.
Months 19–24: Motif–phenotype modeling with scRNA-seq/epigenomics; variant enrichment analyses; cross-study replication; preprint 1.
Months 25–30: Final atlas and software release; documentation and tutorials; working group synthesis paper; capstone training workshop; long-term hosting plan.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- 3D genomics informatics (Hi-C/Micro-C processing, domain calling, single-cell contact modeling).
- Quantitative imaging/microscopy experts (FISH/super-resolution data interpretation, segmentation QC, imaging-derived metrics).
- Polymer physics/modeling (coarse-grained polymer priors, simulation, ABC/Bayesian calibration).
- Statistical modeling/causal inference (hierarchical models, uncertainty quantification, enrichment analyses).
- Machine learning (multimodal representation learning, clustering stability, domain adaptation).
- Research software engineering (workflow automation, containers, documentation, CI/CD).
This breadth is essential: no single lab typically has deep expertise across Hi-C, super-resolution imaging, polymer physics, and hierarchical statistical modeling, and the synthesis requires coordinated standards and shared tooling consistent with NCEMS working group goals.

Expected Outcomes: Deliverables
1) Atlas of chromatin nanodomain motifs across mammalian cell types: A public, versioned resource that defines a motif dictionary (discrete motif classes with interpretable feature signatures) and provides genome-wide motif occupancy tracks for prioritized human and mouse cell types. Outputs will include BED/BigWig tracks, per-region motif probabilities, and uncertainty estimates.

2) Joint inference toolkit for contacts + imaging: Open-source software implementing pipelines to (i) extract nanodomain-scale features from Hi-C/Micro-C, (ii) extract imaging-derived geometric constraints (distance distributions and domain geometry summaries), and (iii) perform joint calibration of polymer-based reconstructions. The toolkit will emphasize modularity so users can swap in alternative normalizations, domain callers, or polymer priors.

3) Quantitative motif–phenotype models: Statistical models linking motif composition to emergent regulatory phenotypes, including gene expression dispersion (as a proxy for transcriptional noise/bursting), enhancer responsiveness proxies (e.g., association with enhancer marks and coexpression), and lineage-associated expression stability. Results will be released as model objects, summary tables, and reproducible notebooks.

4) Variant-context synthesis: A resource quantifying enrichment of GWAS Catalog and ClinVar noncoding variants in specific motif classes and motif boundaries, with matched-control analyses. This will provide a mesoscale organizational lens for interpreting noncoding variation beyond single-loop narratives.

Mechanistic advances in mesoscale emergence
This project’s core impact is to move from descriptive catalogs of loops/TADs/compartments to a mesoscale theory of emergent regulation grounded in a compact motif vocabulary. By explicitly integrating imaging geometry with contact maps, we will clarify which contact-derived patterns correspond to physically distinct nanodomain shapes and separations, addressing a major ambiguity in 3D genome inference. The motif dictionary will provide a mesoscale “state space” in which chromatin organization can be compared across cell types, species, and conditions.

We expect to establish quantitative relationships between motif composition and emergent transcriptional behaviors. If motifs explain expression dispersion beyond molecular covariates, it would support the idea that mesoscale topology is not merely a reflection of epigenomic state but an organizing principle that shapes regulatory noise and responsiveness. Such findings would contribute to a mechanistic understanding of how stable cell identities arise from fluctuating molecular interactions: cell-type-specific combinations of mesoscale motifs could buffer or amplify transcriptional variability, thereby influencing lineage stability.

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
- A unifying framework across modalities: The field currently has parallel literatures—Hi-C-centric and imaging-centric—that often disagree in interpretation. A joint inference framework will provide a common language, enabling more rigorous cross-validation and improving confidence in structural conclusions.
- Improved interpretability for AI in genomics: Rather than black-box predictors, motif classes offer interpretable mesoscale units that can be used as features in downstream predictive models of gene regulation, differentiation, and disease.
- Comparative and evolutionary insights: Cross-species motif transfer analyses can reveal which mesoscale organizational principles are conserved and which are lineage-specific, informing how genome regulation evolves.
- Disease relevance without new experiments: By synthesizing variant catalogs with motif contexts, we can generate testable mechanistic hypotheses for why certain noncoding variants have outsized regulatory effects (e.g., by destabilizing hub-like motifs or weakening insulation), guiding future experimental work by the community.

Enabling future research
The atlas and tools will enable investigators to (i) annotate any region of interest with motif probabilities, (ii) compare motif composition across cell types, and (iii) integrate new public datasets as they appear. Because the project focuses on synthesis and standards, it will lower barriers for labs to incorporate imaging constraints into 3D genome analyses and to interpret contact maps at the nanodomain scale.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: At least two major manuscripts are anticipated: (1) methods paper describing joint inference and motif discovery; (2) synthesis paper reporting the motif atlas and motif–phenotype relationships.
- NCEMS-style workshops: Annual working group meetings and a capstone training workshop focused on multimodal 3D genome synthesis (contacts + imaging + epigenomics), with hands-on tutorials.
- Public resources: Deposited motif tracks and metadata schema in community repositories (e.g., Zenodo for versioned releases; GitHub for code; links and descriptors suitable for indexing by 4DN/ENCODE portals where permitted).

Long-term sustainability
We will design the resource as a lightweight, versioned data product with clear provenance and automated rebuilds. Continuous integration will re-run key pipelines when upstream references change (e.g., genome build patches, updated annotations). We will provide a governance document for community contributions, including how new datasets can be added, how motif dictionary updates are versioned, and how to cite releases via DOIs (Zenodo). The emphasis on open formats, containerized workflows, and thorough documentation will allow the atlas and tools to persist beyond the funding period and be extended by the broader community.

Budget and Resources: Budget philosophy and alignment with NCEMS
This project is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring substantial coordination, shared computational infrastructure, and dedicated personnel for data engineering, multimodal modeling, and open-science productization. Funds are requested to support a distributed working group spanning multiple labs and disciplines; no funds are requested for experimental data generation.

Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (2–3 years):
  1) Multimodal 3D genomics postdoc (Hi-C/Micro-C feature extraction, motif discovery, cross-dataset replication).
  2) Quantitative modeling postdoc (hierarchical models linking motifs to scRNA-seq phenotypes; variant enrichment analyses).
- 1 Research software engineer / scientific programmer (2–3 years): workflow automation (Snakemake/Nextflow), containerization, CI/CD, documentation, and packaging of tools for community use.
- 1 Graduate student (2–3 years, partial support): imaging-derived feature extraction pipelines, QC metrics, and integration with contact-derived features under mentorship from imaging and genomics leads.
- Trainee support (supplemental): short-term support for additional graduate students/postdocs participating in working group sprints, ensuring training and broad participation.
Justification: Synthesis at this scale requires sustained engineering and statistical capacity beyond typical single-lab staffing, especially for reproducible workflows and multimodal harmonization.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or HPC allocations: required for processing large Hi-C/Micro-C matrices, running polymer simulations/ABC calibration, and training multimodal representation learning models.
- Storage: budget for secure, redundant storage of downloaded public datasets (where permitted) and large intermediate files; emphasis on storing derived features rather than duplicating raw archives.
Justification: Joint inference and cross-validation across many cell types requires repeated model fitting and simulation; shared compute prevents bottlenecks and enables reproducibility.

Working group meetings and travel
- Annual in-person working group meetings (2–3 meetings total): support travel for PIs, postdocs, graduate students, and key collaborators across institutions to conduct intensive synthesis, align standards, and accelerate integration across modalities.
- Targeted travel to disseminate outcomes: conference travel for trainees and key personnel to present the atlas/toolkit and recruit adopters.
Justification: NCEMS’s value is catalyzing transdisciplinary integration; in-person meetings materially improve coordination between genomics, imaging, polymer physics, and statistics teams.

Workshops and training events
- Capstone training workshop (in-person, final year): venue costs, training materials, and travel support for trainees from diverse institutions (including those with fewer resources) to broaden participation.
- Quarterly virtual tutorial series: minimal costs for webinar hosting, captioning, and archiving.
Justification: Training the next-generation data-savvy workforce is a core NCEMS goal; workshops ensure broad, lasting impact beyond publications.

Open science infrastructure
- Zenodo DOI-backed releases for data products; costs for curation time and preparation.
- Web hosting for documentation (e.g., GitHub Pages) and optional lightweight registry site for atlas browsing.
- Professional support for accessibility (captioning tutorials, documentation QA) where feasible.
Justification: Open, reproducible science requires time and infrastructure to make resources discoverable and usable.

Overall resource justification
Each budget category directly enables synthesis: personnel build and validate integrated pipelines; compute supports large-scale multimodal inference and replication; travel and meetings create the cross-disciplinary cohesion that no single lab can achieve; and open-science infrastructure ensures that the community can reuse, audit, and extend the resulting atlas and tools.

criteria.justification: The proposal squarely targets mesoscale (50–300 nm) chromatin nanodomains and explicitly frames enhancer communication, insulation, and transcriptional bursting as emergent behaviors arising from collective topology.

Jointly learning a cross-cell-type “motif dictionary” from contacts plus imaging constraints and linking motifs to expression variability is highly innovative and could substantially advance interpretability in 3D genomics, though similar multimodal integration efforts exist in narrower forms.

The workflow is logically structured with explicit validation (cross-study replication, held-out imaging prediction, downsampling sensitivity), but key risks remain around modality alignment, identifiability of polymer calibration, and operationalizing “bursting” from scRNA-seq dispersion proxies.

The 30-month plan is plausible but ambitious given the breadth (Hi-C/Micro-C, diverse imaging formats, polymer ABC/Bayesian calibration, multimodal deep clustering, cross-species transfer, and variant enrichment), and success will likely depend on narrowing to a well-curated set of cell types with strong multi-omic overlap.
The project is explicitly and exclusively based on publicly available datasets and focuses on integration and reanalysis rather than generating new experimental data.

The proposal includes concrete open-science deliverables (containerized workflows, CI, versioned Zenodo releases with DOIs, public tracks and tutorials), though governance for sensitive/large imaging data redistribution and clear licensing/attribution handling across heterogeneous sources could be more fully specified.

The proposal explicitly centers on mesoscale chromatin nanodomains and how their collective topology gives rise to emergent regulatory behaviors like transcriptional bursting, perfectly aligning with the call's focus.

The concept of defining a 'motif dictionary' for chromatin topology by integrating contact maps with imaging constraints is highly innovative and addresses a critical gap in understanding structure-function relationships.
The methodology is exceptionally detailed and rigorous, employing advanced joint inference frameworks, polymer physics calibration, and robust validation strategies like cross-modality prediction.

The timeline is realistic but ambitious given the complexity of harmonizing diverse data types; however, the inclusion of dedicated research software engineering support significantly enhances feasibility.
The project is a pure synthesis effort that strictly utilizes existing public data (4DN, ENCODE, BioImage Archive) without generating new experimental data, fitting the solicitation perfectly.
Data sources are identified with high specificity, and the proposal demonstrates a sophisticated understanding of limitations (e.g., contact degeneracy) and how to mitigate them.

The proposal demonstrates an exemplary commitment to open science, budgeting for a Research Software Engineer to ensure reproducible pipelines, containerization, and long-term resource sustainability.

The proposal directly and explicitly addresses mesoscale emergent phenomena, focusing on how chromatin nanodomains (50-300 nm) produce emergent regulatory behaviors like enhancer-promoter communication, insulation, and transcriptional bursting that cannot be inferred from individual molecular components.

The proposal presents a highly novel approach by creating a joint inference framework that integrates contact maps with imaging data to define a 'motif dictionary' of chromatin organization. This represents a significant conceptual advance beyond current single-modality analyses of 3D genome organization.

The methodology is well-articulated with clear aims, specific analytical approaches (multi-resolution community detection, polymer modeling with ABC calibration, unsupervised representation learning), and explicit validation strategies including cross-dataset replication and held-out testing. Minor concerns exist about the complexity of integrating such diverse data types.

Title: A Cross-Cell-Type Atlas of Biomolecular Condensate Material States and Their Emergent Control of Gene Expression Noise

Background: Biomolecular condensates organize cellular biochemistry through mesoscale assemblies that sit between molecular interactions and organelle-scale structures. At the mesoscale (roughly 10–1000 nm), condensates exhibit emergent behaviors—viscoelasticity, percolation, arrested coarsening, and multiphase organization—arising from collective interactions among proteins and RNAs. These properties are not predictable from individual components alone: the same set of proteins can form a fluid droplet in one context and a gel-like, dynamically arrested network in another, depending on concentration, multivalency, post-translational modifications, and the surrounding molecular milieu. The central challenge for molecular and cellular biosciences is to convert the descriptive catalog of condensate components into quantitative, predictive models of condensate material states and their downstream functional consequences.

A growing body of literature has established that many nuclear and cytoplasmic bodies—including nucleoli, nuclear speckles, Cajal bodies, stress granules, and P-bodies—share hallmarks of phase separation and dynamic exchange. Public databases now curate condensate-associated proteins and their biophysical features: UniProt provides canonical sequences and annotations; Pfam catalogs modular domains; MobiDB and DisProt provide intrinsic disorder annotations; and specialized LLPS resources such as PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, and DrLLPS compile experimentally supported condensate components and contexts. These resources collectively suggest that condensate proteins are enriched for intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), low-complexity sequences, RNA-binding domains, and multivalent interaction motifs. In parallel, imaging repositories such as the Image Data Resource (IDR), BioImage Archive, and the Cell Image Library host microscopy datasets that capture condensate morphology, puncta distributions, and in some cases time series. The Human Protein Atlas (HPA) provides immunofluorescence images across many cell lines, offering a systematic, albeit heterogeneous, view of subcellular localization and punctate patterns for thousands of proteins.

Despite this abundance, two gaps limit progress. First, most analyses treat condensates as categorical entities (e.g., “stress granule protein” vs. not) rather than as occupying a continuum of mesoscale material states. Yet mesoscale material state—capturing properties such as internal mobility, network connectivity, and substructure size distributions—is precisely where emergent behavior manifests. Second, functional consequences are often assessed qualitatively (e.g., “condensates regulate transcription”) without quantitative linkage to measurable cellular phenotypes. Gene expression noise—cell-to-cell variability driven by transcriptional bursting and regulatory fluctuations—is an especially relevant emergent phenotype because it integrates stochastic molecular events into population-level distributions. Single-cell transcriptomic resources such as the Human Cell Atlas, Tabula Sapiens, and the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) provide extensive data on transcriptional variability across cell types and conditions, while multiome datasets (scRNA+scATAC) enable partial separation of transcriptional and chromatin contributions to variability.

The proposed synthesis addresses a long-standing puzzle: why do condensates sometimes buffer gene expression (reducing noise) while in other contexts they amplify variability (increasing noise and enabling plasticity)? Existing studies point to mechanisms including local concentration of transcription factors, sequestration, modulation of RNA processing, and changes in chromatin accessibility. However, these mechanisms are rarely unified under a mesoscale framework that treats condensate material state as a tunable variable. Polymer physics and soft-matter theory predict that transitions from liquid-like to gel-like states alter diffusion, reaction kinetics, and residence times—features expected to influence transcriptional bursting by changing the effective on/off rates of promoter-associated complexes. Yet no community-scale, cross-cell-type atlas currently links condensate material features to transcriptional noise in a standardized way.

Synthesis research is uniquely suited to close these gaps because the necessary evidence is distributed across disparate public resources: protein sequence and disorder annotations, curated LLPS membership lists, heterogeneous imaging datasets with puncta morphologies, and large-scale single-cell transcriptomes capturing variability. Integrating these data requires harmonization across modalities (sequence, images, expression), batch effects, and inconsistent metadata. It also requires methodological innovation: extracting mesoscale features from images at scale; learning low-dimensional representations (manifolds) that correspond to material states; and connecting those representations to cell-type-specific gene expression noise through probabilistic models.

Mesoscale emergent phenomena are important because they represent the level at which cells convert molecular interactions into robust, regulatable structures that impact phenotypes. Understanding condensate material states could explain context-dependent gene regulation, disease-associated aberrant phase transitions, and evolutionary design principles of IDR “sequence grammars.” Moreover, a cross-cell-type atlas would provide a reference for interpreting perturbation signatures from public resources such as LINCS L1000 (chemical/genetic perturbation transcriptional profiles) and DepMap CRISPR screens (gene essentiality and genetic dependencies), which include many regulators implicated in RNA granules and nuclear bodies. By leveraging the existing, rapidly expanding public data ecosystem, NCEMS can catalyze a community-scale synthesis that transforms fragmented observations into a coherent mesoscale theory linking condensate material state to emergent gene expression noise.

This project aligns directly with NCEMS’s mission: it targets emergent mesoscale properties; leverages AI and data science to synthesize publicly available molecular, imaging, and single-cell data; and requires a multidisciplinary working group spanning biophysics, polymer theory, bioimage analysis, and statistical genomics. The outcome will be a reusable, open, reproducible resource that enables the broader community to test mechanistic hypotheses without generating new experimental data, thereby accelerating discovery and training data-savvy scientists in best practices for synthesis research.

Research Questions: This project centers on the idea that “condensate material state” is a latent mesoscale variable—emergent from collective molecular interactions—that can be inferred from heterogeneous public data and used to predict downstream gene regulatory phenotypes. We focus on transcriptional bursting and cell-to-cell gene expression noise as emergent cellular outcomes that integrate many molecular events. Our working group will address four tightly defined research questions (RQs) with testable hypotheses (Hs) and measurable predictions.

RQ1: Can condensate material states be represented as a low-dimensional manifold that is conserved across cell types and imaging modalities?
H1 (Material-state manifold): Imaging-derived mesoscale features (puncta size distributions, spatial clustering, texture metrics, coarsening proxies, and FRAP-derived recovery parameters where available) combined with composition/sequence features (IDR fraction, charge patterning, aromatic content, multivalency motifs, RNA-binding domains) will map onto a low-dimensional manifold (e.g., 2–6 latent dimensions) that captures continuous variation from liquid-like to gel-like/aged states and from single-phase to multiphase substructured states.
Predictions: (i) Canonical condensate classes (nucleolus, speckles, stress granules, P-bodies) will occupy partially separable regions of the manifold, but with overlaps reflecting context dependence. (ii) The same condensate class will shift position across cell types and perturbations in ways consistent with known regulators (e.g., chaperones, kinases, RNA abundance).
Validation using existing data: We will test manifold stability via cross-dataset validation (train on IDR/BioImage Archive subsets, evaluate on HPA images), and assess whether known FRAP-annotated proteins occupy expected manifold positions (liquid-like fast recovery vs. gel-like slow recovery).

RQ2: Which sequence grammars and interaction motifs predict mesoscale transitions between liquid-like and arrested/gel-like condensate substructures?
H2 (Grammar-to-state mapping): Specific “sequence grammar” features—e.g., sticker-spacer architectures, aromatic and arginine content, charge blockiness (kappa), prion-like low complexity, and modular RNA-binding domains—will predict manifold coordinates corresponding to material state, beyond what is explained by simple disorder fraction.
Predictions: (i) Proteins enriched in aromatic stickers and balanced charge patterning will associate with more liquid-like regions; (ii) proteins with high prion-like content, strong homotypic interaction propensity, or predicted beta-aggregation segments will associate with more arrested/gel-like regions; (iii) multiphase condensates (e.g., nucleolar subcompartments) will be associated with compositional heterogeneity and proteins with distinct grammar clusters.
Validation using existing data: Predictions will be tested by correlating sequence-derived features (from UniProt/Pfam/MobiDB/DisProt) with imaging-inferred manifold coordinates across proteins and cell types, controlling for expression level proxies (from scRNA-seq) and localization.

RQ3: Does condensate material state systematically tune transcriptional bursting parameters and gene expression noise across cell types?
H3 (State-to-noise coupling): Condensates in more liquid-like states will be associated with reduced extrinsic noise for target gene programs (buffering via rapid exchange and averaging), whereas more arrested/gel-like states will be associated with increased burst size variability and/or altered burst frequency (amplification via prolonged residence times and heterogeneous microenvironments). The direction and magnitude of effects will depend on condensate function (e.g., transcriptional hubs vs. RNA decay granules).
Predictions: (i) Cell types where nuclear speckle-associated factors map to more liquid-like manifold coordinates will show lower noise in splicing- and transcription-coupled gene sets; (ii) stress granule/P-body arrested states will correlate with increased noise in stress-response transcripts and altered mean–variance relationships; (iii) within a cell type, perturbations predicted to shift material state (from LINCS/DepMap) will correspond to predictable changes in inferred bursting parameters.
Validation using existing data: We will infer bursting parameters from scRNA-seq distributions using hierarchical Bayesian models (e.g., negative binomial/Poisson-beta frameworks) and quantify noise metrics (CV^2, Fano factor, residual variance after mean correction). We will link these to condensate state estimates at the level of (protein, cell type) and to gene programs using curated target sets (e.g., speckle-associated transcripts, stress granule-enriched mRNAs from published lists).

RQ4: Which regulators causally shift condensate material state and thereby modulate gene expression noise?
H4 (Regulatory control points): Perturbations affecting post-translational modification pathways (e.g., phosphorylation), RNA metabolism, chaperone systems, and chromatin regulators will emerge as causal drivers that move condensates along specific manifold directions and produce consistent changes in noise.
Predictions: (i) Perturbations in kinases/phosphatases implicated in LLPS will shift material state coordinates and yield coherent transcriptional variability signatures in LINCS L1000; (ii) CRISPR dependencies (DepMap) for condensate regulators will cluster by inferred material-state directionality; (iii) causal discovery will identify a small set of “state control nodes” whose perturbation effects generalize across cell contexts.
Validation using existing data: We will use causal inference and discovery on perturbation–expression datasets (LINCS L1000, GEO perturbation scRNA where available) and integrate with genetic dependency data (DepMap) to triangulate regulators. Validation will rely on replication across independent perturbation datasets and on known positive controls (e.g., stress granule regulators such as G3BP1/2; speckle factors such as SRRM2/SON) without performing any new experiments.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses are designed to yield mechanistic insights at the mesoscale: how collective material properties emerge from sequence and composition, how those properties vary across cellular contexts, and how they propagate upward to emergent gene expression variability. The emphasis is on measurable predictions that can be adjudicated using existing public data, enabling rigorous synthesis without new data generation.

Methods: Overview and synthesis strategy
The project will create an integrated, cross-modal atlas that links (A) condensate composition and sequence-derived interaction grammars, (B) imaging-derived mesoscale morphology/dynamics, and (C) single-cell transcriptional variability and perturbation signatures. The core methodological idea is to infer a shared latent “material state manifold” from heterogeneous features and then test associations and putative causal relationships between manifold position and gene expression noise.

Specific data sources (publicly available)
1) Condensate membership and annotation
- PhaSepDB, LLPSDB, DrLLPS: curated condensate-associated proteins, condensate types, and experimental contexts.
- UniProt: protein sequences, isoforms, subcellular annotations.
- Pfam: domain architectures (RNA-binding, low complexity-associated domains).
- MobiDB and DisProt: intrinsic disorder annotations and curated disordered regions.
- Optional interaction resources for context: BioGRID and IntAct for protein–protein interactions; RNAcentral for RNA annotations.

2) Imaging repositories and localization
- Human Protein Atlas (HPA) Cell Atlas immunofluorescence images: puncta/localization across many cell lines.
- Image Data Resource (IDR): curated microscopy datasets with metadata.
- BioImage Archive: deposited microscopy datasets, including time series where available.
- Cell Image Library: additional microscopy datasets.
- Published FRAP time series and recovery curves available in supplementary materials or linked repositories (where explicitly public); we will only use datasets with clear reuse permissions.

3) Single-cell expression and multiome resources
- Human Cell Atlas (HCA) scRNA-seq: diverse tissues/cell types.
- Tabula Sapiens: human multi-tissue scRNA-seq.
- GEO and ArrayExpress: scRNA-seq datasets with perturbations or matched imaging contexts (when metadata permits).
- Public scRNA+scATAC multiome datasets (e.g., from GEO) to estimate chromatin accessibility variability when available.

4) Perturbation and dependency resources
- LINCS L1000: transcriptional signatures for chemical and genetic perturbations.
- DepMap (CRISPR screens): gene dependency profiles and co-dependency networks.

Data harmonization and entity resolution
- Protein identifiers: map across UniProt accessions, gene symbols, and database-specific IDs using UniProt mapping tables; maintain versioned mapping files.
- Condensate type ontology: build a controlled vocabulary aligning PhaSepDB/DrLLPS terms (e.g., “nuclear speckle” vs “speckles”) and map to Gene Ontology cellular component terms when possible.
- Cell-type harmonization: use Cell Ontology labels for scRNA-seq; map HPA cell lines to standardized identifiers (Cellosaurus).
- Metadata normalization: extract imaging modality, magnification, staining channel, and segmentation-relevant parameters from IDR/BioImage Archive metadata; record missingness explicitly.

Feature extraction
A) Sequence/composition features (per protein)
- Disorder metrics: fraction disordered, number/length of disordered segments (MobiDB/DisProt).
- Domain composition: counts of Pfam domains (RRM, KH, DEAD-box, etc.).
- Grammar features computed from UniProt sequences: amino-acid composition (aromatic, glycine, arginine), charge patterning (kappa), low complexity (SEG), prion-like propensity (PLAAC where permissible as an algorithm), predicted coiled-coils.
- Multivalency proxies: number of repeats, motif density (e.g., RG/RGG, SYGQ-rich segments).

B) Imaging-derived mesoscale features (per protein, cell line, dataset)
- Standardized puncta segmentation: train/finetune deep learning models (e.g., U-Net/Cellpose-style architectures) using weak supervision from existing annotations where available; otherwise apply self-supervised/transfer learning across datasets. Training uses only existing images.
- Puncta statistics: count per cell, size distribution, intensity distribution, spatial clustering (Ripley’s K), radial distribution relative to nucleus.
- Texture and morphology: Haralick features, fractal dimension proxies, shape descriptors.
- Dynamics proxies: where time series exist, compute coarsening proxies (change in size distribution over time), fusion/fission event rates via tracking.
- FRAP features: extract recovery half-time, mobile fraction, and fit parameters from published curves; where raw time series exist, re-fit using standardized models.

C) Single-cell noise and bursting inference (per gene program, cell type)
- Preprocessing: adopt standardized scRNA pipelines (e.g., Scanpy/Seurat equivalents) but implement in open workflows; apply ambient RNA correction when metadata supports it; rigorously document filtering.
- Noise metrics: mean–variance residuals, CV^2, Fano factor, and overdispersion parameters per gene, adjusted for mean expression and detection rate.
- Bursting models: hierarchical Bayesian models (Poisson-beta / negative binomial with latent transcription rate states) to infer burst frequency and burst size proxies; compare multiple models and use posterior predictive checks.
- Gene program mapping: define condensate-associated gene sets using curated lists (e.g., speckle-associated splicing factors’ targets; stress granule-enriched mRNAs from published compilations) and compute program-level noise.

Latent “material state manifold” modeling
- Multi-view representation learning: integrate sequence features and imaging features using methods such as variational autoencoders (multi-modal VAE), factor analysis with shared/private factors, or canonical correlation analysis variants. The output is a low-dimensional embedding with uncertainty.
- Interpretability: align latent axes with physical interpretations by regressing latent dimensions against FRAP parameters (where available) and against known liquid/gel annotations from LLPSDB contexts.
- Batch correction: use hierarchical modeling and domain-adversarial approaches to reduce modality-specific and dataset-specific artifacts while preserving biological variation.

Linking material state to gene expression noise
- Hierarchical association models: mixed-effects models linking manifold coordinates to noise metrics, with random effects for dataset/cell type and covariates (mean expression, cell cycle scores, technical factors).
- Mediation-style analyses: test whether perturbation-induced expression signatures (LINCS) associated with condensate regulators predict inferred state shifts and noise changes.
- Causal discovery: apply constraint-based and score-based methods (e.g., PC algorithm variants, NOTEARS-style continuous optimization) on perturbation graphs where interventions are known (LINCS perturbations), focusing on edges between regulator modules, material state coordinates, and noise outcomes. Emphasize robustness and sensitivity analyses rather than definitive causality claims.

Validation (no new experiments)
- Positive controls: known condensate markers (G3BP1/2 for stress granules; DCP1A for P-bodies; FBL for nucleolus; SON/SRRM2 for speckles) should map to expected manifold regions and show coherent imaging features.
- Cross-dataset replication: train embeddings on one repository (e.g., HPA+IDR) and test stability on another (BioImage Archive); replicate noise associations across HCA and Tabula Sapiens.
- Holdout strategies: cell-type holdouts, protein holdouts, and dataset holdouts; evaluate predictive performance for FRAP parameters (when available) and for noise outcomes.
- Sensitivity analyses: quantify dependence on segmentation choices, scRNA normalization, and cell-cycle correction.

Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6: Working group formation; ontology/ID mapping; assemble benchmark datasets; initial segmentation pipeline; initial sequence feature computation.
Months 7–12: Large-scale imaging feature extraction (HPA, IDR); compile FRAP-curated subset; first-generation manifold model; release v0.1 code and data schema.
Months 13–18: Integrate scRNA noise/bursting inference (HCA, Tabula Sapiens); link cell types and gene programs; preliminary state–noise models; internal replication.
Months 19–24: Perturbation integration (LINCS, DepMap); causal discovery analyses; refine manifold with multi-view learning; release atlas v1.0.
Months 25–30: Manuscripts and preprints; NCEMS-hosted training workshop; finalize open resource, documentation, and long-term hosting plan.

Team composition and roles (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Polymer/soft-matter physicists: interpret manifold axes in terms of viscoelasticity, percolation, and coarsening; guide physically grounded feature design.
- Protein biophysicists/sequence analysts: implement sequence grammar metrics; connect motifs to interaction models.
- Bioimage analysts/computer vision experts: scalable segmentation, tracking, and harmonization across modalities.
- Statistical geneticists/single-cell methodologists: noise decomposition, bursting inference, covariate control, and replication.
- Causal inference/data science experts: perturbation graph modeling, robustness checks.
- Research software engineers: workflow automation, documentation, packaging, continuous integration.

All activities are strictly limited to synthesis of existing publicly available datasets and computational analyses; no new experimental data, imaging, sequencing, or sample generation is proposed.

Expected Outcomes: Deliverables
1) Cross-cell-type atlas of condensate material states
We will release an integrated atlas that assigns probabilistic “material state” coordinates (with uncertainty) to condensate-associated proteins across cell lines/cell types and condensate classes. The atlas will include: (i) standardized protein-level sequence/grammar features, (ii) imaging-derived puncta and morphology metrics with provenance to source images, (iii) FRAP-derived parameters where publicly available, and (iv) links to cell-type-specific gene expression noise summaries.

2) Open computational toolkit for condensate mesoscale feature extraction
A reusable software suite will implement standardized pipelines for puncta segmentation, feature extraction, and quality control across HPA, IDR, and BioImage Archive datasets. This toolkit will include model weights (where licensing permits), evaluation benchmarks, and guidance for applying the pipeline to new public imaging datasets.

3) Statistical models connecting mesoscale state to emergent transcriptional variability
We will provide validated hierarchical models that quantify how condensate material state coordinates associate with transcriptional noise and inferred bursting parameters across cell types. Outputs will include effect size estimates, credible intervals, and sensitivity analyses that explicitly account for technical confounders and dataset structure.

4) Candidate regulatory “state control nodes” from perturbation synthesis
By integrating LINCS L1000 perturbation signatures and DepMap co-dependency networks with the atlas, we will generate ranked lists of regulators predicted to shift condensate material state along specific manifold directions, together with predicted consequences for gene expression noise programs. These are not experimental claims but synthesis-derived hypotheses grounded in multiple independent public datasets.

5) Community benchmarks and ontologies
We will deliver a condensate-type controlled vocabulary mapping across LLPS databases and imaging resources, plus benchmark sets of proteins/images for evaluating segmentation and manifold inference methods. These benchmarks will lower barriers for future methodological development.

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergent phenomena
This project advances a central NCEMS theme: understanding how new properties emerge at intermediate scales of organization. Condensate material state is inherently mesoscale—it reflects collective network connectivity, internal mobility, and substructure organization at tens to hundreds of nanometers. By learning a data-driven manifold of material states and anchoring it to physical proxies (FRAP, coarsening metrics), we will transform qualitative descriptions (“liquid-like”, “gel-like”) into quantitative, comparable coordinates across datasets.

The key conceptual advance is linking this mesoscale variable to an emergent cellular phenotype: gene expression noise. Noise is not a property of any single molecule; it emerges from stochastic processes distributed across promoters, chromatin, transcription machinery, RNA processing, and degradation. Condensates may modulate these processes by altering reaction-diffusion environments and residence times. Our synthesis will test whether a conserved relationship exists between condensate state and bursting parameters across cell types, providing a unifying framework for context-dependent condensate function.

Broader impacts
- Molecular and cellular biology: The atlas will help interpret why the same condensate-associated factor can have different regulatory outcomes in different contexts, supporting more accurate models of gene regulation.
- Disease relevance (via public data): Many neurodegenerative and cancer-related proteins are condensate-associated; our resource will enable hypothesis generation about how aberrant state shifts could influence transcriptional heterogeneity, a hallmark of tumor evolution and stress adaptation.
- Methodological innovation: Standardized, open pipelines for bioimage feature extraction and multi-modal manifold learning will be broadly applicable beyond condensates (e.g., cytoskeletal assemblies, endomembrane substructures).
- Workforce development: Trainees will gain cross-domain skills in reproducible bioimage analysis, single-cell statistics, and multi-modal integration—skills directly aligned with NCEMS’s training goals.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: At least two major manuscripts are anticipated: (i) the material-state manifold and imaging/sequence synthesis; (ii) the state–noise coupling and perturbation/causal synthesis.
- Preprints and open peer feedback: Preprints will be posted with open issue trackers for community input.
- Workshops: An NCEMS-hosted workshop will train participants to use the atlas and pipelines; tutorial notebooks will be published.
- Data deposition: The atlas (tables, embeddings, metadata, and links) will be deposited in long-term repositories (e.g., Zenodo and/or Figshare) with DOIs; code will be archived with releases.

Long-term sustainability
We will design the atlas as a versioned, modular resource: new imaging datasets, LLPS database updates, and scRNA compendia can be incorporated via reproducible workflows. Sustainability will be supported by (i) clear data schemas, (ii) containerized pipelines, (iii) continuous integration tests, and (iv) community governance practices (contribution guidelines, code of conduct, and an advisory group). By emphasizing interoperability with existing repositories (HPA, IDR, BioImage Archive, HCA), the resource will remain useful even as upstream datasets evolve.

Overall, the project will produce a durable community-scale synthesis that elevates condensate biology from component lists to predictive mesoscale theory and provides practical tools and training to accelerate future discovery—without generating any new experimental data.

Budget and Resources: Budget philosophy
Because this is a synthesis-only project, the budget prioritizes personnel time for data integration and method development, compute for large-scale image processing and model fitting, and NCEMS-centered collaboration/training activities. No funds are requested for experiments, reagents, sample collection, or instrument time.

Personnel (primary cost drivers)
1) Two postdoctoral researchers (2.0 FTE total)
- Postdoc A (bioimage/ML): develop and maintain segmentation, tracking, and feature extraction pipelines across HPA/IDR/BioImage Archive; implement QC and benchmarking.
- Postdoc B (statistical genomics/Bayesian modeling): implement scRNA noise and bursting inference, hierarchical association models, and replication analyses across HCA/Tabula Sapiens/GEO.
Justification: The project’s scale requires dedicated experts to ensure robust, validated pipelines across modalities.

2) One research software engineer / programmer analyst (1.0 FTE)
- Build workflow automation (Nextflow/Snakemake), containerization, CI testing, documentation, and release engineering for atlas versions.
Justification: Community-scale synthesis requires production-grade, reproducible software and data releases beyond typical single-lab capacity.

3) Graduate students (1–2 trainees, 0.5–1.0 FTE total)
- Projects include sequence grammar feature development, manifold learning experiments, and perturbation/causal discovery analyses.
Justification: Directly supports NCEMS training goals and expands capacity for exploratory analyses under mentorship.

4) Faculty/senior personnel (effort support as allowed)
- Modest support for coordination, supervision, and cross-disciplinary integration (biophysics, polymer theory, causal inference).
Justification: Ensures rigorous interpretation of mesoscale variables and alignment with emergence-focused aims.

Computing resources
- Cloud compute credits and/or HPC allocations for:
  - Large-scale image segmentation and feature extraction (GPU-intensive).
  - Multi-modal representation learning and Bayesian model fitting (CPU/GPU, memory-intensive).
- Storage for intermediate derived data (feature matrices, embeddings) and caching of permissible image subsets.
Justification: Processing thousands of microscopy images and fitting hierarchical models across large scRNA compendia exceeds typical lab compute; centralized resources enable standardized, reproducible runs.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings at NCEMS (e.g., 2–3 in-person meetings over 30 months) to integrate disciplines, conduct hackathons, and coordinate releases.
- Travel support for trainees and geographically distributed team members to ensure inclusive participation.
- Conference travel for dissemination (computational biology, cell biology, bioimage analysis), emphasizing presentations and workshops.
Justification: The project’s success depends on sustained cross-lab integration and community dissemination.

Workshops and training events
- Budget for an NCEMS-hosted training workshop (hybrid): venue costs, A/V, instructional materials, and participant support (especially trainees and underrepresented institutions).
Justification: Directly addresses NCEMS’s mandate to train the next-generation data-savvy workforce and to catalyze community uptake.

Open science infrastructure
- Costs for long-term archiving and dissemination: Zenodo (free) supplemented by optional paid storage or institutional repository fees if needed for large derived artifacts; domain/website hosting for documentation; DOI-enabled releases.
- Professional data curation support (if available through NCEMS) to ensure metadata quality and FAIR compliance.
Justification: Sustainability and reuse depend on well-curated, versioned releases with persistent identifiers.

Summary of resource necessity relative to synthesis goals
This budget is justified by the need to (i) harmonize and process heterogeneous public datasets at scale, (ii) develop and validate robust computational methods across modalities, (iii) maintain open, reproducible infrastructure suitable for community reuse, and (iv) convene a truly multidisciplinary team whose combined expertise and coordination requirements exceed what any single lab can provide.

criteria.justification: The proposal directly targets mesoscale emergent properties of biomolecular condensates (material state, viscoelasticity, multiphase organization) and explicitly links them to an emergent cellular phenotype (gene expression noise). Emergence is central to the hypotheses, modeling strategy, and intended outputs.

Creating a cross-cell-type, multi-modal “material state manifold” and connecting it to transcriptional bursting/noise is a highly innovative synthesis direction with potential to unify disparate condensate observations. Significance is high, though the transformative impact depends on whether heterogeneous imaging and scRNA proxies can robustly support material-state inference.

The methods are generally well-grounded (multi-view representation learning, hierarchical Bayesian noise/bursting models, cross-dataset holdouts, positive controls, sensitivity analyses) and include explicit validation plans. Key rigor risks remain around confounding/identifiability (e.g., linking protein-level imaging features to cell-type scRNA noise without matched samples) and the reliability of FRAP/time-series proxies across studies.

The scope is ambitious: large-scale segmentation across heterogeneous repositories, manifold learning, scRNA bursting inference across atlases, and perturbation/causal discovery within 30 months. Milestones are sensible, but feasibility hinges on data availability/metadata quality (especially FRAP and time series) and on narrowing to tractable, well-annotated subsets if harmonization proves difficult.

The project is explicitly synthesis-only, relying on publicly available sequence/LLPS databases, imaging repositories, scRNA/multiome atlases, and perturbation resources, with no new experimental data generation. Integration across modalities and repositories is the core deliverable.

Data sources are clearly enumerated (PhaSepDB/LLPSDB/DrLLPS, HPA/IDR/BioImage Archive, HCA/Tabula Sapiens/GEO, LINCS/DepMap) with concrete feature plans and entity-resolution steps. Limitations are acknowledged in general (heterogeneous modalities/metadata, batch effects), but the proposal could more explicitly address licensing/usage constraints for images/FRAP supplements and the expected scarcity/non-comparability of dynamic measurements.

The proposal commits to open pipelines, versioned atlas releases, containerized workflows, CI, DOIs, and training materials, aligning well with reproducible team science. It would be stronger with more explicit governance details (authorship/contribution model, data-use compliance plan per repository, and a concrete plan for releasing derived features/embeddings when raw images cannot be redistributed).
The proposal places mesoscale emergent properties (viscoelasticity, percolation) at the center of the research, explicitly linking them to emergent cellular phenotypes (gene expression noise).

The concept of a 'material state manifold' derived from static data to predict dynamic transcriptional outcomes is highly innovative and addresses a critical gap in understanding context-dependent condensate function.

The methodology is exceptionally rigorous, combining physics-informed feature extraction, deep learning for segmentation, and hierarchical Bayesian modeling with clear validation strategies using holdout datasets.
The 30-month timeline is realistic but ambitious given the challenge of harmonizing heterogeneous imaging modalities; however, the detailed milestones and team expertise suggest high feasibility.
The project is a pure synthesis effort, explicitly stating it will generate no new experimental data and relying entirely on integrating diverse public repositories.
Data sources (HPA, IDR, HCA, LINCS, etc.) are identified with high specificity, and limitations regarding data heterogeneity and proxies are acknowledged and addressed methodologically.
