This requires team science across virology, quantitative imaging, network biology, and statistical modeling, and it relies entirely on integrating diverse public datasets. NCEMS support is crucial to coordinate cross-virus data harmonization, establish open standards for compartment annotation, and train trainees in integrative, reproducible computational virology focused on emergent mesoscale organization.

Background: Viruses remodel host cells to create replication compartments (RCs)—mesoscale structures typically ~100–1000 nm that concentrate viral genomes, polymerases, and recruited host factors while excluding or modulating antiviral sensors. Across virus families, RCs appear as membraneless inclusions (often described as liquid-like or gel-like condensates), membrane-bound organelles (e.g., double-membrane vesicles and spherules), or hybrid assemblies combining scaffolded membranes with phase-separated interiors. The mesoscale is central: it is the scale at which many weak molecular interactions, crowding, and transport constraints collectively produce new system properties (reaction acceleration, shielding, spatial segregation) that cannot be inferred from any one protein’s biochemistry. In this sense, viral RCs are a tractable and data-rich model for emergent mesoscale organization in cells.

Current understanding is fragmented across virology subfields. For positive-strand RNA viruses, electron microscopy (EM) studies have documented membrane curvature and invagination to generate spherules, convoluted membranes, or double-membrane vesicles, while fluorescence microscopy has revealed dynamic viral protein foci that coalesce and mature over time. For negative-strand RNA viruses and many DNA viruses, large cytoplasmic or nuclear inclusions assemble, often in association with stress granule components, RNA-binding proteins, chaperones, and cytoskeletal or trafficking machinery. A growing literature suggests that some RCs exhibit hallmarks of biomolecular condensation (concentration-dependent assembly, spherical morphology, fusion events), whereas others are clearly constrained by membrane geometry and organelle contact sites. Yet, a unified framework to compare RC architectures across unrelated viruses is lacking, in part because evidence is distributed across imaging modalities, cell types, and annotation practices.

Public data resources now make cross-virus synthesis feasible at community scale. Imaging data relevant to RC morphology and substructure are increasingly deposited in the BioImage Archive, Image Data Resource (IDR), and EMPIAR, including correlative light and electron microscopy in some systems. Host–virus protein interaction (HV-PPI) data are curated in IntAct, BioGRID, and VirHostNet, enabling cross-study integration of physical and functional interactions. Functional genomics screens for host dependency factors—CRISPR knockout, CRISPRi, and RNAi—are available in repositories such as GEO and SRA, and in aggregated resources including DepMap’s viral perturbation collections where available, as well as numerous published screens with accessible count matrices and hit lists. Transcriptomic responses to infection (bulk RNA-seq, microarray, and in some cases single-cell atlases) are also available in GEO and ArrayExpress, and increasingly in cell atlas initiatives that include infection perturbations or time courses. Finally, structural information about viral scaffolds and host complexes has expanded via the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and AlphaFold DB, enabling mechanistic interpretation of interaction modules and potential multivalency that drives mesoscale assembly.

Despite this abundance, key gaps persist that synthesis research is uniquely positioned to address. First, RC morphology is typically described qualitatively and within a single virus system; quantitative, standardized feature extraction across viruses is rare. Second, HV-PPI networks and genetic dependency screens are usually analyzed separately, leading to inconsistent conclusions about which host processes are central versus context-dependent. Third, replication phenotypes (e.g., viral titers, reporter expression, replication markers) are often reported in heterogeneous units and experimental contexts, limiting cross-study comparability. Fourth, the emergent link between mesoscale organization and replication efficiency—how compartment architecture and host module recruitment jointly produce system-level outcomes—has not been tested systematically across viruses.

NCEMS’s emphasis on mesoscale emergence and synthesis makes RCs an ideal target. RCs sit between molecules and organelles, precisely the mesoscale where emergent behaviors arise from collective interactions, crowding, and geometry. A cross-virus synthesis can reveal whether seemingly different RCs implement convergent “design principles” (e.g., selective permeability, spatial segregation of replication/transcription/assembly, organelle tethering) and whether a small set of host modules repeatedly acts as mesoscale organizers. Importantly, these questions are beyond a single lab: they require harmonizing imaging, interaction, genetic, transcriptomic, and structural datasets across many viruses and laboratories, and developing shared standards for RC annotation.

This proposal leverages existing publicly available datasets to build a comparative, mechanistic understanding of RC emergence. By integrating quantitative imaging-derived morphotypes with network modules and functional dependencies, we will move from virus-specific narratives to generalizable mesoscale principles. The payoff is twofold: fundamental insight into how mesoscale cellular organization emerges under viral perturbation, and practical identification of conserved host “organizer modules” whose disruption may broadly impair RC formation and replication. This synthesis will also produce reusable datasets and workflows for the broader community studying mesoscale compartments, condensates, and organelle remodeling in diverse biological contexts.

Research Questions: This working group will address the overarching question: do viral replication compartments (RCs) share universal mesoscale design principles across unrelated viruses, and can those principles be expressed as measurable, predictive relationships between (i) RC morphotype features, (ii) recruited host factor modules, and (iii) replication efficiency phenotypes? We focus on emergent mesoscale properties—organization, permeability proxies, spatial coupling to organelles, and dynamic assembly—rather than on single-protein enzymology.

Research Question 1 (RQ1): Can RC architectures across diverse viruses be represented in a common quantitative feature space that yields a robust, cross-virus taxonomy of morphotypes?
Prediction 1A: When EM and fluorescence datasets are mapped into standardized features (size distributions, shape descriptors, internal texture/subcompartmentalization, membrane association, proximity to organelles, and time-resolved assembly proxies), RCs will cluster into a small number of recurrent morphotypes (e.g., membrane-invaginated spherules; double-membrane vesicle networks; membraneless inclusion bodies; hybrid membrane/condensate assemblies) that transcend viral phylogeny.
Prediction 1B: Morphotype clusters will be stable across imaging modalities and laboratories after harmonization and batch correction, with uncertainty quantifiable via bootstrap resampling and leave-one-study-out validation.
Validation using existing data: We will test clustering robustness using independent imaging datasets from BioImage Archive/IDR and EMPIAR, applying modality-specific feature extraction and then aligning features via domain adaptation and batch-effect models. Known exemplar systems (e.g., well-characterized spherules vs double-membrane vesicles) serve as positive controls for separability.

Research Question 2 (RQ2): Are there conserved host “mesoscale organizer” modules that are preferentially recruited into RCs and that predict RC morphotype?
Hypothesis 2: Across viruses, RC assembly depends on a limited set of host modules that repeatedly appear as highly central, enriched, and functionally required—such as RNA metabolism/RNP granule proteins, membrane trafficking and curvature machinery, lipid remodeling pathways, chaperones/proteostasis, and cytoskeletal transport.
Measurable predictions:
- 2A: Community detection on integrated HV-PPI networks will identify recurrent host modules whose membership is conserved across multiple viruses more than expected by degree-preserving randomization.
- 2B: These modules will be significantly enriched among hits from CRISPR/RNAi dependency screens (GEO/SRA; DepMap viral screens where available), after harmonizing gene identifiers and applying meta-analysis across studies.
- 2C: Module activity inferred from transcriptomic signatures (bulk and single-cell where available) will correlate with RC morphotype and/or replication outcomes, consistent with module recruitment and functional engagement.
Validation using existing data: We will validate module recurrence by comparing results across interaction databases (IntAct vs BioGRID vs VirHostNet) and across screen types (CRISPR vs RNAi). We will also use curated host complexes (CORUM) and pathways (Reactome, KEGG) as external references to test biological coherence.

Research Question 3 (RQ3): How do RC morphotype and host module recruitment jointly determine emergent replication efficiency across viruses?
Hypothesis 3: Replication efficiency is an emergent outcome determined by a small number of mesoscale variables—compartment capacity (size/volume proxies), organization (subcompartmentalization/texture), coupling to organelles (e.g., ER, mitochondria, Golgi proximity), and selective recruitment of organizer modules—rather than by any single interaction.
Measurable predictions:
- 3A: Multilevel models incorporating morphotype features plus module-level predictors will explain replication phenotypes (viral titers, reporter readouts, replication marker expression) better than models using only viral taxonomy or only single-gene effects.
- 3B: Causal graph analyses will support directed relationships consistent with “module recruitment → morphotype stabilization → replication efficiency,” with alternative explanations (e.g., replication level driving apparent compartment size) evaluated via time-course ordering and sensitivity analyses.
- 3C: The same organizer modules will predict replication outcomes across multiple viruses, indicating broad-spectrum leverage points.
Validation using existing data: We will assemble replication phenotype measures from published datasets (often in GEO/SRA-linked studies) and standardize them to comparable effect sizes within study, then meta-analyze across studies. Time-course transcriptomics and imaging timepoints (when available) will support temporal constraints in causal modeling.

Research Question 4 (RQ4): Do structural features of viral scaffold proteins and recruited host complexes explain convergent mesoscale assembly strategies?
Hypothesis 4: Viral proteins that nucleate RCs exhibit convergent structural properties—multivalency, intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs), modular interaction motifs, and/or membrane-binding/curvature-inducing domains—that align with the inferred assembly strategy (phase separation, membrane scaffolding, or hybrid).
Predictions:
- 4A: Structural annotations from PDB and AlphaFold DB (disorder propensity, predicted interaction interfaces, oligomerization likelihood, membrane association motifs) will associate with morphotype cluster membership.
- 4B: Host complexes recruited as organizer modules will show compatible structural/biophysical features (e.g., RNA-binding multivalency; coatomer/ESCRT architecture; lipid-modifying enzyme complexes) consistent with mesoscale assembly.
Validation using existing data: We will quantify structural features using established predictors and curated annotations, then test associations with morphotypes and network modules using permutation tests and hierarchical models.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses yield a rigorous, testable synthesis agenda: define a cross-virus mesoscale feature language; identify conserved organizer modules; and build predictive, mechanistic models linking mesoscale organization to emergent replication efficiency—entirely through integration and reanalysis of publicly available datasets.

Methods: Overview and scope (synthesis-only): We will conduct a community-scale synthesis integrating five public data modalities—imaging, host–virus interactions, functional genetic screens, transcriptomics, and structural models—across multiple viruses (initial focus: coronaviruses, flaviviruses, and herpesviruses; expandable to additional families as data density permits). No new experiments, samples, or data generation will occur. All analyses will use existing publicly available datasets and metadata.

A. Specific data sources (by modality)
1) Imaging (RC morphology and spatial context)
- BioImage Archive (EMBL-EBI): infection imaging datasets with fluorescence microscopy and metadata.
- Image Data Resource (IDR): curated multi-dimensional microscopy studies, including infection-related datasets.
- EMPIAR: raw EM datasets, including virus-induced membrane remodeling and replication organelles.
- Supplementary imaging from published studies when deposited in the above archives; we will only use data that are publicly accessible.
2) Host–virus protein interactions (HV-PPI)
- IntAct (EMBL-EBI): curated molecular interactions, including virus–host.
- BioGRID: host–pathogen interaction datasets.
- VirHostNet: integrated virus–host interaction knowledgebase.
- Optional cross-references: STRING (for host-only network context; used cautiously with confidence thresholds).
3) Functional screens (host dependency)
- NCBI GEO and SRA: CRISPR knockout/CRISPRi and RNAi screens with available count matrices or hit lists.
- DepMap (Broad Institute): where viral perturbation screens or relevant host essentiality context can be leveraged for interpretation and priors.
- PubChem BioAssay / ChEMBL (optional): for reported antiviral perturbations with mechanistic annotations, used only as existing data to contextualize “mesoscale disruptors.”
4) Transcriptomics
- NCBI GEO and ArrayExpress: bulk RNA-seq/microarray infection time courses.
- Single-cell infection atlases where public (e.g., COVID-19 Cell Atlas and other scRNA-seq infection datasets deposited in GEO/ArrayExpress); also Human Cell Atlas where infection perturbation datasets are available.
5) Structural data
- Protein Data Bank (PDB): experimentally determined structures of viral scaffolds and host complexes.
- AlphaFold DB: predicted structures for viral and host proteins lacking PDB coverage.
- UniProt: domain annotations, subcellular localization, and sequence features.

B. Data harmonization and governance
- Entity normalization: unify virus names/strains, host species/cell lines, gene/protein identifiers (HGNC/Ensembl/UniProt), and experimental conditions using controlled vocabularies.
- Metadata schema: develop an RC-centric metadata model extending existing standards (OME for imaging; PSI-MI for interactions), capturing virus, time post-infection, cell type, imaging modality, markers, and reported replication readouts.
- Batch and study effects: record study-level covariates and implement hierarchical models and ComBat-like adjustments where appropriate; for imaging, use domain adaptation to reduce modality/lab differences.
- Provenance: every derived dataset will include provenance links (accession IDs, versioned downloads, checksums) and transformation logs.

C. Imaging feature extraction and RC morphotyping
Goal: produce a standardized mesoscale feature framework.
1) Preprocessing
- Convert microscopy formats using Bio-Formats/OME tools; standardize voxel sizes and intensity scaling when metadata permit.
- For EMPIAR volumes/micrographs, apply established denoising and contrast normalization pipelines (parameterized and documented).
2) Segmentation and compartment detection (existing images)
- Use a combination of classical and ML-assisted segmentation, relying on pretrained models where available (e.g., Cellpose/StarDist for fluorescence; EM segmentation via ilastik or pretrained U-Net models). We will not train on new labeled data; if labels exist publicly within IDR studies, they may be used.
- Generate uncertainty estimates by ensembling methods and quantifying agreement.
3) Feature computation (mesoscale descriptors)
- Size/shape: area/volume proxies, equivalent diameter, eccentricity, surface roughness.
- Internal organization: texture features (Haralick), radial intensity profiles, subcompartment counts via watershed/peak detection.
- Spatial context: distances to organelle markers (ER, Golgi, mitochondria, nucleus) when channels exist; proximity to membranes in EM via boundary detection.
- Dynamics proxies: when time-lapse exists, track RCs to estimate fusion frequency, growth rates, and mobility; otherwise infer “assembly stage” from timepoint metadata.
4) Morphotype taxonomy
- Build a joint embedding of features using variational autoencoders or contrastive learning with modality labels as nuisance variables; assess stability with repeated subsampling.
- Cluster using HDBSCAN or Gaussian mixture models; select cluster number via stability metrics.
- Output: a probabilistic morphotype assignment per dataset/timepoint with confidence intervals.

D. Network synthesis: HV-PPI integration and module discovery
1) Construct virus-specific bipartite networks (virus proteins ↔ host proteins) from IntAct/BioGRID/VirHostNet; retain evidence codes and publication provenance.
2) Harmonize interaction confidence: map database-specific scores to a unified scale using calibration against replicated interactions.
3) Embed and detect modules
- Compute host-side embeddings using node2vec/DeepWalk on projected host networks, and/or graph neural network embeddings with virus identity as feature.
- Identify host modules via Leiden/Louvain community detection and overlapping community methods (e.g., link communities) to capture multifunctional proteins.
4) Module interpretation
- Enrich modules for Reactome/KEGG pathways, Gene Ontology, and CORUM complexes.
- Define “recurrent organizer modules” as modules that (i) appear across multiple viruses, (ii) are enriched for screen hits, and (iii) show consistent association with morphotypes.

E. Functional screen meta-analysis (CRISPR/RNAi)
1) Curate screens from GEO/SRA and published supplementary tables; include only those with sufficient metadata and accessible results.
2) Standardize effect sizes
- For CRISPR: use MAGeCK-style summary statistics when available; otherwise compute log-fold changes and robust z-scores.
- For RNAi: harmonize to gene-level scores and account for off-target propensity using published correction methods.
3) Meta-analysis
- Combine across studies using random-effects models; stratify by virus family, cell type, and assay.
- Map hits to network modules and test module-level enrichment via permutation tests.

F. Transcriptomic integration (bulk and single-cell)
1) Bulk: compute differential expression signatures per condition/timepoint; infer pathway activity (GSVA) and regulator activity (DoRothEA/PROGENy where applicable).
2) Single-cell (where public): harmonize cell annotations; infer infection state; compute module activity scores and heterogeneity metrics.
3) Link to RC features: align transcriptomic timepoints with imaging timepoints when possible; otherwise use coarse staging (early/mid/late) based on reported hours post-infection.

G. Multimodal modeling: linking morphotypes, modules, and replication phenotypes
1) Outcome harmonization: within each study, convert replication readouts (titer, qPCR, reporter) to standardized effect sizes relative to controls; retain units for transparency.
2) Multilevel regression
- Fit hierarchical models with random effects for study and virus, predictors including morphotype probabilities, module enrichment scores, and transcriptomic module activities.
- Evaluate predictive performance with leave-one-virus-out and leave-one-study-out cross-validation.
3) Causal inference (observational)
- Construct causal graphs with constraints from time ordering; apply methods such as invariant causal prediction and sensitivity analyses to unmeasured confounding.
- Compare alternative models (e.g., replication drives size vs size enables replication) using time-course evidence.

H. Validation without new experiments
- Cross-database replication: confirm organizer modules across IntAct/BioGRID/VirHostNet.
- Cross-modality coherence: test whether morphotype-associated modules also show consistent transcriptomic activation.
- Known positive controls: benchmark morphotype assignments against canonical RC descriptions from the literature for selected viruses.
- Negative controls: randomized networks (degree-preserving), permuted gene labels, and shuffled timepoints to assess false discovery.

I. Timeline and milestones (30 months)
Months 0–6:
- Assemble working group; finalize metadata schema; curate initial virus set and datasets; implement reproducible data ingestion.
- Milestone: public registry of included datasets with accession IDs and harmonized metadata v1.
Months 7–12:
- Imaging pipelines operational; first-pass feature extraction; preliminary morphotype clustering.
- Milestone: RC feature dataset v1 and morphotype taxonomy draft.
Months 13–18:
- HV-PPI integration; module discovery; screen meta-analysis; initial module recurrence results.
- Milestone: organizer module catalog v1 with provenance and enrichment analyses.
Months 19–24:
- Multimodal modeling linking morphotypes/modules to replication phenotypes; causal graph analyses; robustness checks.
- Milestone: predictive models v1 and cross-validation reports.
Months 25–30:
- Final synthesis, manuscripts, and community resources; NCEMS workshop; finalize open pipelines and documentation.
- Milestone: public release of datasets/tools v2; preprints and submission-ready manuscripts.

J. Team composition (multi-lab, transdisciplinary)
- Virology experts (RNA and DNA viruses) to ensure biological interpretation and correct mapping of viral life cycle stages.
- Quantitative imaging scientists to lead feature extraction, morphometrics, and modality harmonization.
- Network biologists to integrate HV-PPI, perform module detection, and interpret pathway/complex enrichment.
- Statistical modelers/causal inference experts to build multilevel and causal models with rigorous uncertainty quantification.
- Structural bioinformaticians to quantify scaffold multivalency, disorder, and interaction interface features from PDB/AlphaFold DB.
- Research software engineers to build reproducible pipelines, data packaging, and documentation.
- Trainees (graduate students/postdocs) embedded across tasks, receiving cross-training in imaging, networks, and reproducible computational science.

This integrated approach directly addresses NCEMS priorities: mesoscale emergence, synthesis of existing public data, cross-disciplinary collaboration beyond a single lab, and production of open, reusable resources for the community.

Expected Outcomes: Deliverable 1: A cross-virus replication compartment (RC) feature atlas and morphotype taxonomy. We will release a standardized, quantitative feature dataset describing RCs across viruses, imaging modalities, and timepoints, with probabilistic morphotype assignments and uncertainty estimates. This atlas will include harmonized metadata (virus, strain where available, host cell type, time post-infection, imaging modality, markers) and will be linked to the original BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR accession identifiers. The taxonomy will provide a shared language for describing RC mesoscale organization—moving beyond qualitative labels to measurable, comparable descriptors.

Deliverable 2: An integrated catalog of conserved host “mesoscale organizer” modules. By synthesizing IntAct, BioGRID, and VirHostNet interactions with CRISPR/RNAi screen meta-analyses (GEO/SRA; DepMap context where relevant) and transcriptomic module activity (GEO/ArrayExpress; public single-cell infection datasets), we will produce a ranked set of host modules recurrently recruited and required across viruses. Each module will be accompanied by evidence provenance (interaction sources, screen studies, enrichment statistics), functional annotations (Reactome/KEGG/GO, CORUM complexes), and network centrality measures. This catalog will help the field distinguish broadly conserved organizers from virus- or context-specific factors.

Deliverable 3: Predictive, interpretable models linking mesoscale organization to replication efficiency. We will deliver multilevel predictive models that estimate replication outcomes (standardized within-study effect sizes derived from public replication readouts) from RC morphotype features and module-level predictors. Importantly, these models will be interpretable: we will report which mesoscale features (e.g., size distribution shifts, increased internal subcompartmentalization, organelle proximity signatures) and which host modules contribute most strongly, with uncertainty and cross-validation results. Where time-course data permit, causal graph analyses will propose directional relationships (e.g., organizer module engagement preceding morphotype stabilization) and quantify robustness to confounding.

Deliverable 4: Mechanistic synthesis of convergent assembly strategies across viruses. Integrating structural annotations (PDB, AlphaFold DB, UniProt) with the morphotype and module results, we will generate mechanistic hypotheses about convergent mesoscale assembly strategies: (i) phase-separation–dominated RCs driven by multivalent RNA-binding and disordered viral scaffolds; (ii) membrane-curvature–scaffolded RCs driven by viral membrane proteins and host trafficking/curvature modules; and (iii) hybrid RCs combining membrane topology with condensate-like interiors. The impact is a generalizable conceptual framework for how mesoscale organization emerges from ensembles of weak interactions, geometry, and cellular resource allocation.

Scientific impact on mesoscale emergent phenomena. This project advances NCEMS’s mission by providing a concrete, quantitative example of emergence at the mesoscale: RCs exhibit system-level properties—selective concentration, shielding, kinetic enhancement, spatial segregation—that arise from collective organization rather than from single molecules. By comparing across unrelated viruses, we can separate universal mesoscale principles (e.g., modular recruitment, permeability proxies, organelle coupling) from lineage-specific implementations. The resulting framework can inform broader cell biology questions about condensates, organelle contact sites, and mesoscale reaction engineering in living cells.

Broader impacts and downstream utility. The outputs will enable multiple future research directions without requiring new data generation by this project: (i) hypothesis generation for antiviral strategies targeting organizer modules or mesoscale assembly processes; (ii) improved annotation standards for infection imaging datasets; (iii) transfer of methods to other mesoscale compartments (stress granules, P bodies, autophagosomes, centrosomal material); and (iv) benchmarking datasets for AI methods in multimodal biological synthesis. By providing standardized feature sets and module definitions, we lower barriers for diverse researchers—including those outside virology—to contribute to mesoscale emergence science.

Dissemination plan. We will produce at least two major manuscripts: (1) the RC morphotype atlas and feature framework; (2) the multimodal organizer-module and replication-efficiency synthesis with predictive/causal models. We will release preprints and submit to open-access journals when possible. We will host an NCEMS-aligned workshop (virtual + in-person) to train participants in using the pipelines and interpreting the atlas, and we will present at cross-disciplinary venues spanning virology, quantitative cell biology, and network science.

Long-term sustainability. All datasets will be packaged with stable identifiers and deposited in long-lived repositories (e.g., Zenodo for derived datasets and code releases; links back to BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR for primary imaging; interaction and transcriptomic resources referenced by accession). We will design the atlas as an extensible resource: new viruses and datasets can be incorporated by running the same containerized workflows and adding metadata-compliant entries. Sustainability will be reinforced through community engagement—inviting external groups to contribute additional public datasets and annotations via documented contribution guidelines and periodic “data sprints.”

Budget and Resources: Budget rationale (2.5–3 years; synthesis-only). The proposed work is computationally intensive and coordination-heavy, requiring personnel across multiple disciplines, robust computing, and dedicated resources for open science dissemination and training. All items below are justified by the need to integrate and harmonize heterogeneous public datasets at community scale—beyond the capacity of a single lab.

Personnel
1) Two postdoctoral researchers (computational synthesis focus).
- Postdoc A (quantitative imaging + morphometrics): leads imaging ingestion from BioImage Archive/IDR/EMPIAR, feature extraction, morphotype taxonomy, and uncertainty quantification.
- Postdoc B (network biology + multimodal modeling): leads HV-PPI integration (IntAct/BioGRID/VirHostNet), screen meta-analysis (GEO/SRA), and multilevel/causal models linking modules and morphotypes to replication phenotypes.
Justification: The project’s core deliverables require sustained, expert-level integration across modalities; two postdocs provide parallel progress and cross-validation.

2) One graduate student (integrative analysis + training pipeline).
- Focus on transcriptomic integration (GEO/ArrayExpress; public single-cell infection datasets), module activity inference, and contribution to causal/time-course analyses.
Justification: Provides structured training in data synthesis and contributes to deliverables; aligns with NCEMS workforce goals.

3) Research software engineer/programmer (0.5–1.0 FTE depending on award size).
- Builds and maintains Snakemake/Nextflow pipelines, containers (Docker/Singularity), CI, documentation, and data packaging for Zenodo releases.
Justification: Reproducibility and sustainability require professional engineering support; essential for open workflows usable by the community.

4) PI/co-PI effort (fractional) across participating labs.
- Supports coordination, scientific integration, mentoring, and dissemination.
Justification: Multi-lab synthesis demands active leadership, consensus building on standards, and oversight of open science practices.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or institutional HPC allocations for:
  (i) large-scale image processing (segmentation, feature extraction) from EMPIAR and high-content fluorescence datasets;
  (ii) graph embedding/community detection on large interaction networks;
  (iii) model fitting with cross-validation and bootstrapping.
- Storage for cached public downloads and intermediate artifacts (tens of TB depending on imaging volume), with backup.
Justification: Imaging datasets and repeated analyses at scale exceed typical lab compute; centralized resources ensure consistent, reproducible runs.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (1–2 in-person per year) to coordinate standards (RC feature specification, metadata schema), resolve integration issues, and conduct hands-on analysis sprints.
- Conference travel for dissemination at cross-disciplinary venues (virology, quantitative cell biology, network science) and to recruit additional community contributors.
Justification: NCEMS-style synthesis benefits from intensive, face-to-face integration and broad dissemination to maximize reuse.

Workshops and training events
- Budget for hosting an NCEMS-aligned workshop (venue, A/V, materials, limited trainee travel support) and a virtual tutorial series.
Justification: Training is a core program goal; workshops accelerate adoption of tools and standards and build the next-generation workforce.

Open science infrastructure costs
- Zenodo/DOI-associated release preparation (person-time), potential costs for long-term data hosting of derived artifacts if needed, and web hosting for documentation (e.g., GitHub Pages) and a lightweight project portal.
Justification: Ensures deliverables remain accessible, citable, and maintainable beyond the award period.

Overall, the budget prioritizes the essential elements of a community-scale synthesis project: dedicated integrative personnel, scalable compute for multimodal reanalysis, strong coordination across labs, and robust open-science dissemination and training that extend impact well beyond the immediate team.

title: CYTOKINETIC BOTTLENECKS OF HEAT WAVES
author: Human
abstract_original: The lack of motility makes plants highly vulnerable to environmental anomalies such as periods of extreme high temperature known as heat waves. Plants can search for better habitats by exploiting seed mobility, which relies on completing the life cycle and producing seeds. Formation of reproductive organs and seed development requires the production of cells through cell division. The last stage of cell division, cytokinesis, encompasses many key cellular processes, including vesicle trafficking, cell wall biosynthesis, cytoskeletal dynamics, and signaling. While cytokinesis is highly sensitive to heat stress in plants adapted to temperate climates, cytokinesis is more resilient in species adapted to tropical zones. However, how heat stress affects cytokinesis and the mechanisms of cytokinetic robustness across different plant species remains unknown. This project aims to compare changes in cytokinetic components under heat stress in susceptible and hardy species to characterize differential responses of genetic circuits responsible for specific cellular events during cytokinesis. The long term goal is to harness this data for identifying the bottlenecks of cytokinetic robustness. The experimental approach here will be systematic analysis of publicly available data from single-cell and whole-organ omics data collected under control and high-temperature conditions including transcriptomics, translatomics, and proteomics. Predicting cytokinetic bottlenecks will inform future experimental design for their functional characterization leading to better understanding of cellular adaptation mechanisms to heat stress. This knowledge may provide insight into evolutionary strategies of plant adaptation to different climates and improve predictions for heat resiliency at the level of individual plants and populations.
full_draft_original: Introduction 4.1. Problem overview. 4.1.1. Cytokinesis is critical for plant life. The majority of planetary plant biomass derives from cytokinesis. Plant cytokinesis occurs via the formation of a specialized membrane compartment, the cell plate, between daughter cells. The cell plate gradually matures into a cell wall after cytokinesis is complete. One of the key processes accompanying this transition is replacing callose, the main polysaccharide in the cell plate lumen, with cellulose. A plant-specific polarized secretory module, the phragmoplast, is responsible for constructing the cell plate. The phragmoplast consists of microtubules and actin cytoskeleton, vesicles, and associated proteins. As the phragmoplast diameter is commonly smaller than the cell width, completing the cell plate construction requires phragmoplast expansion. The expansion is driven by microtubules and requires coordination between microtubule dynamics, membrane and cell-wall-component trafficking, exocytosis, vesicle fusion, and endocytosis. Phragmoplast expansion encompasses four steps: establishment of microtubule overlap, vesicle recruitment, vesicle fusion and remodeling, and microtubule depolymerization. Each step requires a dedicated genetic network comprising structural proteins, enzymes, and signaling components. 4.1.2. Cytokinesis is sensitive to heat stress. Exposing tobacco tissue culture cells to 38°C for 2 h causes cytokinetic arrest and elongation of phragmoplast microtubules while cells remain viable; subsequently, microtubule organization does not recover even by 2 hours at normal temperature, indicating that the arrest is long-term. In meiotic Arabidopsis cells treated at 36–38°C, chromosome segregation is disrupted and microtubule density in the phragmoplast is reduced. In the flowering sea grass Cymodocea nodosa, treatment at 38°C for 2 h depolymerizes some phragmoplast microtubules but does not block cytokinesis. The graded heat stress responses among species will allow us to identify both common and distinct resilience mechanisms of cytokinesis. 4.1.3. Outcomes of prior studies 4.1.3.1. Cytokinesis is differentially sensitive to heat stress within the plant lineage. Arabidopsis plants are killed at about 35°C whereas maize plants are killed by temperatures at least 10 degrees higher. Consequently, maize cytokinesis could be resilient to heat stress. We compared the impact of heat stress on cytokinesis in these species. On the basis of published data 38°C was used to induce stress. Exposure of 6-day-old Arabidopsis seedlings to 38°C for 1 hour caused cell plate tilting and disorganization, as indicated by the cytokinetic vesicle marker RABA2a. Cell plate assembly failed resulting in formation of cell wall stubs and phragmoplasts were aberrantly long. We examined microtubule stability in the elongated phragmoplasts using fluorescence recovery after photobleaching and found very slow recovery of the fluorescent signal. As the signal recovery requires microtubule depolymerization, this outcome suggests that heat stress suppressed depolymerization of phragmoplast microtubules. Oppositely, in 3-week-old maize seedlings the phragmoplast morphology appeared unaltered and no cell wall stubs were detected even after exposure to 42°C or 45°C. Thus, cytokinesis is heat-resilient in maize. This outcome is consistent with the report that the 2021 heat wave caused yield losses to all dryland farming crops except maize. Therefore, comparing the impact of 38°C on cytokinetic components in Arabidopsis and tobacco with those in maize will likely inform on mechanisms of cytokinetic robustness. 4.1.3.2. Impact of heat stress on transcription and translation of cytokinetic genes. While analyzing the impact of heat stress on circadian clock-regulated genes, we discovered changes in both the abundance of mRNAs and in the ribosome-binding fraction encoding key cytokinetic genes. For example, the phragmoplast-localized kinesin HINKEL was reduced after heat treatment on both transcriptome and translatome levels. AIR9 transcripts were not significantly affected by heat treatment. Heat stress resulted in lower transcription and translation of multiple cytokinetic genes with the exception of the midzone localized formin homology protein AtFH8 whose translation was specifically upregulated. AtFH8 might contribute to the stabilization of microtubule plus-ends at the phragmoplast midzone. Up-regulation of this protein could be a mechanism to sustain phragmoplast organization under heat stress. Therefore, comparison of transcriptome and translatome data captures the complexity of cytokinetic gene regulation in responses to stresses. 4.1.4. Conceptual framework. According to the theory of biological robustness, genetic networks for individual traits contain specific robustness alleles instead of a master robustness allele acting across multiple networks. Consequently, known robustness alleles for other traits are unlikely to contribute to heat resiliency of cytokinesis. Instead, cytokinetic robustness must be achieved by temporally controlling and genetically buffering distinct cytokinetic processes in a modular fashion. When a genetic network experiences an interruption, both the central hubs and less connected nodes could either limit or maintain resiliency. Consequently, identifying cytokinetic bottlenecks requires generating cytokinetic protein networks and comparing their behaviour under normal and stress conditions. Construction of cytokinetic networks is hindered by limited information about their components. Despite genetic screens for cytokinetic mutants having already identified multiple players, many cytokinetic genes remain unidentified either due to genetic redundancy or lethality. Furthermore, despite biophysical modeling indicating that callose provides the spreading force for membrane remodeling during cell plate expansion, there are numerous knowledge gaps about other carbohydrates and corresponding enzymes during cytokinesis. 4.2. Goals. The long-term goal of our research is to determine the rules and limits of cytokinetic robustness under heat stress and harness this knowledge for improving plant resiliency. Although it has been shown that high temperatures perturb membrane assembly and cytoskeletal dynamics during cytokinesis the underlying molecular mechanisms of such changes remain unknown. The objective of this project is to exploit available data to predict bottlenecks of cytokinesis. A bottleneck is defined as a gene whose product becomes dysfunctional or less functional in response to heat stress. The rationale for this project is based on the following elements: heat stress induces transcriptional changes of genes encoding cytokinetic proteins; plants adapted to hotter environments likely evolved mechanisms to buffer the effects of heat stress on cell division; analysis of available data can inform on differences of cytokinetic responses in heat resilient and heat tolerant species. We plan to achieve the main objective through three specific aims below. 5. Proposed Activities. 5.1. Aim 1. Construct cytokinetic networks using single-cell omics data. Our knowledge about cytokinetic components is limited to several dozens of cytokinesis-defective mutants, a few protein-protein interaction maps, and information about mitotic transcripts. Many proteins required for cytokinesis remain unknown. This aim will take a holistic approach to identify the cytokinetic gene networks using single-cell transcriptomics data from plant species including Arabidopsis thaliana, Zea mays, Oryza sativa, Sorghum bicolor, and Nicotiana tabacum to identify conserved cytokinetic transcripts as well as species-specific cytokinetic transcripts. Raw data will be reprocessed following a standardized pipeline for all omics datasets to allow for effective comparative analysis and interpretation of the data. For single-cell transcriptomics, the analysis for count normalization, dimensionality reduction, clustering visualization, trajectory analysis, and differential gene expression analysis may vary depending on the lab. Therefore, data reprocessing will account for variation and enable statistically significant perturbations to be compared. Then the following pipeline will be used. First, a list of mitotic-related genes including paralogs will be compiled for Arabidopsis from published data. Second, a standardized pipeline such as an orthology inference method will identify orthologous genes from maize, sorghum, rice, and tobacco. Third, the single-cell transcriptome data will be either analyzed or reanalyzed to identify co-expressed transcripts. Fourth, transcripts that are only expressed in cells expressing known mitotic-specific transcripts will be selected as benchmark transcripts to identify coexpressing transcripts. Then, transcripts that appear in fewer than half of the datasets per organism will be more closely assessed for removal from the list. The expected outcome would be a table of Arabidopsis mitosis and cytokinesis proteins and their homologs in other plant species. 5.2. Aim 2. Compare cytokinetic responses to heat stress in heat susceptible and resilient species. Our preliminary experiments demonstrate that cytokinesis is heat-sensitive in tobacco and Arabidopsis thaliana, and heat-tolerant in Zea mays. This aim will compare omics data of Zea mays and other heat-tolerant species with those of heat-sensitive species. As in Aim 1, the raw data will be reprocessed. Analysis will focus on identifying responses that are different between tolerant and susceptible species for each type of omics analyses. We will also identify the transcription factors and cis-regulatory components of these genes that act specifically in heat stress response using available datasets. Completing this aim will inform on which pathways are affected by heat stress in heat tolerant and susceptible species. 5.3. Aim 3. Predict cytokinetic bottlenecks through integration of available datasets. The activities in this aim will construct multi-layered cytokinetic-specific networks and compare their changes under heat stress conditions in susceptible and tolerant species. The first step will be single-layer analysis within a single type of omics data. Analyses for each layer will include differential analysis, correlation network analysis, time series clustering, and association networks. The second stage will be construction of a multiplex network that combines single-layer networks from different omics datasets into a multilayer model. Connections, or edges, between the layers indicate inter-layer relationships. Analysis of networks is expected to generate candidate molecular features with potential influence on differences in cytokinetic responses. These comparisons are predicted to identify cytokinetic bottlenecks under heat stress. We will write a manuscript on this topic and submit it towards the end of year 2. 5.4. Potential problems could arise from the datasets being generated using plants grown under different conditions as well as due to the differences in how the normalization and further analysis were performed. To address this problem we will reanalyze all datasets as outlined in Specific Aim 1, and also including a large number of datasets will help to average the noise caused by variable growth conditions. 6. Outcomes. We anticipate this project will predict cytokinetic bottlenecks under heat stress. This information will be used to formulate the theory of cytokinetic responses to heat stress. The theory will aim to answer the following questions. Which changes to cytokinetic processes in response to heat stress measured either at the transcript or the protein level are common to all species or species-specific? Are there specific subsets of cytokinesis genes or paralogs that have a differential response to heat stress? Do plants eliminate proteins or transcripts or stabilize them to adapt to heat stress? Would these changes promote or block cytokinesis? We will publish this theory as a review article. The theory will inform on the experiments that will lead to the identification of novel genetic, biochemical, and cellular markers of plant heat stress response. Such markers would enable predicting the performance of individual species and stability of entire ecosystems under elevated temperatures, identifying resilient genotypes among the available germplasm for urban ecosystems and afforestation projects, breeding crops with higher yield in hotter environments, developing new approaches for engineering heat-resilient landscaping plant species to contribute to sustainable habitats for humans and animals. 7. Rationale for a working group approach. Our team possesses expertise in cell biology of plant cytokinesis, membrane trafficking, heat stress impact on plant physiology, and protein biochemistry. We collectively have a deep mechanistic understanding of cytokinesis. Further, we collected preliminary data showing that heat stress does not break cytokinetic processes in susceptible plant species, but prevents cytokinetic progression through the arrest of cellular dynamics. The next logical step is to identify cytokinetic pathways affected by the heat stress, and compare them in tolerant and susceptible species using a bioinformatics approach. We want to team up with a synthesis center for the next important stage in understanding the impact of heat stress on cytokinesis. 8. Rationale for support. We hope to gain access to professional expertise in bioinformatics and complex data analysis. Publicly available single-cell and whole-tissue heat stress omics data offers rich material for predicting cytokinetic bottlenecks. Collaboration will lower the barriers of analyzing publicly available omics data for the investigators. Our cell biological data suggests that there will be differentially regulated cytokinetic pathways in heat tolerant and susceptible organisms and we can predict them using bioinformatics analyses. There is currently no alternative funding mechanism to support the transition from an initial concept to an experimental analysis. This project will contribute to developing the theory of cytokinetic robustness and help us to design experiments to test it. 9. Requested resources. To successfully perform the work described in the aims above, a staff scientist with bioinformatics expertise is requested for 4 months per year and an assistant staff scientist for 6 months per year for 2 years. Computational resources for storage and data processing are also needed to successfully implement and achieve the above aims. To accommodate the download and storage of the publicly available datasets listed in the data sources table and support the analyses we estimate and are requesting 50 terabytes of storage and 25,000 CPU hours.

criteria.justification: The proposal targets cytokinesis as a mesoscale, multi-component process whose robustness/failure under heat stress emerges from coordinated cytoskeletal, trafficking, and cell-wall networks. However, the emergent-phenomena framing is more implicit than explicitly operationalized with measurable emergent properties.

Cross-species, multi-omics synthesis to infer cytokinetic “bottlenecks” and robustness mechanisms under heat waves is a novel and potentially high-impact angle with clear relevance to plant adaptation. The significance would be strengthened by sharper, testable predictions and clearer definitions of what constitutes a bottleneck across data modalities.

The overall logic (reprocess datasets, infer orthology, build coexpression and multilayer networks, compare heat responses) is sound, but key methodological details are underspecified (dataset inclusion criteria, batch correction strategy, cross-species comparability, network inference choices, and validation/robustness checks). Without explicit statistical plans for heterogeneity and confounding, rigor is good but not yet very strong.

Reprocessing and integrating single-cell and bulk multi-omics across 5 species plus heat-stress conditions within 2 years is achievable but ambitious, especially given expected heterogeneity in experimental designs and limited staffing time. Feasibility would improve with a staged plan (pilot species/datasets first) and explicit go/no-go milestones.

The project is explicitly and exclusively based on reanalysis and integration of publicly available single-cell and whole-organ omics datasets, with no new data generation. The aims are centered on synthesis across datasets, modalities, and species.

The proposal names organismal scope and data types but does not clearly enumerate specific repositories/accessions, heat-stress regimes, tissues, developmental stages, or minimum dataset requirements. Limitations from growth conditions and normalization are acknowledged, but additional constraints (cell-cycle annotation quality, orthology ambiguity, tissue mismatch, and stress protocol non-equivalence) are not fully analyzed.

While the work inherently uses public data and plans manuscripts, the proposal does not provide concrete open-science implementation details (e.g., preregistered analysis plan, public code/workflows, containerized pipelines, versioned releases, data products, or governance for team/reproducible practices). A clearer commitment and plan are needed to meet the call’s expectations.
The proposal focuses on the robustness of the phragmoplast and cytokinetic machinery, which are complex, self-organizing mesoscale structures, fitting the definition of emergent phenomena.

The comparative approach between heat-resilient and susceptible species using synthesized omics data to find specific genetic 'bottlenecks' is a novel and significant strategy for understanding plant adaptation.
The methodology includes a logical pipeline for data reprocessing, orthology inference, and network construction, with specific attention paid to normalization issues across diverse datasets.
The two-year timeline with requested bioinformatics staff support appears realistic for the proposed scope of data reanalysis and network modeling.
The project is a pure synthesis effort, relying entirely on existing public omics data without generating new wet-lab results, perfectly aligning with the call's requirements.

The proposal identifies specific species and data types (transcriptomics, translatomics, proteomics) and explicitly acknowledges limitations regarding variable growth conditions and data normalization.

While the proposal mentions publishing results and a review article, it lacks a specific, detailed plan for sharing the analysis workflows, code, or intermediate datasets in accordance with open science principles.

The proposal addresses cytokinesis as a complex cellular process involving multiple interacting components (cytoskeleton, vesicle trafficking, signaling), which represents emergent behavior at the cellular level. However, the focus on heat stress responses rather than explicitly framing the work around emergent phenomena makes this connection indirect rather than central.

The comparative approach between heat-tolerant and heat-susceptible species to identify cytokinetic bottlenecks is innovative and addresses an important agricultural and ecological question. The integration of transcriptomics, translatomics, and proteomics data across multiple species represents a significant advancement in understanding plant stress responses.

The methodology is generally logical with a clear pipeline for data reprocessing and analysis, including orthology inference and network construction. However, some aspects lack specificity, such as the criteria for identifying 'benchmark transcripts' and the specific methods for multiplex network analysis, which raises concerns about reproducibility.

The two-year timeline with requested bioinformatics support is reasonable for the proposed aims, though the scope is ambitious given the complexity of integrating multiple omics datasets across five species. The acknowledgment of potential problems with dataset heterogeneity and the plan to address them through reanalysis is appropriate but may require more time than allocated.

The proposal clearly focuses on synthesizing existing publicly available omics data without generating new experimental data. The integration of single-cell transcriptomics, translatomics, and proteomics across multiple species demonstrates a strong synthesis approach, though the preliminary experimental data mentioned suggests some original data generation occurred prior to this proposal.

While the proposal mentions using publicly available datasets from multiple species and references a 'data sources table,' the specific datasets are not explicitly identified in the proposal text. The limitations of cross-species comparisons and variable growth conditions are acknowledged but not thoroughly analyzed.

The proposal mentions publishing manuscripts and a review article but lacks explicit commitment to open science principles such as sharing analysis workflows, code repositories, or making intermediate data products publicly available. There is no discussion of reproducibility practices or data management plans beyond the final publications.

title_norm: emergent ribosome assembly landscapes: integrating cryo-em intermediates, rrna processing maps, and proteomics to explain assembly robustness
title: Emergent Ribosome Assembly Landscapes: Integrating Cryo-EM Intermediates, rRNA Processing Maps, and Proteomics to Explain Assembly Robustness
author: gpt-5.2
abstract_original:
Ribosome biogenesis involves mesoscale ribonucleoprotein intermediates (20–30 nm) that undergo coordinated folding, processing, and factor exchange. The emergent phenomenon is robust, directional assembly arising from collective interactions among rRNA, ribosomal proteins, and dozens of assembly factors—behavior not deducible from any single component. This project will synthesize structural and functional datasets to infer universal principles governing assembly pathway robustness and failure modes.

We will integrate: (i) cryo-EM structures of ribosome assembly intermediates and associated factors (EMDB, PDB), (ii) time-resolved rRNA processing and modification maps (RNA-seq and specialized datasets in GEO/SRA; MODOMICS for modifications), (iii) quantitative proteomics of assembly factors and ribosomal proteins under perturbations (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iv) genetic interaction and essentiality data for assembly factors (BioGRID, DepMap; yeast genetic interaction networks), and (v) subcellular localization/imaging of nucleolar subcompartments (Human Protein Atlas; IDR datasets).

Title: Emergent Ribosome Assembly Landscapes: Integrating Cryo-EM Intermediates, rRNA Processing Maps, and Proteomics to Explain Assembly Robustness

Abstract: Ribosome biogenesis involves mesoscale ribonucleoprotein intermediates (20–30 nm) that undergo coordinated folding, processing, and factor exchange. The emergent phenomenon is robust, directional assembly arising from collective interactions among rRNA, ribosomal proteins, and dozens of assembly factors—behavior not deducible from any single component. This project will synthesize structural and functional datasets to infer universal principles governing assembly pathway robustness and failure modes.

We will integrate: (i) cryo-EM structures of ribosome assembly intermediates and associated factors (EMDB, PDB), (ii) time-resolved rRNA processing and modification maps (RNA-seq and specialized datasets in GEO/SRA; MODOMICS for modifications), (iii) quantitative proteomics of assembly factors and ribosomal proteins under perturbations (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), (iv) genetic interaction and essentiality data for assembly factors (BioGRID, DepMap; yeast genetic interaction networks), and (v) subcellular localization/imaging of nucleolar subcompartments (Human Protein Atlas; IDR datasets).

Using probabilistic graphical models and energy landscape concepts, we will infer transition probabilities and identify bottlenecks. Comparative analysis across bacteria, yeast, and human will reveal conserved vs lineage-specific modules. We will also apply network controllability analysis to identify minimal sets of factors that steer assembly away from dead-end states.
