Expected insights include a cross-species atlas of assembly intermediates aligned to processing timelines, quantitative identification of fragile transitions, and mechanistic explanations for why some perturbations cause global collapse while others are compensated. Methodological advances include pipelines to harmonize heterogeneous cryo-EM intermediate annotations and to integrate structural states with sequencing-based processing data.

This project requires collaboration among cryo-EM structural biologists, RNA processing experts, network scientists, and disease geneticists, and it depends entirely on integrating numerous public datasets beyond any single lab’s scope. NCEMS support will enable community curation, open workflows, and trainee-led hackathons to produce reusable resources for understanding emergent mesoscale assembly in RNP machines.

Background: Ribosome biogenesis is among the most complex and consequential self-assembly processes in cells. It transforms long precursor rRNAs and dozens of ribosomal proteins into a functional ribonucleoprotein (RNP) machine through a coordinated sequence of rRNA folding, chemical modification, endo/exonucleolytic processing, and exchange of transient assembly factors. The key mesoscale entities in this process are pre-ribosomal particles—20–30 nm RNP intermediates—whose composition and structure evolve over time and space. At this scale, emergent properties arise: directionality (net forward progress despite reversibility of individual steps), robustness (successful assembly under genetic and environmental variability), and quality control (selective degradation or recycling of aberrant intermediates). These behaviors cannot be inferred from any single molecule (an rRNA helix, a ribosomal protein, or an assembly factor) because they result from collective interactions among many components and from the coupling of molecular events to subcellular organization.

Over the last decade, cryo-electron microscopy has produced a rich structural catalog of assembly intermediates in bacteria, yeast, and human. Deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) and Protein Data Bank (PDB), these structures reveal transient factor binding, rRNA domain docking order, and large-scale conformational checkpoints. In parallel, high-throughput sequencing has generated maps of rRNA processing and modification. Public repositories such as NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and Sequence Read Archive (SRA) contain RNA-seq, NET-seq, and specialized rRNA-focused datasets (including pulse-chase and time-course experiments) that quantify precursor rRNA species and processing kinetics under perturbations. MODOMICS and related resources compile known rRNA modifications and the enzymes that install them, providing an additional functional layer that influences folding and factor recruitment.

Quantitative proteomics has further expanded what is known. PRIDE/ProteomeXchange hosts datasets measuring the abundance of ribosomal proteins and assembly factors across conditions, including depletion of specific factors, stress responses, and disease contexts. These data provide system-level readouts of how perturbations redistribute factors, stall intermediates, or trigger compensatory pathways. Genetic interaction resources (BioGRID for curated interactions; comprehensive yeast genetic interaction networks from large-scale screens; and human essentiality/fitness screens such as DepMap) add a complementary view of functional redundancy and pathway buffering. Finally, imaging and localization data—e.g., the Human Protein Atlas and imaging datasets in the Image Data Resource (IDR)—provide spatial context, including nucleolar subcompartment localization and dynamic relocalization of assembly factors.

Despite the abundance of public data, key gaps remain because these datasets are rarely integrated. First, structural intermediates are often annotated inconsistently across studies, species, and labs (e.g., naming of states, factor occupancy, rRNA processing stage). Second, structural snapshots are difficult to align to processing timelines: an intermediate resolved by cryo-EM is not automatically linked to a specific rRNA cleavage or modification state measured by sequencing. Third, robustness and failure modes are not directly visible in any one dataset. A proteomics dataset may show accumulation of factors, but without structural and processing alignment it is hard to interpret which transition failed. Conversely, a structural intermediate may suggest a checkpoint, but without genetic interaction and perturbation data it is unclear whether that checkpoint is buffered by redundancy.

This proposal addresses these gaps through synthesis research: building a unified, cross-species “assembly state graph” that integrates structural states (EMDB/PDB), rRNA processing/modification trajectories (GEO/SRA, MODOMICS), proteomic perturbation responses (PRIDE/ProteomeXchange), genetic buffering (BioGRID, DepMap, yeast interaction networks), and mesoscale spatial organization (Human Protein Atlas, IDR). The central significance is that ribosome assembly is a canonical mesoscale emergence problem: a large RNP transitions through a landscape of partially ordered states, where local molecular interactions are shaped by global constraints (particle topology, factor availability, nucleolar organization) and where robustness emerges from modularity and redundancy.

Understanding these emergent principles has broad implications. Ribosome biogenesis defects underlie ribosomopathies and cancer-associated nucleolar stress, yet tissue-specific vulnerability remains puzzling. A synthesis framework can identify which transitions are fragile (low redundancy) and therefore more likely to produce disease phenotypes. More generally, ribosome assembly provides a tractable testbed for mesoscale emergence in RNP machines, with parallels to spliceosome assembly, ribonucleoprotein granules, and viral capsid maturation.

Existing public data now make this synthesis feasible at community scale. The breadth of cryo-EM intermediate structures, the depth of sequencing-based processing maps, and the diversity of perturbation proteomics and genetic interaction datasets collectively enable inference of transition structure, directionality constraints, and buffering mechanisms. However, harmonizing these heterogeneous resources requires coordinated expertise (structural biology, RNA biology, proteomics, network science, statistical modeling, and disease genetics) and substantial curation and computational infrastructure—well beyond a single lab. NCEMS support is essential to convene a multidisciplinary working group, build reusable open workflows, and produce a community resource that converts disparate public datasets into mechanistic insight about emergent mesoscale assembly robustness.

Research Questions: This project is organized around precise questions about how robust, directional ribosome assembly emerges from the collective behavior of mesoscale pre-ribosomal particles. We focus on inference and prediction using only publicly available data, with validation performed by cross-dataset consistency checks, held-out datasets, and benchmarking against well-established checkpoints described in the literature.

Research Question 1: What is the minimal set of mesoscale assembly states and transitions that explains the diversity of observed cryo-EM intermediates across studies and species?
Hypothesis 1A (state modularity): Cryo-EM intermediates can be represented as combinations of a limited number of conserved structural modules (e.g., rRNA domain docking modules, factor-binding modules) that recur across datasets, generating apparent diversity by recombination.
Measurable predictions: (i) clustering intermediates by factor occupancy and rRNA conformational descriptors will yield a small set of reproducible “module signatures” shared across independent studies; (ii) module presence will correlate with specific rRNA processing/modification milestones.
Validation using existing data: We will test reproducibility by training module definitions on a subset of EMDB/PDB entries and evaluating whether held-out intermediates from different labs/species map to the same module signatures with high confidence.

Research Question 2: How are structural intermediates coupled to rRNA processing and modification timelines to produce directionality?
Hypothesis 2A (processing-gated transitions): Directionality emerges because certain structural transitions are conditionally permitted only after specific rRNA cleavage or modification events, effectively gating transitions and preventing backtracking.
Measurable predictions: (i) inferred transition probabilities in the assembly state graph will increase sharply after specific processing events (e.g., cleavage at defined sites in pre-rRNA); (ii) perturbations that slow a processing step (as observed in GEO/SRA time courses) will shift occupancy toward pre-gated structural states (as observed in cryo-EM and proteomics).
Validation using existing data: We will align rRNA processing kinetics from published time courses with structural state occupancy inferred from cryo-EM and proteomics perturbation datasets; consistency will be assessed via likelihood-based model comparison (gated vs ungated models).

Research Question 3: What network features explain robustness to loss or fluctuation of assembly factors?
Hypothesis 3A (redundant, partially ordered pathways): Robustness arises from redundant alternative routes through the state graph, enabled by partially ordered modules and compensatory factor exchange.
Measurable predictions: (i) factors with many synthetic genetic interactions (yeast networks in BioGRID and large-scale screens) will correspond to nodes/edges with high alternative-path counts; (ii) proteomics under perturbation will show compensatory upregulation/relocalization of factors predicted to provide alternative routes.
Validation using existing data: We will compute redundancy metrics (k-shortest paths, edge-disjoint paths) and test correlation with genetic interaction degree and with proteomic compensation signatures across PRIDE datasets.

Research Question 4: How does mesoscale spatial organization in the nucleolus map onto the assembly state graph?
Hypothesis 4A (spatial compartmentalization of graph regions): Distinct nucleolar subcompartments correspond to contiguous regions of the state graph (sets of states/transitions) characterized by shared factor localization and processing events.
Measurable predictions: (i) factors localized to fibrillar center/dense fibrillar component/granular component (from Human Protein Atlas and IDR) will preferentially associate with early/mid/late graph regions; (ii) transitions that cross these regions will coincide with known trafficking or maturation steps.
Validation using existing data: We will integrate localization annotations with factor occupancy in structural states and test for enrichment of subcompartment labels along inferred pseudotime ordering of states.

Research Question 5: Why do disease-associated mutations produce tissue-specific vulnerability despite ubiquitous ribosome biogenesis?
Hypothesis 5A (fragile transitions drive vulnerability): Ribosomopathy-associated genes disproportionately affect low-redundancy transitions (bottlenecks) in the state graph, leading to context-dependent failure when factor supply or stress differs by tissue.
Measurable predictions: (i) genes implicated in ribosomopathies (curated from OMIM/ClinVar and literature) will be enriched among controllability-critical nodes/edges (network controllability and betweenness); (ii) DepMap dependency patterns will align with predicted bottlenecks, with cell lines exhibiting high dependency on bottleneck factors showing expression/proteomic signatures consistent with limited buffering.
Validation using existing data: Enrichment tests (permutation-based) will quantify whether disease genes map to fragile transitions more than expected by chance, controlling for annotation bias and gene essentiality.

Collectively, these questions and hypotheses aim to produce mechanistic insight into mesoscale emergence: how a large RNP navigates an energy- and information-constrained landscape, how gating and modularity produce directionality, how network redundancy yields robustness, how spatial compartmentalization organizes the landscape, and how fragility explains pathological failure modes—all inferred and tested through synthesis of existing public structural, sequencing, proteomic, genetic, and imaging data.

Methods: Overview and guiding principle (synthesis-only): All analyses will use publicly available datasets; no new experiments, samples, or data collection will be performed. The working group will focus on harmonization, integration, and modeling to infer an emergent assembly landscape across bacteria, yeast, and human.

1) Data sources (specific repositories)
Structural intermediates:
- Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB): density maps and metadata for pre-ribosomal particles.
- Protein Data Bank (PDB): atomic models and factor annotations for intermediates.
- UniProt: protein identifiers, domains, isoforms, and cross-references.
- Pfam/InterPro: domain architecture for assembly factors.

rRNA processing and modification:
- NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) and Sequence Read Archive (SRA): RNA-seq and specialized datasets reporting pre-rRNA intermediates, processing defects, and time courses.
- ENA (European Nucleotide Archive) as mirrored access where relevant.
- MODOMICS: curated rRNA modification types, positions, and enzymes.
- RiboMethSeq and related published datasets (as deposited in GEO/SRA) for 2’-O-methylation profiles.

Proteomics:
- PRIDE / ProteomeXchange: quantitative proteomics of ribosome biogenesis factors and ribosomal proteins under perturbations.

Genetic interactions and essentiality:
- BioGRID: physical and genetic interactions for assembly factors.
- DepMap (Cancer Dependency Map): CRISPR/RNAi gene dependency scores and expression for human cell lines.
- Published yeast genetic interaction matrices (available via repositories and supplementary data; indexed through BioGRID where possible).

Subcellular localization and imaging:
- Human Protein Atlas (HPA): subcellular localization annotations and images.
- Image Data Resource (IDR): curated microscopy datasets including nucleolar markers and protein localization.

Disease variant resources (for mapping, not experimentation):
- ClinVar and OMIM (where accessible) and curated literature lists of ribosomopathy genes.

2) Data ingestion, identifier harmonization, and curation
- Establish a unified identifier mapping layer across species using UniProt accessions, Ensembl gene IDs, and NCBI Gene IDs; orthology mapping via eggNOG or OrthoDB.
- Create controlled vocabularies for assembly factors, ribosomal proteins, and processing steps (cleavage sites, ITS/ETS regions) and map synonyms from EMDB/PDB metadata and publications.
- Structural metadata standardization: parse EMDB/PDB entries to extract factor occupancy, rRNA segments present, resolution, organism, and assigned maturation stage (when provided). Where stage labels are inconsistent, derive standardized labels via computed descriptors (below).

3) Feature extraction from cryo-EM intermediates
- Represent each structural intermediate as a feature vector capturing:
  a) Factor occupancy (binary/probabilistic from model annotations).
  b) rRNA conformational descriptors: presence/absence of major rRNA domains, inter-domain contacts, and global compaction metrics derived from atomic coordinates (PDB) or segmented maps (EMDB).
  c) Ribosomal protein incorporation status.
- Compute similarity between intermediates using mixed-type distance metrics (e.g., Jaccard for occupancy + continuous distances for geometric descriptors).
- Cluster intermediates using consensus clustering (e.g., hierarchical + Leiden on similarity graphs) to define reproducible state families. Stability assessed by bootstrap resampling across entries.

4) Aligning structural states to rRNA processing/modification timelines
- For each organism, curate processing events (cleavage sites, trimming steps, modification installation) from GEO/SRA datasets and literature-linked metadata.
- Where time-course data exist, infer processing pseudotime using probabilistic models (e.g., hidden Markov models on precursor abundance trajectories).
- Link structural states to processing stages by probabilistic matching: states with factor signatures known to associate with certain processing steps serve as priors; posterior assignments refined by maximizing agreement with perturbation datasets (below).

5) Integrating proteomics perturbations to estimate state occupancies
- From PRIDE/ProteomeXchange, select datasets with perturbations to assembly factors (knockdown/knockout/degradation systems already performed by original authors) and quantify differential abundance of relevant factors and ribosomal proteins.
- Use a deconvolution approach: treat observed proteomic changes as mixtures of underlying state occupancy shifts, where each state has an expected factor composition. Fit mixture weights via constrained regression (nonnegative least squares / Bayesian deconvolution) with uncertainty estimates.

6) Building the “assembly state graph” and inferring transitions
- Nodes: harmonized structural state families.
- Directed edges: candidate transitions constrained by (i) monotonicity of processing events (cleavage/modification order) and (ii) feasible factor exchange (gain/loss patterns).
- Infer edge weights (transition probabilities) using probabilistic graphical models:
  - Dynamic Bayesian networks / hidden Markov models where latent states are structural nodes and emissions are processing/proteomics observables.
  - Regularization to favor sparse, interpretable graphs.
- Energy landscape interpretation: define an effective potential over states derived from negative log stationary probabilities and transition asymmetries; identify barriers and metastable basins.

7) Robustness, redundancy, and controllability analyses
- Redundancy metrics: number of alternative paths between early and late states; edge-disjoint path counts; sensitivity of reachability to edge removal.
- Bottleneck detection: betweenness centrality, minimum cut sets, and transition entropy.
- Network controllability: apply structural controllability frameworks to identify minimal driver nodes/factors whose modulation (inferred from perturbation datasets) can steer the system away from dead-end basins.
- Map genetic interaction data (BioGRID, yeast matrices) onto graph features: test whether synthetic sick/lethal interactions concentrate around predicted bottlenecks or low-redundancy modules.

8) Spatial mapping to nucleolar subcompartments
- Use HPA/IDR localization annotations to label factors by nucleolar subcompartment when available.
- Compute enrichment of localization labels across graph regions (early/mid/late) and across modules; test compartment boundaries against predicted high-barrier transitions.

9) Disease mapping and cross-species comparison
- Map ribosomopathy genes/variants (ClinVar/OMIM/literature) onto factors and graph positions.
- Compare bacteria/yeast/human graphs via orthology-mapped modules; identify conserved cores vs lineage-specific branches.
- Use DepMap dependencies to test whether bottleneck factors show higher essentiality and context dependence.

10) Validation (no experiments)
- Cross-dataset validation: hold out subsets of cryo-EM intermediates or proteomics datasets and test predictive likelihood of the inferred graph.
- Positive controls: known checkpoints (e.g., established factor dependencies) should appear as high-barrier transitions or strong gating constraints.
- Negative controls: randomized identifier mappings and permuted interaction networks to ensure signals exceed null expectations.

11) Timeline and milestones (30 months; adaptable to NCEMS cycle)
Months 0–6: Working group kickoff; ontology/identifier layer; initial EMDB/PDB ingestion; first reproducible pipeline release.
Months 6–12: Structural feature extraction; consensus state families; first cross-species mapping draft; trainee-led hackathon on curation.
Months 12–18: Processing timeline inference from GEO/SRA; probabilistic alignment of states to processing; first assembly state graph per organism.
Months 18–24: Proteomics deconvolution; transition inference with graphical models; robustness and controllability analyses.
Months 24–30: Spatial compartment mapping; disease and DepMap integration; finalize atlas, manuscripts, and public resource portal.

12) Team composition (multilab, transdisciplinary)
- Cryo-EM structural biologists (annotation standards, structural descriptors).
- RNA processing/modification experts (processing event curation, interpretation).
- Proteomics specialists (dataset selection, normalization, batch correction).
- Network scientists/statisticians (graph inference, controllability, uncertainty quantification).
- Computational biologists/software engineers (workflow infrastructure, packaging).
- Disease geneticists/clinician-scientists (variant curation, ribosomopathy interpretation).
- Trainees (graduate students/postdocs) embedded across tasks, leading reproducible notebooks and hackathon modules.

NCEMS support is essential for convening these perspectives, sustaining community-scale curation, and providing neutral infrastructure for open, reproducible synthesis products that no single lab can produce alone.

Expected Outcomes: Deliverables (concrete, reusable products)
1) Cross-species Ribosome Assembly Atlas (public resource):
- A harmonized catalog of cryo-EM pre-ribosomal intermediates from EMDB/PDB, standardized with consistent factor occupancy, rRNA domain descriptors, and mapped organism/stage metadata.
- A curated library of rRNA processing and modification events linked to GEO/SRA accessions and MODOMICS entries, with standardized cleavage/modification nomenclature.
- Integrated perturbation summaries from PRIDE/ProteomeXchange that quantify how factor/ribosomal protein abundances shift across conditions.

2) Assembly State Graphs and inferred landscapes:
- For bacteria, yeast, and human: directed assembly state graphs with estimated transition probabilities, uncertainty intervals, and inferred gating constraints tied to processing events.
- Identification of metastable basins (stall states), high-barrier transitions, and alternative routes that contribute to robustness.

3) Robustness and controllability toolkit:
- Open-source software implementing redundancy metrics, bottleneck identification, and network controllability analyses tailored to assembly graphs.
- A standardized reporting format (“assembly graph schema”) enabling other groups to add additional RNP machines or new public datasets without reengineering.

4) Mechanistic synthesis insights (testable, literature-grounded explanations)
- A quantitative explanation of how partially ordered modules and redundant routes generate robust directionality at the mesoscale, even when individual steps are reversible.
- A map of which processing events act as gates and which factor exchanges are most predictive of forward progression.
- A spatially informed model linking nucleolar subcompartments to contiguous regions of the assembly landscape, providing a mesoscale bridge between molecular events and organelle-scale organization.

5) Disease-relevant interpretations without new experiments
- A ranked list of “fragile transitions” disproportionately impacted by ribosomopathy genes/variants, with mechanistic rationales grounded in graph redundancy and controllability.
- Integration with DepMap to contextualize which bottleneck factors show cell-type-dependent essentiality, offering a synthesis-based explanation for variable vulnerability.

Impact on understanding mesoscale emergent phenomena
This project directly advances NCEMS’s mission by explaining an emergent mesoscale phenomenon—robust, directional RNP assembly—through community-scale synthesis of heterogeneous public data. Rather than treating ribosome biogenesis as a linear pathway, we will formalize it as a landscape of states and transitions whose global properties (robustness, fragility, compartmentalization) emerge from network structure and gating constraints. The resulting framework will clarify how mesoscale particles navigate competing interactions, how redundancy is distributed across the landscape, and how the nucleolus organizes and constrains assembly.

Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
- Generalizable methodology: The assembly graph schema and inference pipeline will be transferable to other mesoscale assembly systems (spliceosome, proteasome assembly, viral capsid maturation, mitochondrial ribosome biogenesis), enabling broader synthesis efforts.
- Improved interpretability of perturbation datasets: By providing a state-based model, the project will help researchers interpret existing proteomics and transcriptomics perturbations in terms of which assembly transitions are affected.
- Training and workforce development: Trainees will gain experience in integrative analysis across structural biology, omics, and network science, aligned with NCEMS’s goal of training data-savvy scientists.

Enabling future research
While this project will not generate new data, it will substantially increase the value of existing datasets by making them interoperable and mechanistically interpretable. The atlas and tools will allow future investigators to:
- Rapidly map new public cryo-EM intermediates into a shared state space.
- Predict which processing steps or factors are likely to be compensable vs catastrophic when perturbed.
- Formulate targeted hypotheses for future experimental work (outside the scope of this proposal) based on identified bottlenecks and gates.

Dissemination plan
- Publications: at least two major manuscripts (methods/resource paper; biological synthesis insights across species and disease mapping), plus organism-specific or module-focused collaborative papers.
- Workshops: NCEMS-hosted working group meetings and open tutorials on using the atlas and pipelines.
- Public portal: a lightweight web interface (e.g., static site + downloadable artifacts) to browse state graphs, modules, and linked datasets, with programmatic access via APIs.

Long-term sustainability
- Persistent archiving: versioned releases deposited in Zenodo with DOIs; container images archived in public registries.
- Community governance: a contributor guide and curation policy enabling ongoing additions, with issue tracking for annotation disputes.
- Interoperability: adoption of standard identifiers (UniProt/Ensembl) and export formats (JSON schema, TSV, GraphML) to ensure the atlas remains usable as repositories evolve.

Overall, the project will produce a durable, open, community resource that transforms fragmented public data into a coherent mechanistic understanding of emergent mesoscale ribosome assembly landscapes and their robustness and failure modes.

Budget and Resources: Budget philosophy and NCEMS fit
This is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring coordinated curation, integration, and modeling across multiple public repositories. Funds are requested to support personnel time for data engineering and analysis, compute for large-scale integration (cryo-EM feature extraction and multi-omics modeling), and working-group activities that enable cross-disciplinary collaboration and trainee training. No funds are allocated for experiments, sample acquisition, or new data generation.

Personnel (primary cost driver)
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (computational focus; 2–3 years):
  1) Structural/graph modeling postdoc to lead cryo-EM feature extraction, state clustering, and graph inference.
  2) Multi-omics integration postdoc to lead processing timeline inference, proteomics deconvolution, and cross-dataset validation.
- 2 Graduate research assistants (part-time over 2–3 years):
  Support curation (ontology, identifier mapping), documentation, and notebook-based reproducibility; trainees will lead hackathon modules and tutorials.
- 1 Research software engineer / programmer analyst (50–100% FTE depending on award size):
  Build and maintain ETL pipelines, workflow automation (Snakemake/Nextflow), containerization, CI testing, and the public portal.
- PI/Co-PI effort (modest, distributed across participating labs):
  Coordination, scientific oversight, and integration across disciplines; emphasis on enabling team science rather than duplicative analysis.

Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or HPC allocations:
  Needed for batch downloading and parsing EMDB/PDB, computing structural descriptors at scale, running Bayesian/graphical models with resampling, and generating reproducible containers.
- Data storage and backup:
  Storage for derived feature matrices, intermediate files, and cached public datasets (within repository terms). Costs include secure backups and long-term archiving of releases.

Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings (2 in-person meetings per year, plus virtual meetings):
  Travel support for geographically distributed participants, with priority for trainees and early-career researchers and for inclusion of investigators from primarily undergraduate institutions and under-resourced institutions.
- Conference dissemination:
  Limited travel for presenting synthesis outputs at relevant meetings (e.g., ASCB, RNA Society, Gordon Conferences on Ribosome Biogenesis, cryo-EM meetings), emphasizing outreach and recruitment of contributors.

Workshops and training events
- Annual open workshop hosted through NCEMS:
  Hands-on training in using the atlas, running workflows, and contributing annotations; includes support for instructional materials, venue/virtual platform costs, and trainee participation.
- Trainee-led hackathons (1–2/year):
  Microgrants for trainee participation, facilitation, and compute to run reproducibility checks and curation sprints.

Open science infrastructure
- Zenodo archiving (no direct cost, but effort allocated):
  Personnel time to prepare versioned releases, metadata, and DOIs.
- Web dissemination:
  Minimal hosting costs for a static documentation/portal site (e.g., GitHub Pages) plus optional lightweight server costs if interactive graph browsing is implemented.

Justification relative to synthesis goals
Personnel support enables the intensive, expert curation and integration required to harmonize heterogeneous datasets and build validated assembly graphs—work that cannot be accomplished by a single lab. Compute resources are essential for scalable structural feature extraction and probabilistic modeling. Travel and workshops are integral to NCEMS’s working-group model, ensuring diverse expertise, training the next generation, and producing community-adopted standards. All budget categories directly support synthesis, integration, open dissemination, and workforce development, fully aligned with NCEMS funding requirements and the constraint of no new data generation.

criteria.justification: The proposal directly targets mesoscale emergent properties of ribosome biogenesis (directionality, robustness, failure modes) and frames them explicitly as arising from collective interactions among many components and spatial organization.

Integrating cryo-EM intermediates with rRNA processing/modification kinetics, proteomics perturbations, genetic buffering, and nucleolar spatial data into an inferred state graph is highly innovative and could yield broadly useful principles and resources, though similar “state landscape” ideas exist in adjacent systems.

The workflow is logically structured (harmonization → feature extraction → alignment → graph inference → validation) with appropriate statistical controls and holdout validation, but key steps (cross-species state comparability, deconvolution identifiability, and uncertainty propagation across layers) need sharper methodological specification to be fully convincing.

The 30-month plan is plausible for building organism-specific atlases and pipelines, but the full cross-species integration plus spatial compartment mapping and disease/DepMap interpretation is ambitious given expected heterogeneity, missingness, and curation burden across repositories.
The project is explicitly synthesis-only, relying entirely on public repositories and emphasizing integration, harmonization, and modeling rather than any new experimental data generation.

Major repositories and data types are clearly enumerated (EMDB/PDB, GEO/SRA, MODOMICS, PRIDE, BioGRID, DepMap, HPA/IDR, ClinVar/OMIM), but limitations are discussed mostly at a high level and would benefit from more explicit risk mitigation for sparse time courses, inconsistent cryo-EM annotations, batch effects in proteomics, and uneven availability of nucleolar subcompartment labels.

The proposal includes concrete open-science deliverables (versioned Zenodo releases, containers, CI-tested workflows, schemas, public portal, contributor governance, hackathons), though it could further specify licensing, data redistribution constraints (e.g., EMDB/PDB/GEO terms), and a reproducibility standard (e.g., required minimal metadata and benchmark suites).
The proposal centers entirely on explaining how macroscopic properties like robustness and directionality emerge from mesoscale interactions in ribosome assembly.

The timeline is well-structured with clear milestones, though the cross-species scope is ambitious and will require tight coordination of the multidisciplinary team.

The proposal directly and explicitly addresses mesoscale emergent phenomena, focusing on how robust, directional ribosome assembly emerges from collective interactions among rRNA, ribosomal proteins, and assembly factors. The 30-month timeline is ambitious given the scope of integrating five distinct data types across three species, building probabilistic models, and producing a comprehensive atlas. While milestones are well-defined, the complexity of data harmonization and the challenge of achieving consensus state definitions across heterogeneous cryo-EM datasets may require more time than allocated.

The proposal is an exemplary synthesis project that exclusively uses existing publicly available data from EMDB, PDB, GEO/SRA, PRIDE, BioGRID, DepMap, Human Protein Atlas, and other repositories. No new experimental data generation is proposed, and the integration plan across data types is comprehensive.

Data sources are explicitly and comprehensively identified with specific repository names and data types. The proposal acknowledges key limitations such as inconsistent annotations across cryo-EM studies and the challenge of aligning structural snapshots to processing timelines, though a more detailed discussion of data completeness and coverage gaps across species would strengthen this section.

The proposal demonstrates exemplary commitment to open science with detailed plans for Zenodo archiving with DOIs, containerized workflows, a public web portal, standardized export formats (JSON, TSV, GraphML), community governance with contributor guides, and trainee-led hackathons. The dissemination plan includes workshops, tutorials, and programmatic API access.
