Background: Mesoscale cell biology (approximately 10–1000 nm) is where molecular composition becomes collective material state. In this regime, the cytoplasm and nucleoplasm behave neither like dilute solution nor like a simple polymer melt; instead they exhibit emergent properties—effective viscosity, viscoelasticity, anomalous diffusion, and spatially heterogeneous crowding—that arise from the combined concentrations, sizes, shapes, interactions, and organization of proteins, RNAs, and macromolecular assemblies. These emergent physical states influence reaction kinetics, encounter rates, phase behavior, and spatial signaling, yet remain difficult to predict from the properties of individual molecules. Understanding how mesoscale material properties emerge from proteome composition is a fundamental challenge aligned with NCEMS’s vision: to explain how new system properties appear across scales, especially at the mesoscale where biomolecules give rise to organelle-level behaviors.

A large body of work has established that intracellular diffusion deviates from Brownian motion for many probes, showing subdiffusion or heterogeneous dynamics depending on probe size and binding (e.g., fractional Brownian motion or continuous-time random walk phenomenology). Fluorescence recovery after photobleaching (FRAP), fluorescence correlation spectroscopy (FCS), and single-particle tracking (SPT) studies have repeatedly demonstrated that diffusion coefficients can vary by orders of magnitude across compartments, cell types, and conditions, and that stress responses can globally slow diffusion. Parallel research in soft-matter and polymer physics provides mechanistic frameworks—obstruction models, effective medium theories, and viscoelastic models—that connect excluded volume and interaction potentials to transport. In vitro reconstitutions and simulations further show that mixtures of globular proteins, intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs), and ribonucleoprotein complexes can generate nontrivial rheology and anomalous diffusion. However, most quantitative links between composition and transport remain qualitative or system-specific.

At the same time, the data landscape has changed dramatically. Quantitative proteomics repositories such as ProteomeXchange (including PRIDE) and abundance compendia such as PaxDB provide organism- and condition-specific protein abundance estimates, including absolute copy numbers for many systems. Subcellular localization resources (Human Protein Atlas) and spatial proteomics datasets (e.g., hyperLOPIT and related fractionation-based localization maps deposited in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange) make it possible to estimate compartment-specific proteome composition rather than whole-cell averages. Structural databases (Protein Data Bank) and large-scale structure predictions (AlphaFold DB) enable estimation of protein size/shape descriptors relevant to excluded volume, while MobiDB provides disorder annotations that relate to soft interactions, entanglement-like effects, and binding promiscuity. Complex Portal and related resources curate stable assemblies and stoichiometries that influence mesoscale packing. Metabolomics resources such as Metabolomics Workbench provide measurements of osmolytes and metabolites that modulate hydration and macromolecular crowding.

Despite these advances, major gaps remain that are uniquely addressable by synthesis research. First, diffusion/viscosity measurements are scattered across publications, supplementary tables, and imaging repositories (e.g., Image Data Resource and BioImage Archive), with heterogeneous reporting standards (probe identity, size, temperature, cell cycle stage, analysis model, photophysics). This fragmentation prevents the community from building predictive models across systems. Second, proteome abundance and localization data are typically analyzed for pathways, not for their collective physical consequences. Third, existing models often treat crowding as a single scalar (e.g., volume fraction) and do not incorporate spatial heterogeneity and composition-dependent soft interactions (e.g., charge patterning, disorder content, oligomerization) that can create compartment-specific “crowding fields.” Finally, it is unclear whether cells maintain conserved “crowding setpoints” in specific compartments (cytosol vs nucleoplasm) across evolution and perturbation, or whether they tune material state as a regulatory layer.

This proposal addresses these gaps by synthesizing publicly available proteomics, spatial localization, structural/biophysical annotations, metabolomics, and imaging-derived transport measurements into a unified, open, community-scale resource and modeling framework. The significance is twofold. Conceptually, it reframes intracellular transport and reaction kinetics as emergent mesoscale outcomes of proteome organization, enabling mechanistic hypotheses about how cells regulate physical state to control biochemical networks. Practically, it provides predictive tools that allow researchers to infer diffusion regimes and effective viscosity landscapes from omics and localization data, supporting reinterpretation of phenotypes (e.g., slowed signaling under stress, altered metabolic flux) as consequences of mesoscale state shifts.

The project requires NCEMS-scale coordination because no single lab typically has (i) deep expertise in quantitative proteomics and spatial proteome mapping, (ii) biophysical microscopy and transport modeling, (iii) soft-matter theory for crowded heterogeneous media, and (iv) modern Bayesian/ML methods for calibration across heterogeneous datasets—nor the capacity to curate and harmonize the dispersed diffusion/viscosity literature into a reusable database with community standards. NCEMS support will enable working-group meetings, shared infrastructure, and open-science governance to produce durable, reusable synthesis products. By leveraging existing data only, the project turns the community’s accumulated measurements into a coherent framework for understanding how mesoscale crowding emerges and how it regulates cellular function.

Research Questions: This working group will address the overarching question: Can emergent mesoscale transport properties (effective viscosity, diffusion coefficients, and anomalous diffusion exponents) be predicted from compartment-specific proteome composition and organization across organisms and conditions using only existing public data? We decompose this into precise, testable research questions with measurable predictions.

RQ1: Are there conserved compartment-specific “crowding setpoints” across cell types and organisms? Here, a “setpoint” refers to a constrained range of inferred excluded-volume fraction and/or calibrated effective viscosity in a given compartment (e.g., cytosol, nucleoplasm, mitochondrial matrix) despite large variation in proteome identity and abundance. 
H1: For major compartments, inferred crowding metrics (e.g., effective volume fraction, calibrated obstruction parameter, or Bayesian posterior mean viscosity) fall within a narrow, conserved range across diverse eukaryotes under baseline conditions, even when total protein concentration differs. 
Predictions: (i) After harmonization for temperature and probe class, diffusion coefficients for standardized probe categories (e.g., GFP-like proteins, ribosomes, endogenous enzymes) will cluster by compartment more strongly than by species; (ii) inferred crowding-field parameters will show lower variance within compartments across species than across compartments within a species. 
Validation using existing data: We will test clustering and variance partitioning using diffusion/FRAP/FCS/SPT datasets from IDR/BioImage Archive and literature, aligned with compartment proteome estimates derived from Human Protein Atlas and spatial proteomics (hyperLOPIT) plus abundance from PaxDB/ProteomeXchange.

RQ2: Which proteome features disproportionately control emergent viscosity and anomalous diffusion? 
H2: A small number of “crowding hubs”—protein classes with high abundance and strong soft interactions—dominate mesoscale transport outcomes. Candidate classes include ribosomal proteins/ribosomes, chaperones, cytoskeletal polymers, and IDP-rich proteins. 
Predictions: (i) Models that include features capturing IDP content (MobiDB), multivalency/oligomerization (Complex Portal), and assembly size (PDB/AlphaFold-derived hydrodynamic radius proxies) will outperform models based on total protein concentration alone in predicting diffusion and anomalous exponents; (ii) Shapley-value or posterior inclusion analyses will identify consistent high-impact features across datasets (e.g., fraction of mass in large complexes; fraction of residues disordered; abundance of ribosome-associated proteins). 
Validation: We will evaluate predictive performance via cross-dataset validation (train on one organism/condition set, test on another) and compare nested models (total concentration only vs concentration + composition + interaction proxies).

RQ3: Can condition-dependent shifts in mesoscale diffusion landscapes be inferred from omics and metabolomics without direct transport measurements? 
H3: Stress, cell cycle, and differentiation shift mesoscale transport primarily through coordinated changes in (i) proteome mass reallocation to large assemblies and (ii) osmolyte/metabolite profiles that modulate hydration and effective interactions. 
Predictions: (i) In conditions with known global slowing of diffusion (e.g., osmotic stress, heat shock), proteomics will show increased abundance of chaperones and/or stress granule-associated proteins and increased predicted disorder/multivalency; (ii) metabolomics will show shifts in osmolytes (e.g., trehalose in yeast; amino acid/osmolyte changes in mammalian cells) that correlate with inferred viscosity parameters. 
Validation: We will link condition-labeled proteomics (ProteomeXchange) and metabolomics (Metabolomics Workbench) to transport measurements where available; where transport measurements are absent, we will test whether the inferred crowding-field shifts align with known qualitative phenotypes reported in literature (e.g., slowed cytosolic diffusion under hyperosmotic shock) and with independent proxies such as measured cell volume changes or macromolecular concentration estimates when reported.

RQ4: Do mesoscale “crowding fields” exhibit spatial heterogeneity that is predictable from spatial proteomics and compartment architecture? 
H4: Spatial proteomics supports the inference of heterogeneous crowding fields within broad compartments (e.g., perinuclear vs peripheral cytosol; nucleolus vs nucleoplasm), and these fields predict spatially varying diffusion regimes observed by SPT/FRAP. 
Predictions: (i) Where spatial proteomics provides multi-localization probabilities or gradient-like distributions, inferred local excluded volume will correlate with spatially resolved diffusion maps in imaging datasets; (ii) compartments enriched for large complexes and RNA-binding proteins will show stronger subdiffusion (lower anomalous exponent) than compartments dominated by small globular enzymes at similar total concentration. 
Validation: We will use imaging datasets with spatially resolved transport (IDR/BioImage Archive) and align them to compartment/subcompartment annotations; model fit will be assessed by posterior predictive checks and spatial correlation metrics.

Mechanistically, these hypotheses aim to establish that mesoscale transport is not merely a byproduct of “how much protein is present” but an emergent state governed by compositional allocation to assemblies, disorder-mediated soft interactions, and spatial organization. The synthesis will yield quantitative, falsifiable relationships between proteome organization and transport parameters, enabling a predictive mesoscale biophysics layer that can be integrated with signaling and metabolic models without generating any new experimental data.

Methods: Overview and synthesis strategy. The project will build an integrated, analysis-ready knowledge base linking compartment-specific proteome composition to measured transport/viscosity outcomes, then fit mechanistic and data-driven models that map composition to emergent mesoscale parameters. All activities are synthesis: we will only download, curate, standardize, and analyze existing publicly available datasets and literature supplements; no new experiments, samples, or data generation will be performed.

1) Data sources (public repositories and curated literature)
A. Quantitative proteomics and absolute abundance
- ProteomeXchange Consortium datasets, primarily via PRIDE (mass spectrometry raw/processed files and sample metadata).
- PaxDB (integrated protein abundance and copy-number estimates across organisms and tissues).
- Where available, organism-specific absolute proteome resources linked from PaxDB and ProteomeXchange metadata (e.g., yeast and bacterial absolute proteomes deposited publicly).
B. Spatial localization and compartment abundance
- Human Protein Atlas (subcellular localization annotations; where quantitative, use intensity/abundance proxies).
- Spatial proteomics datasets such as hyperLOPIT and related subcellular fractionation maps deposited in PRIDE/ProteomeXchange (multi-compartment probability assignments).
- UniProt subcellular location annotations (as a harmonization layer for non-human organisms).
C. Transport/viscosity and anomalous diffusion measurements
- Image Data Resource (IDR) and BioImage Archive for deposited FRAP/SPT/FCS imaging datasets and derived measurements when provided.
- Published datasets with diffusion coefficients/anomalous exponents in supplementary tables; we will curate these into a structured database with explicit provenance (DOI, figure/table, analysis method).
- When repositories provide raw trajectories or time series, we will reanalyze using standardized, published algorithms (analysis of existing data is permitted; no new data collection).
D. Metabolomics and osmolytes
- Metabolomics Workbench (condition-labeled metabolite profiles; osmolytes and metabolites affecting hydration and crowding).
E. Structural and biophysical annotations
- Protein Data Bank (PDB) for experimentally determined structures and complex assemblies.
- AlphaFold Protein Structure Database for predicted structures to estimate size/shape proxies broadly.
- MobiDB for intrinsic disorder annotations and disorder content.
- Complex Portal for curated macromolecular complexes and stoichiometries.
- Optional supporting resources: BioGRID/IntAct for interaction degree (as a proxy for binding propensity), used cautiously to avoid confounding by study bias.

2) Harmonization and integration
A. Entity resolution
- Map proteins across datasets using UniProt accessions and gene identifiers; maintain organism-specific namespaces.
- Standardize compartments using Gene Ontology Cellular Component (GO-CC) terms; build a compartment ontology mapping (e.g., “cytosol” vs “cytoplasm” vs “cytoplasmic matrix”) with explicit rules.
B. Condition and metadata normalization
- Create a controlled vocabulary for conditions (stress type, osmolarity, temperature, cell cycle stage, differentiation state) using existing ontologies where possible (e.g., EFO terms in sample metadata).
- Standardize units: diffusion coefficients (µm^2/s), viscosity (Pa·s or cP), temperature (K), probe size (nm), timescales, and analysis model used.
C. Measurement-model harmonization
- For FRAP, record fitting model (single exponential, diffusion model, reaction-diffusion) and extract comparable summary parameters (effective diffusion, mobile fraction) with uncertainty.
- For SPT, standardize MSD computation windows and fit anomalous diffusion MSD ~ t^α to obtain α and generalized diffusion coefficient; apply published localization-error corrections when raw trajectories are available.
- For FCS, record model (1- vs 2-component, anomalous exponent) and extract comparable parameters.
D. Data quality scoring
- Assign quality flags based on metadata completeness, probe identity, calibration reporting, and replicate availability. Analyses will be repeated under “strict” and “broad” inclusion criteria to assess robustness.

3) Constructing mesoscale “crowding fields” from composition
A. Compartment proteome composition
- For each organism/condition/compartment, estimate protein concentration distributions using absolute abundance (PaxDB/ProteomeXchange) combined with compartment assignment probabilities (hyperLOPIT/HPA/UniProt).
B. Size/shape and excluded-volume proxies
- Estimate hydrodynamic radius proxies from PDB/AlphaFold structures using computational geometry (e.g., radius of gyration, solvent-excluded volume) and sequence-based predictors when structures are missing.
- Incorporate oligomerization/complex membership (Complex Portal) to adjust effective particle sizes and volume occupancy.
C. Soft interaction and viscoelasticity proxies
- Disorder fraction and low-complexity regions (MobiDB) as predictors of soft interactions and transient binding.
- Interaction propensity proxies (Complex membership counts; curated interactions) to represent transient sticking that can induce subdiffusion.
D. Field representation
- Define a compartment-level crowding state vector: total macromolecular volume fraction estimate, fraction in large complexes, mean/variance of size distribution, disorder-weighted concentration, and an interaction “stickiness” index.
- Where spatial proteomics supports subcompartment gradients, represent the crowding field as a coarse spatial mixture (e.g., two- or three-zone model) rather than a single scalar.

4) Modeling and inference
A. Mechanistic coarse-grained models
- Obstruction/effective-medium models: relate excluded volume to effective diffusion (e.g., D/D0 as a function of volume fraction and size ratio).
- Viscoelastic/anomalous diffusion models: fractional Brownian motion (FBM) and generalized Langevin approaches to connect α to viscoelastic parameters; treat α as an emergent parameter influenced by disorder-weighted concentration and interaction proxies.
B. Bayesian calibration
- Use hierarchical Bayesian models to calibrate mapping from composition features to observed diffusion/viscosity, with random effects for lab/assay/probe and explicit temperature correction.
- Output posterior distributions for crowding parameters and quantify uncertainty propagation from proteomics and localization uncertainty.
C. Machine learning for prediction and feature attribution
- Train supervised models (e.g., gradient-boosted trees, elastic net, and Bayesian additive regression trees) to predict (D, α, viscosity) from crowding state vectors.
- Use cross-validation stratified by dataset/lab to avoid leakage; evaluate generalization across organisms and compartments.
- Interpretability: SHAP values and Bayesian variable inclusion to identify “crowding hubs” and key compositional drivers.

5) Validation without new experiments
- Cross-dataset validation: train on one repository/literature subset and test on independent subsets.
- Positive controls: known trends such as slower diffusion for larger probes, and reported diffusion slowdowns under osmotic stress; verify that models recover these directions.
- Consistency checks: compare inferred viscosity against independent published viscosity estimates (where available) and against metabolomics-predicted osmotic shifts.
- Posterior predictive checks: simulate expected diffusion distributions from inferred crowding fields and compare to observed distributions.

6) Timeline and milestones (30 months; adaptable to 24–36 months)
Months 0–6: Working group kickoff; finalize metadata standards; build ingestion pipelines; initial curation of diffusion/viscosity literature; release v0 schema and minimal dataset.
Months 7–12: Integrate proteomics + localization + structural annotations; compute compartment crowding state vectors; release v1 integrated dataset and documentation.
Months 13–18: Implement mechanistic and Bayesian calibration models; perform cross-dataset validation; preprint on harmonized database and baseline models.
Months 19–24: ML prediction models; feature attribution and “crowding hub” identification; cross-species/condition analyses; release v2 tools and notebooks.
Months 25–30: Community workshop; finalize manuscripts; harden software (containers/workflows); deposit final database snapshots; sustainability handoff plan.

7) Team composition and roles (multidisciplinary, multi-lab)
- Quantitative proteomics experts: curate ProteomeXchange/PaxDB mappings, normalization, batch effects.
- Spatial proteomics/localization experts: interpret hyperLOPIT/HPA, compartment ontology mapping.
- Biophysical microscopy and transport analysts: standardize FRAP/FCS/SPT parameter extraction and error models.
- Soft-matter/biophysical theorists: guide obstruction/viscoelastic modeling and interpretation.
- Statistical learning/Bayesian modelers: hierarchical calibration, uncertainty quantification, ML generalization tests.
- Research software engineers/data curators: build pipelines, database, APIs, documentation, and reproducible workflows.
- Trainees (graduate students/postdocs): lead curation sprints, model development, and open training materials.

NCEMS support is essential to convene these perspectives, support sustained curation and standard setting, and produce community-scale synthesis products that exceed the capacity of any single laboratory.

Expected Outcomes: This synthesis project will deliver a set of durable, open resources and mechanistic insights that collectively advance understanding of emergent mesoscale physical regulation in cells.

1) Primary deliverables
A. An open, curated database of intracellular transport and material-state measurements
- A structured “Cellular Transport & Crowding” database containing diffusion coefficients, anomalous exponents, FRAP recovery parameters, and viscosity estimates extracted from Image Data Resource (IDR), BioImage Archive, and published supplements.
- Rich metadata: probe identity and size class, compartment, organism/cell type, condition, temperature, acquisition modality (FRAP/FCS/SPT), analysis model used, uncertainty/replicates, and provenance.
- A community reporting template (machine-readable) for future deposition of diffusion/viscosity results, aligned with existing imaging metadata standards where possible.
B. An integrated multi-omics “crowding state” atlas
- For each organism/condition/compartment represented, a derived crowding state vector combining: absolute abundance (PaxDB/ProteomeXchange), compartment allocation (Human Protein Atlas/hyperLOPIT), structural size proxies (PDB/AlphaFold DB), disorder content (MobiDB), and complex membership (Complex Portal), with metabolomics covariates (Metabolomics Workbench) when available.
- Versioned snapshots deposited in long-term repositories with clear licensing and citations.
C. Reproducible modeling toolkit
- Open-source pipelines to (i) ingest and harmonize datasets, (ii) compute crowding fields/state vectors, (iii) fit mechanistic and Bayesian calibration models, and (iv) train ML predictors with robust cross-dataset validation.
- Prebuilt notebooks demonstrating key analyses, including uncertainty-aware predictions and feature attribution.

2) Scientific outcomes: mechanistic insights into emergent mesoscale regulation
A. Evidence for (or against) conserved crowding setpoints
- Quantitative assessment of whether cytosol, nucleoplasm, and other compartments maintain constrained ranges of inferred crowding/viscosity across species and baseline conditions.
- If supported, this would suggest that maintaining mesoscale material state is a conserved cellular objective, akin to homeostasis of pH or ion concentration.
B. Identification of “crowding hubs” and compositional control knobs
- A ranked set of protein classes and compositional features that disproportionately influence emergent viscosity and anomalous diffusion (e.g., allocation to ribosomes/large complexes, disorder-weighted concentration, chaperone abundance).
- Mechanistic interpretation linking these hubs to soft interactions and viscoelasticity, providing a physical layer to complement genetic/pathway-centric views.
C. Predictive links from omics to transport landscapes
- Validated models that predict diffusion regimes (D and α) for probe classes given compartment composition, enabling inference in systems where transport has not been directly measured.
- Condition-dependent predictions (stress, cell cycle, differentiation) that connect proteome/metabolome shifts to mesoscale physical consequences, reframing diverse phenotypes as material-state transitions.

3) Broader impacts on molecular and cellular biology
- Integrative understanding: The project will connect proteome allocation and organization to emergent transport constraints that shape signaling, metabolism, and assembly dynamics.
- Reinterpretation of phenotypes: Many reported changes in pathway activity under stress may be partially explained by altered encounter rates and diffusion-limited kinetics; our atlas will help researchers test these ideas quantitatively.
- Methodological advancement: By combining hierarchical Bayesian calibration with mechanistic crowding models and interpretable ML, the project will provide a general blueprint for synthesizing heterogeneous biophysical measurements.

4) Enabling future research (without committing to new experiments)
- The database and standards will lower the barrier for the community to reuse existing imaging datasets and to deposit future measurements in interoperable form.
- The crowding state atlas can be integrated downstream with existing systems biology models (e.g., metabolic network simulations) to incorporate diffusion/viscosity constraints.
- The identified “crowding hubs” will generate testable hypotheses for future experimentalists, but this project itself will not perform experimental validation.

5) Dissemination and sustainability
- Publications: at least two major manuscripts (database/standards paper; cross-species mechanistic/predictive modeling paper) plus method notes.
- Workshops: an NCEMS-hosted training workshop on “Synthesis biophysics of intracellular transport,” including hands-on sessions using the released pipelines.
- Persistent hosting: database snapshots and DOIs via Zenodo; code on GitHub/GitLab; container images on public registries; documentation site (e.g., ReadTheDocs).
- Sustainability plan: governance for community contributions (issue trackers, contribution guidelines, schema versioning), and coordination with existing repository communities (IDR/BioImage Archive, ProteomeXchange) to align metadata fields and reduce duplication.

Collectively, these outcomes will establish protein crowding as a quantitatively predictable, emergent mesoscale regulator and provide the community-scale synthesis infrastructure needed to make intracellular material-state biology a routine, data-driven component of molecular and cellular science.

Budget and Resources: This project is a community-scale synthesis effort requiring sustained curation, multi-repository integration, and advanced modeling. The budget emphasizes personnel time for data harmonization and research software engineering, computational resources for large-scale reanalysis and model fitting, and NCEMS-facilitated collaboration and training.

1) Personnel
- 2 Postdoctoral researchers (2.0 FTE total across participating labs): One focused on biophysical transport modeling (FRAP/FCS/SPT harmonization; mechanistic and Bayesian models) and one focused on proteome/spatial proteomics integration (ProteomeXchange/PaxDB normalization; localization mapping; feature engineering). Postdocs are essential because the project requires deep cross-domain synthesis rather than narrow single-dataset analysis.
- 1 Research software engineer / data curator (1.0 FTE): Builds and maintains ingestion pipelines, database schema, APIs/exports, workflow automation (Snakemake/Nextflow), CI/testing, and documentation. This role is critical for producing reusable community infrastructure.
- 1 Graduate student (0.5–1.0 FTE equivalent): Supports literature curation, quality scoring, and development of training notebooks; gains workforce training in data-centric biophysical cell biology.
- Part-time PI/co-PI effort across multiple institutions: Provides domain oversight (proteomics, spatial proteomics, soft-matter physics, statistical learning), ensures cross-lab integration, and mentors trainees. The multi-PI structure reflects the transdisciplinary nature of the work.

2) Computing resources
- Cloud computing credits and/or institutional HPC allocations: Needed for (i) downloading and processing large imaging datasets from IDR/BioImage Archive, (ii) structural feature computation at scale from AlphaFold DB/PDB, and (iii) Bayesian hierarchical model fitting and cross-validation.
- Data storage: Budget for secure, backed-up storage of intermediate processed files and cache layers (while respecting that authoritative raw data remain in source repositories). Emphasis is on storing derived, analysis-ready representations and provenance.

3) Travel and collaboration
- Working group meetings at NCEMS (or NCEMS-supported venues): Funds for travel and lodging for diverse participants (multiple institutions, career stages, and geographic locations). In-person synthesis meetings accelerate agreement on standards, resolve integration bottlenecks, and support trainee networking.
- Conference dissemination: Targeted travel for presenting results and standards at relevant meetings (computational biology, proteomics, biophysics), maximizing adoption.

4) Workshops and training events
- Budget for at least one hands-on training workshop (hybrid when possible): venue/AV support (if needed), training materials preparation, and trainee participation support.
- Curation sprints and hackathons: modest support for coordination, facilitation, and participant access (e.g., temporary compute accounts) to broaden community contribution.

5) Open science infrastructure
- DOI and archival costs are minimized by using Zenodo and existing repositories, but budget supports: documentation hosting (if needed), automated testing infrastructure, and maintenance time to ensure long-term usability.
- Accessibility and interoperability: resources for implementing standard exports (CSV/Parquet), lightweight APIs, and metadata validation tools.

6) Justification relative to synthesis goals and NCEMS need
The requested resources are necessary because the core challenge is not a single analysis but the creation of a reusable, community-scale synthesis product: a harmonized transport/viscosity database linked to multi-omics and structural annotations, with validated models and reproducible pipelines. This scope exceeds a typical single-lab effort due to heterogeneous data types (omics, imaging, structure, metabolomics), the need for standard setting and provenance-aware curation, and the requirement to produce open, maintained infrastructure and training materials. NCEMS support uniquely enables the coordination, convening power, and open-science scaffolding required to deliver these outcomes without generating any new experimental data.

criteria.justification: The proposal directly targets mesoscale emergent properties (effective viscosity, anomalous diffusion, heterogeneous crowding) and explicitly frames them as collective outcomes of proteome organization across 10–1000 nm scales.

Integrating spatial proteomics, structural/disorder annotations, metabolomics, and heterogeneous transport measurements to predict diffusion regimes from omics is highly innovative and could establish a broadly useful “material-state” layer for cell biology, though success depends on data harmonization quality.

The plan is methodologically well-structured (entity resolution, ontology mapping, quality scoring, hierarchical Bayesian calibration, cross-dataset validation), but key modeling assumptions (e.g., mapping from AlphaFold-derived size proxies and disorder to effective interactions/viscoelasticity) may be difficult to justify uniformly across assays and probe types.

The 30-month timeline is plausible for initial database and baseline models, but the full cross-species/condition “crowding field” atlas plus robust reanalysis of diverse FRAP/FCS/SPT datasets and community standards development is ambitious and likely to encounter metadata and comparability bottlenecks.
The project is explicitly and exclusively based on publicly available datasets and literature-derived measurements, with analysis and reanalysis of existing imaging data as the primary work product.

Major repositories are clearly specified (ProteomeXchange/PRIDE, PaxDB, HPA, IDR/BioImage Archive, Metabolomics Workbench, PDB/AlphaFold, MobiDB, Complex Portal) and heterogeneity is acknowledged, but limitations around sparse matched condition metadata, assay-specific biases, and compartment mapping uncertainty could be more explicitly quantified with fallback strategies.

The proposal includes concrete open-science deliverables (versioned database snapshots with DOIs, open-source pipelines, containers, documentation, reporting templates, workshops, and governance for community contributions) aligned with reproducibility and team science.
The proposal is exceptionally relevant, focusing directly on how mesoscale physical properties like viscosity and crowding emerge from collective proteome behavior.
The concept of mapping 'crowding fields' and identifying 'crowding hubs' via synthesis is groundbreaking and addresses a critical gap between omics and physical cell biology.
The methodology is highly rigorous, employing Bayesian calibration, coarse-grained physical models, and robust validation strategies like cross-dataset testing.
The timeline and milestones are realistic and well-structured, though the harmonization of heterogeneous biophysical data remains an ambitious challenge.
The project is an exemplary synthesis effort, explicitly stating it will use only existing public data from diverse, well-defined repositories.
Data sources are identified with high specificity (e.g., PRIDE, IDR, PaxDB), and limitations regarding data heterogeneity are thoroughly addressed with mitigation strategies.
The proposal demonstrates exemplary commitment through plans for open databases, reproducible pipelines, community standards, and long-term hosting via Zenodo and GitHub.

The proposal directly and explicitly addresses mesoscale emergent phenomena, focusing on how collective protein concentrations give rise to emergent properties like effective viscosity, anomalous diffusion, and spatially heterogeneous crowding at the 10-1000 nm scale. This is precisely the type of emergence the funding call targets.

The approach of synthesizing proteomics, spatial localization, structural data, and transport measurements to predict emergent mesoscale properties is highly innovative. The concept of 'crowding hubs' and conserved 'crowding setpoints' represents significant conceptual advancement, though some individual components build on established frameworks.

The methodology is well-articulated with clear hierarchical Bayesian calibration, mechanistic coarse-grained models, and machine learning approaches. The validation strategy using cross-dataset validation and posterior predictive checks is sound, though some aspects of harmonizing heterogeneous diffusion measurements may prove more challenging than anticipated.

The 30-month timeline is ambitious given the scope of data harmonization across multiple heterogeneous repositories and the complexity of building community standards. While milestones are well-defined, the literature curation of scattered diffusion/viscosity measurements and achieving consensus on reporting standards may require more time than allocated.

The proposal is exemplary in its synthesis focus, explicitly stating it will only use existing publicly available data with no new experimental data generation. The integration plan across proteomics, spatial localization, structural databases, metabolomics, and imaging-derived transport measurements is comprehensive.

Data sources are explicitly and comprehensively identified (ProteomeXchange, PaxDB, Human Protein Atlas, hyperLOPIT, IDR, BioImage Archive, Metabolomics Workbench, PDB, AlphaFold DB, MobiDB, Complex Portal). The proposal acknowledges heterogeneity in reporting standards but could more explicitly address potential gaps in coverage across organisms and conditions.

The proposal demonstrates exemplary commitment to open science with detailed plans for open databases, reproducible pipelines, versioned snapshots on Zenodo, GitHub/GitLab code repositories, container images, documentation, community contribution guidelines, and explicit sustainability planning for long-term maintenance.

title_norm: maitool - llm-powered bioinformatics tools for microbiome analysis
title: MaiTool - LLM-powered bioinformatics tools for microbiome analysis
author: Human
abstract_original: Large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and BioGPT have revolutionized how researchers engage with scientific literature, offering capabilities such as extracting insights, summarizing methodologies, and identifying relevant publications. These models have applications in microbiome research, where they can assist in identifying datasets in repositories like MGnify and MG-RAST. However, LLMs lack the ability to directly analyze datasets, necessitating integration with bioinformatics tools to enable robust computational analysis. This project aims to develop MaiTool, a graphical interface that combines LLM capabilities with bioinformatics workflows for microbiome and ancient DNA research. MaiTool will enable users to explore publications, access public datasets via APIs, and perform dynamic analyses, integrating quality control measures to enhance reliability. Existing GPT systems (e.g., BioGPT, BioMedLM, and GeneGPT) will be evaluated and fine-tuned for microbiome applications. We will assess repositories such as HMP, IMG/M, and SRA for their suitability and develop APIs for seamless data access and integration. By addressing queries such as studies involving specific taxa, MaiTool will allow LLMs to retrieve literature while bioinformatics pipelines analyze and visualize dataset profiles. This approach aims to advance interdisciplinary research workflows and establish a new standard for AI-driven bioinformatics.
full_draft_original: Introduction and Goals The rise of large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT and BioGPT has revolutionized how researchers engage with scientific publications. These models excel at understanding complex queries, enabling intelligent data retrieval tailored to project-specific needs. For instance, they can extract insights from publications, summarize methodologies, and, in the area of microbiome research, say, identify relevant datasets in repositories like MGnify and MG-RAST. However, the direct analysis of datasets remains beyond the core capabilities of such systems. Integrating LLMs with traditional bioinformatics tools offers a promising solution, bridging the gap between natural language understanding and robust computational analysis. This integration could enable on-the-fly analyses of microbiome data while incorporating essential components like quality control to flag potential issues with datasets early in the pipeline. By combining LLMs’ contextual understanding with the computational power of bioinformatics tools, researchers could streamline workflows, ensuring efficient access to both published findings and actionable data. This project aims to develop a graphical interface “MaiTool” that facilitates the exploration of microbiome-related publications, provides seamless access to publicly available data, integrates quality control measures, and enables dynamic lightweight analyses. Such a system will empower researchers to make informed decisions efficiently, fostering innovation and collaboration in microbiome research and beyond. While the primary focus is on microbiome science, we also plan to explore extensions to computational challenges in analyzing ancient DNA sequences, including the microbiome analysis of ancient DNA samples. Proposed Activities: Data Collection, Curation, and Analysis Framework We propose to evaluate various GPT systems (BioGPT, BioMedLM and GeneGPT) to determine their effectiveness in assisting researchers with engaging and extracting insights from the scientific literature. Building on this foundation, we will identify 5–10 key use cases where the integration of bioinformatics tools—focused on quality assurance, data visualization, and lightweight computational analysis—can enhance the relevance and utility of the results. This approach aims to create a synergistic system that combines the contextual understanding of GPT models with the analytical power of bioinformatics to deliver targeted, actionable insights for microbiome research. In addition to evaluating existing GPT systems for their applicability in microbiome research, we will explore the feasibility of enhancing their performance through two approaches: either setting up our own large language model (LLM) tailored to specific microbiome research needs or fine-tuning existing open-source models. This exploration will help determine the optimal balance between leveraging pre-trained models and creating customized solutions to support advanced analysis and research workflows. In microbiome research, several public repositories provide access to microbiome data. Key repositories include MGnify, MG-RAST, the Human Microbiome Project (HMP), the Microbiome Atlas of Mothers and Infants (MAMI), the Integrated Microbial Genomes and Microbiomes system (IMG/M) and the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) from NCBI (further please see Data Sources Table), which is the most comprehensive resource for raw sequencing data. We will evaluate each of these repositories to assess their suitability as sources of analysis results, focusing on their data accessibility, quality, and relevance to specific research needs. Additionally, we plan to develop software tools that leverage the APIs provided by these repositories to facilitate seamless access, integration, and utilization of their datasets within our system. This will enable efficient retrieval and analysis of microbiome data, supporting advanced research workflows. As an example, consider a user interested in determining whether there are studies that include a specific microbiome species of interest, such as the keystone gut species Christensenella minuta or oral species Methanobrevibacter oralis. Using the proposed system, a GPT model would first identify relevant publications that mention this species, extracting key information such as study descriptions, methodologies, and findings and data accessions from the literature. Simultaneously, using the reported accessions, a bioinformatics pipeline could access taxonomic profiles for the associated studies by accessing public microbiome datasets (along with metadata) through APIs. The pipeline may perform additional analyses, such as generating visualizations or conducting statistical analyses to explore patterns and relationships involving C. minuta. In addition, the GPT can provide a pipeline that the user can run themselves. Preliminary Data, Tools and Analytical Approaches We will conduct a systematic investigation of several GPT models, including BioGPT, BioMedLM, and GeneGPT, to evaluate their suitability for applications in microbiome analysis. For each model, we will assess its capabilities and explore the potential for fine-tuning to enhance support for data analysis tasks. Simultaneously, we will examine key microbiome data resources, including MG-RAST, HMP, IMG/M, MAMI, and datasets hosted at NCBI. This evaluation will focus on methods for extracting data, identifying analyses that can be performed dynamically, and establishing effective communication with the APIs provided by each resource. A third focus of our activities will be determining the best approach for implementing the interactive exploration tool MaiTool. MaiTool will serve as the primary interface for users, connecting seamlessly to an API for tasks such as LLM usage, data retrieval, and lightweight microbiome analysis. We intend to develop a standalone application using Java, JavaFX and Gluon, which would provide a highly responsive and feature-rich user experience, running on all platforms. The development of MaiTool will include a dedicated phase for comprehensive testing and usability studies to ensure the system meets the needs of researchers effectively. Outcomes This project will deliver several key outcomes: 1. Enhanced GPT for Microbiome and Ancient DNA Analysis: We will identify or fine-tune a GPT model specifically tailored to support research in microbiome and ancient DNA analysis. 2. Unified Microbiome Data API: A unified API will be developed to facilitate seamless access to microbiome data from multiple resources, streamlining data retrieval and integration. 3. Lightweight Bioinformatics Analysis Framework: We will create a bioinformatics framework to perform lightweight analyses on data obtained through the API, ensuring efficient and accessible computational workflows. (While a GPT may provide the description of a pipeline, the user will have to run it themselves, if they are interested in starting from scratch or raw data .) 4. Integrated AI-Bioinformatics System: A GPT system will be integrated with the developed tools to enable interactive access and analysis of microbiome data, bridging AI capabilities with bioinformatics functionality. 5. MaiTool Software for Analysis: We will develop a user-friendly software tool called MaiTool, designed to support both microbiome and ancient DNA analysis. MaiTool will provide an interactive interface for researchers, connecting seamlessly to APIs and integrating some analysis capabilities. 6. Insights into AI-Bioinformatics Integration: This project will provide valuable insights into the challenges and opportunities of integrating AI-driven systems with traditional bioinformatics software and algorithms, setting a foundation for future advancements in computational biology. These outcomes aim to advance microbiome research by enhancing data accessibility, analysis capabilities, and the synergy between AI and bioinformatics. Rationale for a working group approach This project focuses on integrating large language models (LLMs) with traditional data retrieval and bioinformatics analysis in the fields of microbiome and ancient DNA research. Achieving this goal requires expertise spanning multiple disciplines. • Daniel Huson specializes in developing algorithms and software for metagenomics and ancient DNA analysis, bringing essential computational and methodological expertise to the project. • Laura Weyrich contributes her extensive experience in the analysis of ancient DNA and ancient microbiomes, providing critical domain knowledge and practical insights into data interpretation and validation. • Maik Pietzner has a substantial track record in molecular epidemiology, spearheading the computational integration of multimodal ‘omics data sets in population-based studies with a particular focus on molecular quantitative trait loci. Together, this collaboration combines cutting-edge AI technology with expertise in microbiome and ancient DNA research, ensuring a robust and innovative approach to tackling these complex scientific challenges. Rationale for NCEMS support This project will require substantial computational resources to support the exploration of LLMs and microbiome resources. These resources will also be critical for hosting the GPT model used by MaiTool. Robust computational capacity is essential for running experiments, managing data workflows, and ensuring the scalability and responsiveness of the system. In addition, staff support will be vital for setting up computational workflows and implementing a REST API, ensuring seamless integration between components and efficient operation of the system. To foster innovation and collaboration, the project will also require support for short-term visitations between the labs of Working Group members. These visits will facilitate brainstorming, knowledge exchange, and the development of strategies to address the project’s interdisciplinary challenges. Requested resources The project requires 10–20 TB of storage for the enhancement and optimization of LLMs. Computational resources include 200–500 CPU cores and 10–30 GPUs, each with at least 100 GB of memory, to facilitate model development and optimization. RAM demands may increase up to 1–3 TB when models are combined. This will require approximately 200,000 CPU hours and 25000 GPU hours. We estimate that running the final model on a NCEMS host for users will require about 100GB of runtime memory, based on a estimated model size of 10 billion parameters. A staff scientist (up to 33% FTE) with expertise in LLMs will assist in model optimization, complementing the efforts of our existing experts. In addition, they can help ensure optimal utilization of NCEMS resources, including computational infrastructure, project management, and team science training. Proposed Timeline Year 1 Months 1–3: Conduct initial exploration of GPT models to assess suitability for microbiome and ancient DNA analysis. Begin initial exploration of microbiome resources (MG-RAST, HMP, IMG/M, MAMI, SRA) to evaluate data accessibility and API capabilities. Months 4–9: Design the framework for integrating LLMs with microbiome resources, including methods for extracting sample accessions and structuring data workflows. Months 6–12: Develop and implement APIs for seamless access to various microbiome resources, ensuring compatibility and efficient data retrieval. Months 10–12: Refine the accuracy of LLM-driven dataset selection. Improve presentation of analysis results, focusing on clarity and relevance for microbiome researchers. Year 2 Months 1–6: Develop and deploy a REST API to provide access to an LLM, supporting data access and bioinformatics analysis. Months 4–6: Build and implement the front-end interface for MaiTool, providing an alpha release for initial feedback. Months 7–9: Conduct comprehensive testing of the integrated system. Finalize documentation and address feedback to prepare for a beta release. Months 10–12: Publish results, describing the system’s design, capabilities, and applications. Release the fully functional system to the public.

criteria.justification: The proposal focuses on building an AI-enabled interface and workflow tooling rather than explicitly targeting mesoscale emergent phenomena in molecular/cellular systems. Any connection to emergence (e.g., community-level microbiome patterns) is implicit and not framed as a central scientific objective.

Integrating LLM-driven literature/dataset discovery with executable microbiome workflows is timely and potentially useful, but similar “LLM + tools” paradigms and microbiome workflow platforms already exist. The proposal’s novelty is more in packaging and integration than in a clearly articulated new biological insight or synthesis question.

Key methodological details are underspecified, including evaluation benchmarks for LLM performance (retrieval accuracy, hallucination rates), ground-truthing of accession extraction, QC criteria, and validation of downstream analyses across heterogeneous repositories. The plan reads as software development goals without a rigorous, testable experimental design for assessing scientific reliability.

Delivering a fine-tuned/hosted ~10B-parameter model, unified multi-repository API, robust QC-enabled analysis framework, and cross-platform GUI within 24 months is ambitious, especially given the complexity of repository heterogeneity and model governance. The requested compute (e.g., 10–30 GPUs with ≥100GB each) and staffing assumptions appear high and not well-justified by a phased minimal-viable deliverable plan.

The work is explicitly centered on leveraging and integrating publicly available microbiome repositories and literature, with no new experimental data generation. The synthesis emphasis is strong, though the primary output is infrastructure rather than a defined cross-dataset biological synthesis analysis.

Major repositories are named (MGnify, MG-RAST, HMP, IMG/M, SRA, MAMI), but the proposal provides limited discussion of known limitations (metadata incompleteness, batch effects, differing pipelines/ontologies, access restrictions, controlled-access human data, licensing/terms, and ancient DNA authenticity/contamination issues). More explicit risk mitigation and harmonization strategy is needed.

The proposal does not provide concrete plans for open workflows (versioned code repositories, containers, provenance, reproducible notebooks, benchmark datasets, model cards, prompt logs, or licensing), nor does it address how fine-tuned models and training data will be shared. Open science is implied by tool release but not operationalized.
The proposal focuses primarily on software tool development and data retrieval rather than explicitly addressing fundamental questions related to emergent phenomena or mesoscale biology.

Integrating LLMs with bioinformatics workflows is a novel technical application, but the proposal lacks a specific scientific hypothesis that would lead to significant biological advancement on its own.
The technical plan for software development is logical, but the scientific methodology regarding how the synthesis will answer specific biological questions is vague.
The goals are ambitious, particularly fine-tuning LLMs and maintaining API integrations for multiple repositories within two years, representing a significant engineering challenge.
While the project utilizes existing data, it is structured as an infrastructure building project to enable future synthesis, rather than a synthesis project itself aimed at solving a specific puzzle.

The proposal clearly identifies relevant public repositories (MGnify, MG-RAST, HMP, etc.), though the heterogeneity and limitations of combining these specific data sources could be addressed more thoroughly.
There is a strong commitment to open source development, public release of the MaiTool software, and utilization of open public datasets.

The proposal focuses on developing an LLM-powered bioinformatics tool for microbiome analysis but does not address emergent phenomena at the mesoscale in molecular/cellular biosciences. There is no discussion of emergence, self-organization, or complex systems behavior.

The integration of LLMs with bioinformatics workflows represents a moderately novel approach to data access and analysis. However, similar tools are emerging in the field, and the scientific advancement is primarily methodological rather than addressing fundamental biological questions.

The methodology lacks specificity in key areas such as how LLMs will be fine-tuned, what specific analyses will be performed, and how quality control will be implemented. The proposal reads more as a software development plan than a rigorous scientific approach.

The two-year timeline is reasonable for software development, though the scope is ambitious given the complexity of integrating multiple LLMs, APIs, and developing a user-friendly interface. The computational resource requirements are substantial but appear justified.

While the proposal mentions using existing public databases, the primary focus is on tool development rather than data synthesis. The project does not demonstrate integration of distinct datasets to answer scientific questions but rather creates infrastructure for potential future synthesis.

Multiple data repositories are identified (MGnify, MG-RAST, HMP, IMG/M, SRA), but limitations of these sources are not discussed. There is no analysis of data quality issues, coverage gaps, or compatibility challenges between repositories.

The proposal mentions publishing results and releasing the system publicly but lacks concrete plans for open science practices. There is no discussion of code repositories, documentation standards, reproducibility protocols, or data sharing agreements.

title_norm: intelligent metadata compilation to enhance the reusability and discoverability of mass spectrometry-based proteomics data
title: Intelligent metadata compilation to enhance the reusability and discoverability of mass spectrometry-based proteomics data
author: Human
abstract_original: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics generates vast amounts of data, yet the effective reuse and discovery of these datasets remain challenging due to incomplete and inconsistent metadata. Metadata, which provides critical contextual information such as experimental conditions, sample characteristics, and data processing details, is essential for making data FAIR (findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable). To address these challenges, our working group aims to develop intelligent, automated workflows for comprehensive metadata extraction, harmonization, and integration into PRIDE, the largest public proteomics data repository. We will develop powerful bioinformatics and natural language processing tools to extract metadata directly from raw mass spectrometry files and scientific publications. By leveraging structured data standards, metadata will be enriched with controlled vocabulary terms, enhancing dataset transparency and usability. Community engagement through a machine-learning challenge will further drive innovation in metadata extraction techniques. The outcomes of the working group's activities will include automated metadata compilation workflows integrated into user-friendly tools, advanced dataset querying capabilities in PRIDE, and the creation of educational resources for the scientific community. These efforts will enable researchers to efficiently locate and reuse proteomics datasets, facilitating secondary analyses such as AI model training and large-scale reanalysis.
full_draft_original: Introduction and Goals In line with the FAIR principles—findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable—omics data is increasingly accessible through public repositories tailored to diverse research domains. This surge in data availability has immense potential to accelerate scientific discovery and foster cross-disciplinary innovation. However, the effective findability and reusability of these datasets remain limited, primarily due to a lack of comprehensive metadata. Metadata, which includes details like experimental conditions, sample characteristics, data processing methods, and instrument settings, is critical for transforming raw data into scientifically valuable resources. Unfortunately, metadata is often incomplete, inconsistently structured, or buried in unstructured formats such as free-form text in publications. These shortcomings restrict automated processing, systematic querying, and the discovery of relevant datasets. To bridge this gap, the working group will develop automated methods to extract, refine, and associate high-quality metadata with omics data in public repositories. This initiative will lay the groundwork for improved data discoverability and expanded reusability. While metadata enhancement is relevant across all omics fields, the initial focus is on mass spectrometry-based proteomics due to its complex metadata needs and established annotation frameworks. Specifically, the group will leverage the SDRF-Proteomics format, a structured tab-delimited standard adopted from transcriptomics (MAGE-TAB) by the Proteomics Standards Initiative. SDRF-Proteomics improves data transparency and usability by specifying relationships between samples, assays, and data files. Despite its growing adoption, many datasets remain inconsistently annotated. The group proposes to address this by developing intelligent, automated workflows to systematically gather and associate metadata for proteomics experiments and integrate it into PRIDE, the largest proteomics data repository. The tools will extract technical and biological metadata directly from experimental data, open-access publications, and existing annotations. Extracted metadata will be harmonized using controlled vocabulary and ontology terms and linked to datasets in PRIDE, creating an enriched metadata layer accessible for secondary analyses. To ensure accessibility, a user-friendly interface will be implemented in PRIDE’s web portal, alongside an API for metadata-based queries. Enhanced metadata infrastructure will unlock powerful capabilities for proteomics researchers, such as identifying suitable training datasets for AI tools, enabling automated large-scale reanalyses like differential protein expression profiling, and facilitating re-interpretation of public data in light of new hypotheses. Proposed Activities The project will initially focus on standard bottom-up discovery proteomics workflows, encompassing data-dependent and data-independent acquisition with both label-free and label-based quantitation, as well as post-translational modification-enriched datasets. Time permitting, it will expand to specialized approaches such as crosslinking and hydrogen-deuterium exchange proteomics. This stepwise approach allows controlled validation and extension to other omics disciplines in the future. Metadata retrieval will combine extraction from raw mass spectrometry data with mining of complementary metadata from scientific literature. From raw data, proprietary formats will be converted to mzML, and essential metadata such as instrument type, parameters, and search settings (mass tolerances, digestion enzymes, isobaric labeling strategies) will be derived using existing tools such as Param-Medic. Organism identification will be obtained by matching against reference data, and digestion enzymes and modifications will be determined via open modification searching. These components will be integrated into an automated workflow using Nextflow to streamline extraction and organization. For literature-based metadata, critical contextual information not found in raw data (biological conditions, case/control groupings, disease relevance) will be gathered using a natural language processing pipeline built on large language models fine-tuned for scientific text mining. To ensure accuracy and transparency, the models will indicate unavailable elements, perform self-verification, and use ensemble cross-checking among LLMs. To engage the community, a machine-learning challenge will be launched to drive innovation in metadata extraction. Winning open-source algorithms will be integrated into workflows. Tutorial datasets and documentation will be shared through ProteomicsML, fostering education for both data scientists and proteomics practitioners. To develop and validate the approach, the group will use a curated set of public datasets with SDRF metadata as a gold standard, along with a manually curated private test set as an independent benchmark for evaluating metadata accuracy. Scoring will emphasize precision to ensure high-confidence results. Finally, the workflows will be integrated into user-friendly tools such as lesSDRF, enabling automated metadata compilation during PRIDE submissions. Retrospective metadata generation will also be applied to existing public datasets with support from PRIDE’s data curation team. Enhanced PRIDE functionality will include metadata-driven dataset querying via the website and API. Outcomes The project will deliver multiple key outcomes: automated workflows for metadata extraction from raw data and open-access publications using NLP; a community challenge to produce open-source metadata extraction solutions; educational resources and tutorials through ProteomicsML; enhanced metadata tools integrated with PRIDE submission workflows; advanced metadata-based querying and API retrieval in PRIDE; and several open-access publications describing methodologies and technical innovations. All workflows and outputs will follow open-science principles, with code released on GitHub and manuscripts preprinted with accompanying data. While initially focused on proteomics, this work will create a scalable template for addressing metadata challenges across omics disciplines, beginning with metabolomics and beyond. Rationale for a Working Group Approach The project combines expertise across bioinformatics, machine learning, NLP, proteomics, and data repository management, exceeding the capacity of any single research group. Machine-learning and NLP specialists will design algorithms to extract metadata from raw files and publications, while bioinformaticians will align metadata with structured data standards. Proteomics experts will ensure biological relevance, and repository teams will oversee integration with PRIDE. This coordinated, interdisciplinary effort enables robust, scalable, and biologically meaningful metadata solutions. Rationale for NCEMS Support The project aligns with NCEMS’s mission to leverage public data for large-scale synthesis and develop novel integrative strategies. NCEMS staff scientists will assist with SDRF metadata curation, community challenge support, and workflow integration. CyVerse computational resources will provide scalability for NLP and large-scale metadata extraction. Team science training, project management support, and coordination of tool integration across geographically distributed members will further enhance outcomes. NCEMS’s contribution ensures both technical infrastructure and sustainability for this collaborative initiative. Requested Resources The project requires staff scientist and assistant support specializing in metadata harmonization and proteomics experimental design. These roles will include curation of metadata, support for NLP corpus creation, management of the community challenge, technical guidance, and workflow integration. Computational resources include approximately 15 TB of storage for public data mirroring, 2,500 CPU hours for metadata extraction pipelines, and 500 GPU hours for local fine-tuning of LLMs. Proposed Timeline The project is planned for two years. The first year will focus on metadata compilation, workflow development, and a community challenge launch. The second year will include evaluation of challenge outcomes, integration of workflows into lesSDRF, retrospective metadata generation for PRIDE datasets, and implementation of metadata-based querying functionality. Final deliverables will include completed tools, datasets, and open-access publications disseminated to the research community.

criteria.justification: The work primarily targets infrastructure/methods for metadata enrichment and discovery rather than explicitly interrogating mesoscale emergent molecular/cellular phenomena. It could enable downstream emergence-focused synthesis, but that connection is indirect in the proposal.

Automated, standards-aware metadata extraction from raw MS files plus publication NLP/LLM mining, coupled to PRIDE integration and a community challenge, is a timely and potentially high-impact advance for proteomics reuse. If successful, it would materially improve dataset discoverability and enable new large-scale reanalyses and AI training.

The plan is logically structured (raw-file parsing, SDRF harmonization, NLP extraction, benchmarking, PRIDE integration), but key technical risks are under-specified (LLM error modes/hallucinations, ground-truth creation, and validation across heterogeneous study designs). The use of a private benchmark set also raises questions about reproducible evaluation unless an open alternative is provided.

A two-year timeline is plausible for a first production-grade pipeline and limited PRIDE integration, but the scope is ambitious (raw+literature extraction, LLM fine-tuning, community challenge, retrospective annotation at scale, and new PRIDE query features). Success likely depends on narrowing to a well-defined subset of metadata fields and a staged deployment plan with clear go/no-go milestones.

The project is explicitly based on reusing and integrating existing public proteomics datasets (PRIDE) and associated publications/annotations, with no new experimental data generation. It is a clear synthesis/integration effort aimed at improving reuse of community data.

PRIDE and SDRF-Proteomics are clearly identified, and the proposal notes that key metadata are missing or unstructured in publications, but it provides limited specificity on which journals/corpora, licensing constraints for full-text mining, and how non-open-access papers will be handled. Limitations around proprietary raw formats, incomplete instrument metadata, and cross-study heterogeneity are acknowledged only at a high level.

The proposal commits to open workflows (GitHub), preprints, and public dissemination of tutorials/resources, aligning well with reproducible team science. A more detailed plan for releasing evaluation datasets/labels (or an open benchmark equivalent to the private test set) and for documenting model cards, prompts, and provenance would strengthen compliance.

While the proposed tools will facilitate future research into complex biological systems, the proposal focuses on data infrastructure and metadata rather than directly addressing specific emergent phenomena.
The application of Large Language Models and automated raw file analysis to solve the persistent issue of metadata quality in proteomics is a highly novel and significant contribution.
The methodology is exceptionally rigorous, employing established pipelines (Nextflow), specific extraction tools, and a clear validation plan using gold-standard datasets.
The two-year timeline is realistic and well-structured, though managing the community machine-learning challenge alongside tool development will require careful coordination.
The project is an exemplary synthesis effort, relying exclusively on existing public data repositories (PRIDE) and literature to generate value without new experimental data.
Data sources are comprehensively identified, and the proposal thoughtfully addresses limitations such as proprietary file formats and unstructured text in publications.
The proposal demonstrates exemplary commitment to open science, with clear plans for open-source code, open access publications, and direct integration into public community infrastructure.

The proposal focuses on metadata extraction and harmonization for proteomics data repositories, which is an infrastructure/data management project rather than research addressing emergent phenomena at the mesoscale in molecular/cellular biosciences.

The application of NLP and machine learning to automate metadata extraction from proteomics data and publications represents a novel technical approach with clear significance for data reusability, though it is primarily a methodological/infrastructure advancement rather than scientific discovery.

The methodology is well-articulated with clear steps including raw data extraction, NLP pipelines, validation using gold-standard datasets, and integration with existing tools like lesSDRF and PRIDE. The use of ensemble cross-checking and precision-focused scoring demonstrates thoughtful quality control.

The two-year timeline with phased activities is reasonable, though the scope is ambitious given the complexity of NLP fine-tuning, community challenge organization, and retrospective metadata generation for existing PRIDE datasets. Some deliverables may face delays.

The proposal exclusively uses existing public proteomics data from PRIDE and open-access publications, with clear plans to integrate and harmonize metadata across datasets. However, the focus is on enabling future synthesis rather than conducting synthesis research itself.

PRIDE is clearly identified as the primary data source, and the proposal mentions using curated datasets with SDRF metadata as gold standards. However, specific datasets are not enumerated, and limitations of metadata extraction accuracy from diverse publication formats are not thoroughly discussed.

The proposal demonstrates exemplary commitment to open science with explicit plans for GitHub code release, preprints, open-access publications, community challenges producing open-source algorithms, and educational resources through ProteomicsML.

title_norm: emergent receptor clustering in immune synapses: synthesizing super-resolution and signaling data to model t cell activation thresholds
title: Emergent Receptor Clustering in Immune Synapses: Synthesizing Super-Resolution and Signaling Data to Model T Cell Activation Thresholds
author: claude-opus-4-5
abstract_original: T cell activation emerges from receptor clustering at immune synapses where mesoscale organization determines signaling thresholds—a phenomenon where spatial arrangement creates activation decisions impossible from receptor occupancy alone. This synthesis project will decode emergent T cell activation by integrating imaging, signaling, and structural datasets. We will synthesize super-resolution imaging from published studies and Image Data Resource, phosphoproteomics of TCR signaling from PRIDE, structural data from PDB on TCR complexes, and single-cell RNA-seq from the Human Cell Atlas. The central question is: how does receptor clustering at the mesoscale (100-500 nm microclusters) create emergent activation thresholds that determine T cell responses? We hypothesize that emergent thresholds arise from kinetic segregation of phosphatases, cooperative kinase recruitment, and feedback loops operating within receptor clusters. Our computational approach combines spatial stochastic simulations of TCR signaling, machine learning to predict activation from cluster properties, and network analysis of signaling cascades. We will develop image analysis pipelines to quantify cluster properties across activation states. Integration with functional data will connect cluster organization to T cell fate decisions. Comparative analysis across T cell subsets will reveal how emergent thresholds adapt to different immune functions. This project demands expertise in T cell biology, super-resolution imaging, signaling, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of imaging, signaling, and transcriptomic data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent activation thresholds, identification of key cluster features determining T cell responses, and principles for modulating immune activation. Understanding emergent T cell activation has implications for immunotherapy and autoimmune diseases. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.
