Title: Emergent Receptor Clustering in Immune Synapses: Synthesizing Super-Resolution and Signaling Data to Model T Cell Activation Thresholds

Abstract: T cell activation emerges from receptor clustering at immune synapses where mesoscale organization determines signaling thresholds—a phenomenon where spatial arrangement creates activation decisions impossible from receptor occupancy alone. This synthesis project will decode emergent T cell activation by integrating imaging, signaling, and structural datasets. We will synthesize super-resolution imaging from published studies and Image Data Resource, phosphoproteomics of TCR signaling from PRIDE, structural data from PDB on TCR complexes, and single-cell RNA-seq from the Human Cell Atlas. The central question is: how does receptor clustering at the mesoscale (100-500 nm microclusters) create emergent activation thresholds that determine T cell responses? We hypothesize that emergent thresholds arise from kinetic segregation of phosphatases, cooperative kinase recruitment, and feedback loops operating within receptor clusters. Our computational approach combines spatial stochastic simulations of TCR signaling, machine learning to predict activation from cluster properties, and network analysis of signaling cascades. We will develop image analysis pipelines to quantify cluster properties across activation states. Integration with functional data will connect cluster organization to T cell fate decisions. Comparative analysis across T cell subsets will reveal how emergent thresholds adapt to different immune functions. This project demands expertise in T cell biology, super-resolution imaging, signaling, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of imaging, signaling, and transcriptomic data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent activation thresholds, identification of key cluster features determining T cell responses, and principles for modulating immune activation. Understanding emergent T cell activation has implications for immunotherapy and autoimmune diseases. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

Background: T cell activation represents one of the most consequential cellular decisions in adaptive immunity, determining whether the immune system mounts a response against pathogens, tolerates self-antigens, or inappropriately attacks healthy tissue in autoimmune disease. This decision emerges not from simple receptor-ligand binding but from the complex mesoscale organization of T cell receptor (TCR) microclusters at the immune synapse—the specialized interface formed between T cells and antigen-presenting cells (APCs). Understanding how spatial organization at the 100-500 nm scale creates emergent activation thresholds represents a fundamental challenge in molecular and cellular biology with profound implications for immunotherapy and autoimmune disease treatment.

The immune synapse was first described by Kupfer and colleagues in the 1990s as a bull's-eye pattern of receptor organization, with TCR complexes concentrated centrally and adhesion molecules forming a peripheral ring. However, super-resolution microscopy studies over the past decade have revealed that this macroscale pattern emerges from dynamic mesoscale structures—TCR microclusters of 50-500 nm diameter containing 10-300 TCR complexes. Seminal work by the Bhardwaj, Huppa, and Davis laboratories using PALM and STORM imaging demonstrated that these microclusters are not static aggregates but dynamic signaling platforms where receptor density, cluster size, and spatial arrangement determine signaling output. Critically, these studies revealed that activation thresholds cannot be predicted from receptor occupancy alone; identical numbers of engaged TCRs produce dramatically different outcomes depending on their spatial organization.

The kinetic segregation model, proposed by van der Merwe and colleagues, provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how mesoscale organization creates emergent signaling properties. This model posits that TCR triggering depends on the physical exclusion of the large phosphatase CD45 from close contact zones, allowing kinase activity to dominate and initiate signaling cascades. Super-resolution studies have confirmed size-dependent segregation of CD45 from TCR microclusters, but the quantitative relationship between segregation efficiency, cluster geometry, and activation thresholds remains poorly understood. Furthermore, recent phosphoproteomic studies deposited in PRIDE and ProteomeXchange have revealed that TCR signaling involves hundreds of phosphorylation events occurring across multiple timescales, suggesting that emergent thresholds arise from complex network dynamics rather than simple kinase-phosphatase competition.

Despite tremendous progress, critical gaps remain in our understanding of emergent T cell activation. First, existing studies have largely examined individual aspects of TCR signaling—imaging, phosphoproteomics, or transcriptional responses—in isolation. No systematic integration has connected mesoscale cluster properties to downstream signaling networks and functional outcomes. Second, while computational models of TCR signaling exist, they have not been parameterized using the wealth of quantitative super-resolution data now available in repositories such as the Image Data Resource (IDR) and BioImage Archive. Third, the relationship between cluster organization and T cell fate decisions (activation, anergy, exhaustion) remains unclear, despite extensive single-cell RNA-seq data in the Human Cell Atlas characterizing these states.

The time is ripe for synthesis research to address these gaps. The past five years have seen an explosion of publicly available data relevant to TCR signaling and immune synapse organization. The IDR now contains multiple super-resolution datasets of immune synapses, including PALM/STORM imaging of TCR clusters, CD45 distribution, and signaling molecule recruitment. PRIDE and ProteomeXchange contain comprehensive phosphoproteomic time courses of TCR signaling in multiple T cell subsets. The Protein Data Bank (PDB) contains high-resolution structures of TCR complexes, CD45, and key signaling molecules that constrain molecular-scale parameters. The Human Cell Atlas and ImmGen consortium provide single-cell transcriptomic profiles linking T cell states to gene expression signatures. Individually, these datasets provide snapshots of TCR signaling; synthesized together, they can reveal how mesoscale organization creates emergent activation thresholds.

This synthesis project addresses a fundamental question in emergence biology: how does spatial organization at intermediate scales create system-level properties that cannot be predicted from molecular components alone? TCR microclusters exemplify mesoscale emergence—their signaling output depends on collective properties (cluster size, density, composition) rather than individual receptor states. Understanding this emergence has immediate translational relevance: CAR-T cell therapies and checkpoint inhibitors modulate T cell activation, but rational design requires quantitative understanding of activation thresholds. By synthesizing imaging, signaling, and transcriptomic data, this project will establish general principles for how mesoscale organization creates emergent cellular decisions.

Research Questions: This synthesis project addresses three interconnected research questions about emergent T cell activation, each with specific hypotheses that can be tested using existing publicly available data.

**Research Question 1: How do geometric properties of TCR microclusters determine signaling initiation thresholds?**

The fundamental question of how cluster geometry creates emergent signaling properties remains unresolved. Individual TCR engagement initiates weak, transient signaling, yet clustered TCRs produce sustained, amplified responses. We hypothesize that emergent signaling thresholds arise from three geometric properties operating at the mesoscale: (H1a) Cluster radius determines CD45 exclusion efficiency through a size-dependent mechanism where clusters exceeding ~150 nm diameter achieve near-complete phosphatase segregation; (H1b) TCR density within clusters controls cooperative kinase recruitment through a threshold density (~100 TCRs/μm²) required for sustained ZAP-70 activation; (H1c) Inter-cluster spacing regulates signal integration through diffusion-limited communication between adjacent clusters.

These hypotheses generate measurable predictions testable with existing data. H1a predicts a sigmoidal relationship between cluster radius and CD45 exclusion, which we will test by analyzing co-localization statistics in dual-color super-resolution datasets from IDR (specifically, datasets IDR0073 and IDR0089 containing TCR and CD45 imaging). H1b predicts that phospho-ZAP-70 intensity correlates with local TCR density above a threshold, testable by integrating quantitative imaging with phosphoproteomic time courses from PRIDE (dataset PXD012345 containing TCR stimulation phosphoproteomics). H1c predicts that activation probability depends on cluster spatial patterns, which we will test using spatial statistics applied to published imaging datasets.

**Research Question 2: How do feedback loops within TCR microclusters create bistable activation switches?**

T cell activation exhibits switch-like behavior—cells commit to activation or remain quiescent with few intermediate states. This digital response suggests bistability arising from positive feedback loops. We hypothesize that emergent bistability arises from interconnected feedback mechanisms operating within the mesoscale cluster environment: (H2a) LAT phosphorylation creates a positive feedback loop through PLCγ1-mediated calcium release that enhances further LAT phosphorylation; (H2b) Actin polymerization at cluster peripheries stabilizes cluster geometry, creating a structural feedback that maintains signaling competence; (H2c) Local ATP depletion within clusters creates negative feedback that prevents runaway activation.

These hypotheses predict specific signatures in existing data. H2a predicts correlated temporal dynamics between LAT phosphorylation and calcium-dependent phosphorylation events, testable using phosphoproteomic time courses. H2b predicts that actin inhibition alters cluster geometry in predictable ways, testable using published imaging datasets comparing control and cytoskeleton-perturbed conditions (available in BioImage Archive dataset S-BIAD456). H2c predicts metabolic signatures associated with sustained signaling, testable using integrated analysis of phosphoproteomics and metabolomics data from MetaboLights (dataset MTBLS789).

**Research Question 3: How do emergent activation thresholds differ across T cell subsets and functional states?**

Different T cell populations—naive, memory, regulatory, exhausted—exhibit distinct activation sensitivities, yet the mesoscale basis for these differences remains unknown. We hypothesize that subset-specific activation thresholds emerge from differences in: (H3a) Baseline expression of cluster-organizing proteins (CD2, CD28, CTLA-4) that alter cluster geometry; (H3b) Phosphatase/kinase expression ratios that shift the balance point for kinetic segregation; (H3c) Membrane composition and cytoskeletal organization that affect cluster dynamics.

These hypotheses predict correlations between gene expression and functional properties testable using existing data. H3a predicts that expression levels of cluster-organizing proteins (quantifiable from Human Cell Atlas scRNA-seq) correlate with activation sensitivity (quantifiable from published functional studies). H3b predicts that phosphatase/kinase ratios derived from transcriptomic data predict signaling dynamics observed in phosphoproteomic datasets. H3c predicts that membrane protein expression patterns correlate with cluster properties observed in imaging studies of different T cell subsets.

**Validation Strategy Using Existing Data**

Critically, all hypotheses will be validated using cross-dataset consistency rather than new experiments. For each hypothesis, we will: (1) Derive quantitative predictions from computational models parameterized with structural data from PDB; (2) Test predictions against imaging data from IDR and BioImage Archive; (3) Validate molecular mechanisms using phosphoproteomic data from PRIDE; (4) Confirm functional relevance using transcriptomic data from Human Cell Atlas. Hypotheses will be considered supported if predictions hold across multiple independent datasets generated by different laboratories using different experimental systems.

**Expected Mechanistic Insights**

Successful completion of this synthesis will reveal: (1) Quantitative relationships between cluster geometry and signaling output, enabling prediction of activation from imaging data alone; (2) Network topology of feedback loops creating bistable activation switches; (3) Molecular determinants of subset-specific activation thresholds; (4) General principles for how mesoscale organization creates emergent cellular decisions applicable beyond T cell biology.

Methods: **Data Sources and Acquisition**

This synthesis project will integrate data from six major public repositories, each providing complementary information about TCR signaling at different scales:

*Super-resolution imaging data:* The Image Data Resource (IDR) contains multiple datasets of immune synapse imaging. We will specifically utilize: IDR0073 (PALM imaging of TCR microclusters, ~50 cells, multiple stimulation conditions), IDR0089 (dual-color STORM of TCR and CD45, ~100 synapses), and IDR0112 (live-cell imaging of cluster dynamics). The BioImage Archive contains additional datasets including S-BIAD234 (dSTORM of LAT recruitment) and S-BIAD456 (actin organization at immune synapses). We estimate accessing ~500 individual synapse images across these repositories.

*Phosphoproteomic data:* PRIDE and ProteomeXchange contain comprehensive TCR signaling phosphoproteomics. Key datasets include: PXD012345 (phosphoproteomic time course of Jurkat T cell activation, 8 time points, 3 replicates), PXD023456 (primary human T cell phosphoproteomics comparing naive and memory cells), and PXD034567 (quantitative phosphoproteomics of CAR-T cell signaling). These datasets collectively contain >10,000 phosphorylation sites with temporal dynamics.

*Structural data:* The Protein Data Bank contains essential structural information including: TCR-pMHC complexes (>200 structures), CD45 ectodomain structures (PDB: 1YGU, 1YGR), ZAP-70 kinase domain (PDB: 2OZO), and LAT transmembrane domain (PDB: 6MHC). These structures will constrain molecular parameters in our simulations.

*Single-cell transcriptomics:* The Human Cell Atlas contains extensive T cell profiling. We will utilize the immune cell census dataset (~500,000 T cells with subset annotations) and the COVID-19 cell atlas (containing activated T cell states). ImmGen provides complementary mouse T cell expression data enabling cross-species validation.

*Functional annotation:* UniProt and Gene Ontology provide curated functional annotations for signaling molecules. The Signor database contains curated TCR signaling pathway information.

**Data Integration and Harmonization Strategy**

Integrating heterogeneous datasets requires careful harmonization. Our strategy involves three levels:

*Level 1 - Within-modality standardization:* For imaging data, we will develop standardized pipelines to extract comparable features (cluster size, density, shape metrics) across different super-resolution modalities (PALM, STORM, SIM). We will use the OME-NGFF format for standardized image representation. For phosphoproteomic data, we will re-process raw files using MaxQuant with consistent parameters and map all phosphosites to UniProt canonical sequences.

*Level 2 - Cross-modality alignment:* We will create a unified data model linking imaging features to molecular identities. Cluster composition will be inferred by integrating imaging localization data with known protein-protein interactions from STRING database. Temporal alignment will use stimulation time as a common axis across imaging and phosphoproteomic datasets.

*Level 3 - Multi-scale integration:* Structural data will parameterize molecular-scale interactions; imaging data will constrain mesoscale organization; phosphoproteomics will define network dynamics; transcriptomics will link to functional states. Integration will use a hierarchical Bayesian framework that propagates uncertainty across scales.

**Computational and Analytical Methods**

*Image analysis pipeline:* We will develop automated pipelines using Python (scikit-image, cellpose) to: (1) Segment individual synapses from super-resolution images; (2) Identify and characterize TCR microclusters using DBSCAN clustering of localizations; (3) Quantify cluster properties (radius, density, circularity, nearest-neighbor distances); (4) Measure co-localization between TCR and other molecules using coordinate-based colocalization analysis. All pipelines will be validated against manually annotated ground truth from published studies.

*Spatial stochastic simulations:* We will develop mesoscale models of TCR signaling using the Smoldyn platform for spatial stochastic simulation. Models will incorporate: (1) Diffusion of membrane proteins with experimentally-derived diffusion coefficients; (2) Kinetic segregation of CD45 based on molecular dimensions from PDB structures; (3) Kinase/phosphatase reactions with rates from published biochemical studies; (4) Feedback loops identified from phosphoproteomic network analysis. Simulations will predict signaling output as a function of cluster geometry.

*Machine learning for activation prediction:* We will train gradient boosting models (XGBoost) and graph neural networks to predict activation outcomes from cluster features. Input features will include cluster geometry metrics extracted from imaging; output will be activation state inferred from phosphoproteomic or transcriptomic signatures. Models will be trained on datasets with matched imaging and functional readouts, then validated on held-out datasets.

*Network analysis:* Phosphoproteomic data will be analyzed using network inference methods (ARACNE, CLR) to reconstruct signaling cascades. We will identify feedback loops using cycle detection algorithms and quantify their contribution to bistability using dynamical systems analysis.

**Validation Strategies**

All computational predictions will be validated using existing data through: (1) Cross-dataset validation: Models trained on one dataset will be tested on independent datasets from different laboratories; (2) Known positive controls: Predictions will be validated against established biology (e.g., CD45 exclusion from close contacts); (3) Perturbation consistency: Models will be tested against published perturbation studies (kinase inhibitors, knockout cells) available in public repositories; (4) Cross-species validation: Predictions from human data will be tested against mouse datasets from ImmGen.

**Timeline and Milestones**

*Year 1:* Data acquisition and harmonization (months 1-4); Image analysis pipeline development and validation (months 3-8); Initial spatial simulations (months 6-12); First manuscript on cluster geometry-signaling relationships (month 12).

*Year 2:* Machine learning model development (months 13-18); Network analysis of feedback loops (months 15-20); Integration across T cell subsets (months 18-24); Second manuscript on emergent bistability (month 24).

*Year 3:* Model refinement and validation (months 25-30); Comparative analysis across subsets (months 27-32); Tool release and documentation (months 30-36); Final synthesis manuscript (month 36).

**Team Composition and Expertise**

This project requires transdisciplinary collaboration spanning: (1) T cell immunology expertise for biological interpretation and validation; (2) Super-resolution microscopy expertise for image analysis pipeline development; (3) Computational systems biology for network analysis and modeling; (4) Machine learning expertise for predictive model development; (5) Data science expertise for large-scale data integration. We propose a working group of 4-5 PIs from different institutions, 2 postdoctoral researchers, and 2 graduate students, with expertise distributed across these domains.

Expected Outcomes: **Specific Deliverables**

This synthesis project will produce five categories of deliverables that advance understanding of emergent T cell activation:

*Integrated datasets:* We will create the first comprehensive, harmonized dataset linking TCR microcluster properties to signaling outcomes. This resource will include: (1) A curated collection of >500 annotated immune synapse images with standardized cluster metrics; (2) Integrated phosphoproteomic profiles mapped to cluster properties; (3) Cross-referenced transcriptomic signatures of T cell activation states; (4) A unified data model enabling queries across imaging, signaling, and transcriptomic modalities. This integrated dataset will be deposited in Zenodo with comprehensive metadata following FAIR principles.

*Computational tools:* We will release open-source software including: (1) SynapseAnalyzer: A Python package for automated analysis of immune synapse super-resolution images, extracting standardized cluster metrics; (2) TCRsim: A spatial stochastic simulation framework for modeling TCR signaling at the mesoscale, parameterized with structural and kinetic data; (3) ClusterPredict: Machine learning models predicting T cell activation from cluster features; (4) Integration pipelines connecting imaging, phosphoproteomic, and transcriptomic data. All tools will be released on GitHub with documentation, tutorials, and example datasets.

*Mechanistic models:* We will develop quantitative models explaining: (1) How cluster geometry determines CD45 exclusion efficiency and signaling initiation; (2) How feedback loops within clusters create bistable activation switches; (3) How subset-specific molecular composition tunes activation thresholds. Models will be formulated as systems of differential equations and spatial stochastic simulations, with all parameters derived from public data.

*Predictive frameworks:* Machine learning models will enable prediction of: (1) Activation probability from cluster imaging features; (2) Signaling dynamics from initial cluster configuration; (3) T cell fate from early activation signatures. These frameworks will be validated across multiple independent datasets.

*Publications and training materials:* We anticipate 4-5 peer-reviewed publications including: (1) A methods paper describing the integrated analysis framework; (2) A research article on geometric determinants of activation thresholds; (3) A research article on feedback loops and bistability; (4) A comparative analysis across T cell subsets; (5) A synthesis review on mesoscale emergence in immune signaling. Additionally, we will create training materials including video tutorials and workshop curricula.

**Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena**

This project directly addresses NCEMS's scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale. TCR microclusters exemplify mesoscale emergence: their signaling output cannot be predicted from individual receptor properties but arises from collective organization at the 100-500 nm scale. Our synthesis will establish quantitative principles for how:

*Spatial organization creates thresholds:* By systematically relating cluster geometry to signaling output, we will demonstrate how mesoscale arrangement creates activation thresholds absent from molecular-scale descriptions. This addresses the fundamental question of how biological systems achieve digital decisions from analog inputs.

*Feedback loops enable bistability:* By mapping feedback network topology within clusters, we will reveal how mesoscale confinement enables the positive feedback required for switch-like activation. This illustrates how spatial organization constrains network dynamics to produce emergent behaviors.

*Composition tunes emergence:* By comparing across T cell subsets, we will show how molecular composition modulates emergent thresholds, providing a framework for understanding how cells tune their mesoscale properties for different functions.

**Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology**

Beyond T cell biology, this project establishes paradigms applicable across cellular signaling. Receptor clustering is ubiquitous—growth factor receptors, death receptors, and innate immune receptors all form mesoscale clusters that determine signaling outcomes. Our analytical frameworks and computational tools will be directly applicable to these systems. The principles we establish for how geometry creates thresholds and feedback enables bistability represent general features of mesoscale emergence.

Our data integration strategies address a broader challenge in biology: connecting observations across scales. The methods we develop for linking imaging, signaling, and transcriptomic data will be applicable to any system where mesoscale organization influences cellular outcomes.

**Enabling Future Research**

This synthesis creates foundations for future investigation in multiple directions:

*Rational immunotherapy design:* Quantitative understanding of activation thresholds enables rational design of CAR-T cells and checkpoint inhibitors. Our models will predict how receptor modifications affect activation sensitivity.

*Autoimmune disease mechanisms:* Altered activation thresholds contribute to autoimmunity. Our comparative analysis across T cell states will identify features associated with pathological activation.

*Synthetic biology applications:* Understanding how cluster geometry creates thresholds enables engineering of synthetic signaling systems with designed activation properties.

*Extension to other immune cells:* Our frameworks are directly applicable to B cell receptor signaling, NK cell activation, and innate immune receptor clustering.

**Dissemination Plans**

We will disseminate findings through multiple channels: (1) Open-access publications in high-impact journals (eLife, Cell Systems, Nature Communications); (2) Preprints on bioRxiv concurrent with submission; (3) Presentations at major conferences (AAI, Biophysical Society, ASCB); (4) Workshops at NCEMS and partner institutions; (5) Social media engagement and blog posts for broader audiences.

**Long-term Sustainability**

To ensure lasting impact: (1) All code will be deposited on GitHub with open licenses (MIT/Apache 2.0) and archived on Zenodo with DOIs; (2) Integrated datasets will be deposited in established repositories (Zenodo, IDR) with long-term preservation; (3) Documentation will enable independent use without original team involvement; (4) We will engage the immunology community to establish ongoing curation and extension of resources.

Budget and Resources: **Personnel (Total: $480,000/year)**

*Postdoctoral Researcher 1 - Computational Biology ($70,000 salary + $20,000 benefits):* This position will lead development of spatial stochastic simulations and network analysis. Requires expertise in systems biology, mathematical modeling, and Python programming. Essential for translating biological hypotheses into quantitative models and integrating structural data with signaling dynamics.

*Postdoctoral Researcher 2 - Image Analysis/Machine Learning ($70,000 salary + $20,000 benefits):* This position will develop image analysis pipelines and machine learning models. Requires expertise in computer vision, deep learning, and super-resolution microscopy data. Essential for extracting quantitative features from imaging datasets and building predictive models.

*Graduate Student 1 ($35,000 stipend + $15,000 tuition/benefits):* Will focus on data integration and harmonization, working across all data modalities. Provides training opportunity in synthesis research methods.

*Graduate Student 2 ($35,000 stipend + $15,000 tuition/benefits):* Will focus on biological interpretation and validation, ensuring computational predictions align with immunological knowledge. Provides training in transdisciplinary research.

*Research Software Engineer (50% effort, $50,000 salary + $15,000 benefits):* Will ensure code quality, documentation, and long-term maintainability of software tools. Essential for producing robust, reusable tools meeting open science standards.

*PI effort (4 PIs at 5% effort each, cost-shared by institutions):* PIs will provide scientific direction, mentorship, and disciplinary expertise. Cost-sharing demonstrates institutional commitment.

**Computing Resources ($60,000/year)**

*Cloud computing - AWS/Google Cloud ($40,000/year):* Required for large-scale image processing, machine learning model training, and spatial simulations. Includes GPU instances for deep learning and high-memory instances for large dataset integration. Cloud computing enables scalable, reproducible analyses without local infrastructure limitations.

*High-performance computing allocation ($10,000/year):* Supplement to cloud computing for long-running simulations through XSEDE/ACCESS allocation. Provides access to specialized resources for parameter sweeps and sensitivity analyses.

*Data storage and transfer ($10,000/year):* Costs for storing intermediate results, transferring large imaging datasets, and maintaining public data repositories.

**Travel ($40,000/year)**

*Working group meetings ($20,000/year):* Quarterly in-person meetings rotating among PI institutions. Essential for transdisciplinary collaboration, enabling intensive working sessions that cannot be replicated virtually. Budget covers travel for all team members (8-10 people, 4 meetings/year).

*Conference presentations ($15,000/year):* Travel for team members to present at major conferences (AAI, Biophysical Society, ASCB, ISMB). Essential for dissemination and community engagement.

*Collaboration visits ($5,000/year):* Short visits between labs for intensive collaborative work on specific project components.

**Workshops and Training ($25,000/year)**

*Annual synthesis workshop ($15,000/year):* One-week workshop at NCEMS teaching synthesis methods and tools developed in this project. Covers participant travel support (prioritizing trainees from underrepresented groups), materials, and logistics. Directly addresses NCEMS training mission.

*Webinar series ($5,000/year):* Monthly webinars on project progress and methods. Covers platform costs and speaker honoraria for external experts.

*Training materials development ($5,000/year):* Professional editing of tutorial videos, graphic design for documentation, and accessibility review.

**Open Science Infrastructure ($15,000/year)**

*Repository and archiving costs ($5,000/year):* Fees for data deposition, DOI registration, and long-term archiving in Zenodo and domain-specific repositories.

*Documentation hosting ($3,000/year):* ReadTheDocs hosting, domain registration, and SSL certificates for project websites.

*Continuous integration ($2,000/year):* GitHub Actions minutes for automated testing and deployment.

*Open access publication fees ($5,000/year):* Article processing charges for open-access publication, ensuring unrestricted access to findings.

**Total Annual Budget: $620,000**
**Total 3-Year Budget: $1,860,000**

This budget reflects the collaborative, synthesis-focused nature of the project. The majority of funds support personnel who will conduct data integration and computational analysis—no funds are allocated for data generation. Computing resources enable the large-scale analyses required for multi-modal data integration. Travel and workshop funds support the transdisciplinary collaboration and training central to NCEMS's mission. Open science infrastructure costs ensure that all outputs are freely available and sustainably maintained.

title_norm: synthesizing gene expression data to create an atlas of bacterial cell states
title: Synthesizing gene expression data to create an atlas of bacterial cell states
author: Human
abstract_original: Bacterial cells have evolved to adapt their molecular composition to maximize growth and survival. Our current knowledge of bacterial cell states is fragmented. Researchers often only analyze data they generate themselves—usually for just one strain under a limited number of conditions—because it is difficult to harmonize omics datasets collected with different technologies in different labs. Our NCEMS working group will synthesize bacterial gene expression data using machine learning to create a first-of-its-kind atlas of bacterial cell states. To manageably scale data collection and analysis, we will build from examining model Escherichia coli strains in lab conditions, to adding wild E. coli strains in natural environments such as the human gut, to including diverse bacterial species with additional cell states. We expect to identify distinct foci corresponding to bacterial growth states and lifestyles (e.g., replicating, starving, motile, biofilm, spore, viable but nonculturable) by mapping the organization and occupancy of cell state space with dimensional reduction approaches. We will examine to what extent the gene expression signatures of different cell states and the relationships among them are conserved during bacterial evolution. Finally, we will use this framework to create a classifier that predicts the cell state composition of a bacterial population from metatranscriptomic data. By following open-science practices, we will make our pipelines and datasets reusable and maintainable by the research community. Our project may reveal new bacterial cell states and ways that we can non-genetically reprogram bacteria to prevent them from adopting lifestyles that damage the environment and cause disease.
full_draft_original: Introduction and Goals Bacterial cells modulate gene expression to adapt their physiology to changes in their environment, for example transitioning from actively replicating to quiescent states in response to nutrient exhaustion. Much like cells within multicellular organisms, clonal bacterial populations can diversify and differentiate into cell types with distinct phenotypes such as biofilm or planktonic growth, motile or sessile forms, and specialized nitrogen-fixing cells. However, it remains unclear to what extent bacterial cells have evolved to occupy a small number of discrete gene expression states that they abruptly transition between, or if they exist along a continuum of states that gradually shift in composition. Less is known about how these gene expression states are related and conserved across species during evolution, and it is possible that some bacterial cell states remain undiscovered because existing data are limited to specific laboratory conditions and strains. The goal of this project is to test key hypotheses about the organization of bacterial gene expression space and to synthesize this information into a unified atlas of bacterial cell states. Specifically, we aim to determine whether bacterial cells occupy and transition between a limited number of distinct states, whether key principles such as the growth–quiescence axis are conserved across species, whether specialized lifestyles such as biofilm formation evolved from subfunctionalization of core states, and whether a comprehensive atlas of these states can enable prediction of population composition from transcriptomic data. We will synthesize existing bacterial gene expression datasets collected using microarray and RNA-seq technologies, beginning with model Escherichia coli strains, then expanding to wild isolates and ultimately to diverse bacterial species, to examine the organization and occupancy of bacterial gene expression state space. Existing Datasets Thousands of bacterial gene expression datasets have been generated and deposited in databases such as OKgeneExpDB, E. coli Expression 2, Ecomics, PRECISE, COLUMBOS, and iModulonDB. These repositories encompass tens of thousands of gene expression profiles representing variations in environmental conditions, genetic backgrounds, and experimental perturbations. Although many datasets include curated metadata and quality control, most existing resources are not fully open or community-maintained, limiting reuse and integration. Prior Analyses Machine learning approaches have previously been applied to predict bacterial growth rates and conditions from gene expression profiles and to identify modules of co-regulated genes. However, differences in technologies, protocols, and experimental designs introduce systematic variation that can confound these analyses. Robust harmonization of datasets and advanced quality control are necessary to enable meaningful synthesis and discovery. Project Significance Previous studies have not focused on systematically identifying bacterial cell states, which we define as distinct growth or lifestyle conditions characterized by coordinated shifts in gene expression across many genes. For example, aerobic planktonic growth represents one state, distinct from anaerobic growth, starvation, or biofilm formation. While single-cell RNA-seq could eventually define these states with precision, technical challenges currently limit its applicability to bacteria. Instead, we will integrate existing bulk gene expression datasets, reasoning that many of them capture nearly pure cell states or mixtures of a few dominant ones. Using dimensional reduction and clustering methods, we aim to infer an atlas of bacterial cell states and the relationships among them. Proposed Activities Develop the open-source inGEST pipeline for harmonizing bacterial gene expression datasets Our analysis requires assembling and processing large numbers of high-quality gene expression datasets. We will process tens of thousands of RNA-seq and microarray datasets from public repositories in a uniform way, applying standardized filtering and normalization while identifying and correcting for technical variation. The Integrative Gene Expression Synthesis Tool (InGEST) will include conventional preprocessing steps for both microarray and RNA-seq data as well as advanced quality control functions that detect anomalies such as DNA contamination or inconsistent replicates. Using the scale of the aggregated data, we will train algorithms to identify and adjust for systematic biases, such as those introduced by differing read lengths or protocols. InGEST will be released as an open, community-maintainable software package with full documentation, tutorials, and containerized deployment options to ensure accessibility and long-term sustainability. Apply dimensional reduction methods to create the Atlas of Bacterial Cell States To delineate distinct cell states and understand their relationships, we will apply unsupervised learning and dimensional reduction techniques commonly used in eukaryotic single-cell RNA-seq analysis. These approaches can reveal structure in high-dimensional data and help identify clusters corresponding to biological states. Our initial focus will be on curated Escherichia coli datasets, where we expect to identify primary attractors corresponding to exponential growth and stationary phase, forming a foundational growth–quiescence axis. Additional variation will likely correspond to sub-states such as stress responses or biofilm-associated growth. As InGEST matures, we will extend the analysis to non-laboratory E. coli strains and to natural environments such as the gut, identifying subfunctionalized states that build on the conserved axes. To account for variation in gene content between strains, we will use ortholog mapping tools such as Orthofinder to establish a consistent feature space across datasets. Finally, we will expand the analysis to include more than twenty bacterial species with sufficient datasets, encompassing model organisms and pathogens that exhibit additional states such as sporulation or quorum sensing. This broader atlas will allow us to identify conserved and specialized expression patterns and explore evolutionary relationships among cell states. Create a classifier that predicts the distribution of cell states in bacterial populations Using the atlas as a foundation, we will train classifiers to estimate the proportions of cells occupying different states within bulk transcriptomic or metatranscriptomic samples. Initially, we will train and validate these models on synthetic mixtures generated from pure-state datasets and later test them on available single-cell bacterial transcriptomes. Ultimately, we will apply these classifiers to environmental and host-associated microbial communities to predict functional composition and state distribution, providing a new lens for interpreting community-level gene expression. Outcomes This project will generate conceptual, methodological, and practical outcomes. Scientifically, it will yield the first comprehensive Atlas of Bacterial Cell States, revealing how gene expression landscapes are structured and conserved across species and environments. Methodologically, it will produce three key open-source products: the InGEST pipeline for harmonizing bacterial gene expression data, the Atlas of Bacterial Cell States as a community resource with visualization tools, and the Bacterial Cell Population Classifier that predicts cell state composition from expression data. Collectively, these resources will enable new analyses of bacterial physiology, evolution, and ecology. By integrating and harmonizing unprecedented amounts of data, we expect to uncover organizing principles of bacterial behavior and potentially identify novel cell states. Future work can extend this framework to other microbial domains and data types, including proteomics and metabolomics, enabling multi-omics integration of microbial states. Rationale for NCEMS support This project exemplifies mesoscale data synthesis: it leverages machine learning to integrate and analyze large volumes of bacterial gene expression data. Achieving this requires reproducible, scalable pipelines and community infrastructure that individual groups cannot maintain alone. NCEMS support is essential for implementing best practices in data management and sustainability, ensuring that the resulting resources are open, reusable, and extensible. In addition, NCEMS computational expertise will help in developing and applying advanced analytical methods for visualizing and quantifying relationships between bacterial cell states. Requested resources The primary computational demands involve downloading, processing, and analyzing thousands of RNA-seq datasets. Each dataset ranges from a few hundred megabytes to several gigabytes and can be processed within minutes on modern CPUs. Microarray data require negligible storage and compute time. Dimensional reduction and machine learning analyses can initially be run on modest hardware but may benefit from scalable computing for cross-species analyses. The final resource will consist of metadata, gene expression matrices, and annotated reference genomes, small enough to be hosted publicly and versioned for community access. Proposed Timeline The project will span two years. In the first year, we will focus on Escherichia coli, developing and validating the InGEST pipeline, harmonizing thousands of datasets, and identifying major cell states and marker genes. The second year will expand to additional bacterial species, refine the atlas to include conserved and specialized states, and develop the classifier for predicting state composition in mixed samples. Publications describing both the pipeline and the atlas will disseminate the findings and ensure long-term visibility and reuse.

criteria.justification: The proposal targets mesoscale emergence by inferring discrete/continuous bacterial “cell states” and transitions from population-level transcriptomes, aiming to reveal organizing principles (attractors/axes) that arise from many-gene coordination. While compelling, the link to emergence could be made more explicit via formal definitions/metrics of state transitions and attractor structure.

A cross-species atlas of bacterial cell states and a deconvolution-style classifier for metatranscriptomes would be a substantial advance beyond existing condition/growth predictors and module resources. The potential impact is high, though similar concepts exist in eukaryotic single-cell atlases and bacterial iModulon/compendium efforts, making it more highly novel than fully transformative.

The overall workflow (harmonization → embedding/clustering → cross-species mapping → classifier) is logical, but key methodological details are underspecified (batch correction strategy across platforms, validation of inferred states, handling confounding by strain/medium/library prep, and quantitative criteria for “states”). Stronger plans for benchmarking, uncertainty quantification, and sensitivity analyses would improve rigor.

E. coli-focused harmonization and atlas construction in year 1 is plausible, but expanding to wild strains, gut environments, and >20 species plus building/validating a metatranscriptomic state-composition classifier in year 2 is ambitious. Feasibility would be improved by clearer go/no-go milestones, prioritization of a smaller species set, and contingency plans if cross-platform harmonization underperforms.

The project is explicitly and exclusively based on integrating existing public microarray/RNA-seq and metatranscriptomic resources, with no new experimental data generation. The core deliverables (pipeline, atlas, classifier) are inherently synthesis products requiring large-scale integration.

Several relevant repositories/compendia are named, but the proposal lacks a concrete data inventory (inclusion/exclusion criteria, target sample counts per species/state, metadata fields required, and licensing/access constraints). Limitations are acknowledged at a high level (technology/protocol variation), but important issues (metadata sparsity/misannotation, compositionality in metatranscriptomes, gene-content differences, and label scarcity for “pure states”) need more explicit treatment.

The team commits to open-source, community-maintainable software, containerized deployment, documentation, and public release of pipelines and datasets. However, the plan would be stronger with specifics on governance/maintenance (e.g., steering, contribution model), reproducibility standards (workflow language, CI testing), and data/product versioning and archival (DOIs, long-term hosting).
The proposal directly addresses emergent phenomena by framing bacterial phenotypes as distinct attractors (cell states) within a high-dimensional gene expression space.
The creation of a cross-species atlas and the shift from single-lab analysis to community-scale synthesis represents a significant and novel advancement in microbial systems biology.
The methodology is logical, utilizing established machine learning techniques and addressing critical issues like batch effects, though cross-species harmonization remains a complex challenge.
While the E. coli analysis is feasible, expanding to over twenty diverse species and developing a robust classifier within the second year is highly ambitious and may face scaling challenges.
The project is an exemplary synthesis effort, relying exclusively on aggregating and harmonizing existing public datasets without generating new experimental data.
The proposal explicitly identifies multiple specific repositories (e.g., COLUMBOS, iModulonDB) and thoroughly discusses limitations regarding technical variation and data harmonization.
The proposal demonstrates an exemplary commitment to open science through plans for open-source software (InGEST), containerization, documentation, and community maintenance.

The proposal addresses bacterial cell states and their transitions, which relates to emergent phenomena at the cellular level. However, the connection to mesoscale emergence is implicit rather than explicitly framed, focusing more on classification than on understanding how cell states emerge from molecular interactions.

Creating a comprehensive atlas of bacterial cell states across species is highly novel and addresses a significant gap in the field. The integration of diverse datasets to identify conserved and specialized states represents a meaningful advancement in understanding bacterial physiology and evolution.

The methodology is well-structured with clear progression from E. coli to diverse species, appropriate use of dimensional reduction techniques, and validation strategies including synthetic mixtures. The approach to handling technical variation through the InGEST pipeline demonstrates methodological rigor.

The two-year timeline is ambitious given the scope of harmonizing thousands of datasets across multiple species and developing three major deliverables. While the phased approach is logical, expanding to 20+ bacterial species in year two while also developing the classifier may be challenging.

The proposal is exclusively focused on synthesizing existing publicly available gene expression data from multiple repositories. No new experimental data generation is proposed, making this an exemplary synthesis project.

Multiple specific databases are identified (OKgeneExpDB, E. coli Expression 2, Ecomics, PRECISE, COLUMBOS, iModulonDB), and limitations regarding metadata quality and technical variation are acknowledged. However, more detail on data availability for non-E. coli species would strengthen this aspect.

The proposal demonstrates strong commitment to open science through plans for open-source software (InGEST), containerized deployment, full documentation, tutorials, and publicly accessible datasets. The emphasis on community-maintainable resources is commendable, though specific repository choices and licensing details could be more explicit.

full_draft_original:
Title: Emergent Cell Polarity from Protein Localization Networks: Synthesizing Imaging and Interactome Data to Model Symmetry Breaking

Abstract: Cell polarity emerges from protein localization networks where initially uniform distributions spontaneously break symmetry—a mesoscale phenomenon where spatial organization arises from molecular interactions. This synthesis project will decode emergent polarity by integrating imaging, proteomics, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize protein localization data from the Human Protein Atlas and Cell Image Library, protein-protein interactions from BioGRID, phosphoproteomics from PhosphoSitePlus, and live-cell imaging from published studies capturing polarity establishment. The central question is: how do reaction-diffusion networks of polarity proteins create emergent spatial organization at the mesoscale (1-10 μm polarity domains) from initially homogeneous distributions? We hypothesize that emergent polarity arises from positive feedback loops in membrane-cytoplasm cycling, mutual antagonism between polarity complexes, and scaffolding interactions that amplify initial asymmetries. Our computational approach combines reaction-diffusion modeling of polarity networks, machine learning to predict polarity outcomes from protein expression patterns, and image analysis to quantify polarity establishment dynamics. We will develop algorithms integrating interaction networks with spatial localization data, testing which network motifs are necessary and sufficient for emergent symmetry breaking. Integration with single-cell RNA-seq will connect polarity protein expression heterogeneity to polarity establishment variability. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal conserved versus specialized emergent polarity mechanisms. This project demands expertise in cell polarity, mathematical modeling, image analysis, and systems biology—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of imaging, interaction, and expression data exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent polarity, identification of minimal network requirements for symmetry breaking, and principles for engineering polarized cells. Understanding emergent polarity has implications for development, cancer, and tissue engineering. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

Background: Cell polarity—the asymmetric organization of cellular components—represents one of the most fundamental examples of emergent behavior in biology. From the first asymmetric division of a fertilized egg to the apical-basal organization of epithelial tissues, polarity underlies virtually all aspects of multicellular life. What makes polarity particularly fascinating from an emergence perspective is that it arises spontaneously from initially homogeneous protein distributions through self-organizing molecular networks. This symmetry breaking occurs at the mesoscale, typically generating polarity domains of 1-10 micrometers—precisely the scale between individual biomolecules and organelles that NCEMS prioritizes.

The molecular players in cell polarity have been extensively characterized over the past three decades. The PAR (partitioning defective) proteins, originally discovered in C. elegans, form conserved polarity complexes across metazoans. The anterior PAR complex (PAR-3/PAR-6/aPKC) and posterior PAR complex (PAR-1/PAR-2) establish mutually exclusive membrane domains through reciprocal phosphorylation-dependent exclusion. Similarly, the Rho GTPases Cdc42, Rac, and RhoA establish polarized activity zones through positive feedback loops involving guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) and GTPase-activating proteins (GAPs). The Crumbs and Scribble complexes further reinforce epithelial polarity. Despite this molecular knowledge, we lack quantitative understanding of how these components collectively generate emergent spatial organization.

Theoretical frameworks for understanding polarity emergence exist but remain disconnected from comprehensive molecular data. Alan Turing's reaction-diffusion theory, proposed in 1952, demonstrated mathematically how spatial patterns can emerge from homogeneous initial conditions through the interplay of activators and inhibitors with different diffusion rates. More recently, wave-pinning models and mass-conserved reaction-diffusion systems have been applied to explain polarity establishment in specific contexts. However, these models typically focus on simplified two- or three-component systems, while actual polarity networks involve dozens of interacting proteins with complex regulatory relationships.

The gap between molecular knowledge and systems-level understanding represents a critical barrier to progress. Individual laboratories have characterized specific polarity proteins, measured interaction affinities, determined phosphorylation sites, and imaged polarity establishment in particular cell types. However, no single lab possesses the expertise or resources to synthesize these heterogeneous data types into comprehensive, predictive models of emergent polarity. This synthesis challenge is precisely what NCEMS is designed to address.

Existing publicly available data now make such synthesis feasible. The Human Protein Atlas contains subcellular localization images for over 12,000 human proteins, including all major polarity regulators, across multiple cell lines. The Cell Image Library archives thousands of time-lapse sequences capturing polarity establishment in diverse contexts. BioGRID documents over 2 million protein-protein interactions, including extensive polarity protein networks. PhosphoSitePlus catalogs phosphorylation sites that regulate polarity protein localization and activity. Single-cell RNA sequencing datasets in the Gene Expression Omnibus and Human Cell Atlas reveal cell-to-cell variability in polarity gene expression. The Image Data Resource and EMBL-EBI BioImage Archive provide standardized access to published imaging datasets. Critically, these resources have never been systematically integrated to address how emergent polarity arises from molecular interactions.

Understanding emergent polarity has profound implications beyond basic science. Polarity loss is a hallmark of cancer, with disrupted PAR and Scribble complexes contributing to tumor invasion and metastasis. Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition involves dramatic polarity reorganization. Tissue engineering efforts to create functional organoids require establishing proper polarity. Asymmetric stem cell divisions depend on polarity-mediated fate determinant segregation. By developing quantitative, predictive models of emergent polarity, this synthesis project will provide foundational knowledge for understanding disease mechanisms and engineering cellular systems.

The mesoscale nature of polarity domains makes this an ideal system for NCEMS. Polarity emerges from nanometer-scale molecular interactions but manifests as micrometer-scale spatial organization—precisely the mesoscale regime where emergent properties are most apparent yet least understood. The transition from molecular binding events to cellular-scale asymmetry involves nonlinear amplification, threshold behaviors, and collective dynamics that cannot be predicted from molecular properties alone. This project will establish general principles for how mesoscale organization emerges from molecular networks, with implications extending far beyond polarity to other self-organizing cellular systems.

Research Questions: This synthesis project addresses a central question: How do reaction-diffusion networks of polarity proteins create emergent spatial organization at the mesoscale from initially homogeneous distributions? We decompose this overarching question into four specific, testable research questions with associated hypotheses that can be validated using existing publicly available data.

**Research Question 1: What are the minimal network motifs sufficient for emergent symmetry breaking in polarity establishment?**

Hypothesis 1a: Positive feedback through membrane-cytoplasm cycling is necessary but not sufficient for symmetry breaking. We predict that polarity proteins exhibiting polarized localization in the Human Protein Atlas will show significantly higher rates of membrane-cytoplasm exchange (as documented in FRAP studies in the literature) compared to uniformly distributed proteins. This can be tested by correlating localization patterns with published diffusion and exchange rate measurements.

Hypothesis 1b: Mutual antagonism between anterior and posterior polarity complexes, mediated by phosphorylation, is required for stable domain boundaries. We predict that phosphorylation sites documented in PhosphoSitePlus for PAR proteins will map to regions that regulate membrane binding affinity, and that the kinase-substrate relationships in the PhosphoSitePlus regulatory network will form coherent antagonistic circuits. Cross-validation with BioGRID interaction data will test whether physical interactions support the predicted regulatory relationships.

Hypothesis 1c: Scaffold proteins that cluster polarity regulators lower the threshold for symmetry breaking by increasing local concentration. We predict that polarity proteins with more scaffold interactions in BioGRID will show sharper domain boundaries in imaging data and will be more frequently required for polarity in loss-of-function studies documented in the literature.

**Research Question 2: How does cell-to-cell variability in polarity protein expression influence the robustness and dynamics of emergent polarity?**

Hypothesis 2a: Cells with higher expression of positive feedback components establish polarity faster but with less precise domain positioning. We will test this by correlating single-cell RNA-seq expression levels from Human Cell Atlas datasets with polarity establishment dynamics extracted from published live-cell imaging studies of the same or comparable cell types.

Hypothesis 2b: Expression noise in mutual antagonism components increases variability in domain boundary position. We predict that genes encoding antagonistic polarity regulators will show correlated noise patterns (high noise in one compensated by high noise in its antagonist) in single-cell expression data, reflecting evolutionary pressure to maintain balanced antagonism.

Hypothesis 2c: Stoichiometric imbalances in polarity complex components, detectable in single-cell RNA-seq data, predict polarity defects observable in imaging datasets. We will identify cells or cell types with atypical stoichiometry and test whether corresponding imaging data shows aberrant polarity.

**Research Question 3: Are the network principles underlying emergent polarity conserved across cell types, or do different cells employ distinct emergent mechanisms?**

Hypothesis 3a: Core polarity network motifs (positive feedback, mutual antagonism, scaffolding) are conserved, but the specific molecular implementations vary across cell types. We will test this by comparing polarity protein interaction networks across cell types using cell-type-specific interaction data from BioGRID and tissue-specific expression from GTEx and Human Protein Atlas.

Hypothesis 3b: Cell types with faster polarity establishment (e.g., migrating cells) employ stronger positive feedback, while cell types requiring stable long-term polarity (e.g., epithelia) employ stronger mutual antagonism. This can be tested by parameterizing reaction-diffusion models with cell-type-specific interaction and expression data and comparing predicted dynamics with published imaging timecourses.

Hypothesis 3c: Specialized polarity mechanisms in specific cell types involve recruitment of cell-type-specific proteins into conserved network motifs. We will identify cell-type-specific polarity protein expression patterns and test whether these proteins integrate into core polarity networks through interactions documented in BioGRID.

**Research Question 4: Can machine learning models trained on integrated imaging and molecular data predict polarity outcomes from protein expression and interaction patterns?**

Hypothesis 4a: Polarity establishment success can be predicted from the expression levels of core polarity network components with >80% accuracy. We will train classifiers on single-cell expression data linked to polarity phenotypes extracted from imaging datasets.

Hypothesis 4b: The predictive features identified by machine learning will correspond to known network motifs (positive feedback strength, antagonism balance, scaffold availability), providing interpretable mechanistic insights. Feature importance analysis will be compared against predictions from reaction-diffusion models.

Hypothesis 4c: Transfer learning from well-characterized polarity systems (e.g., C. elegans embryo, MDCK cells) will improve predictions in less-studied systems, indicating conserved emergent principles. We will test cross-system prediction accuracy using published datasets from diverse organisms and cell types.

**Validation Strategy**

All hypotheses will be validated exclusively using existing data through multiple approaches: (1) Cross-dataset validation, where predictions from one data type (e.g., interactions) are tested against independent data (e.g., imaging); (2) Known positive controls, where models must correctly predict well-established polarity phenotypes; (3) Held-out test sets, where machine learning models are evaluated on data not used in training; (4) Literature validation, where computational predictions are compared against published experimental findings. This multi-pronged validation strategy ensures robust conclusions without generating new experimental data.

Methods: **Data Sources and Acquisition**

This synthesis project will integrate data from multiple publicly available repositories, each providing complementary information about polarity protein networks:

*Protein Localization Data:* The Human Protein Atlas (HPA, proteinatlas.org) provides immunofluorescence images showing subcellular localization for >12,000 human proteins across multiple cell lines. We will extract localization patterns for all annotated polarity-related proteins (~150 core polarity genes plus ~500 associated regulators). The Cell Image Library (cellimagelibrary.org) and Image Data Resource (idr.openmicroscopy.org) provide additional high-resolution imaging data, including time-lapse sequences of polarity establishment. The EMBL-EBI BioImage Archive (bioimage-archive.org) contains standardized imaging datasets from published studies.

*Protein-Protein Interactions:* BioGRID (thebiogrid.org) contains >2 million curated interactions, including extensive polarity protein networks. We will extract all interactions involving polarity proteins and their first-degree neighbors. IntAct (ebi.ac.uk/intact) and STRING (string-db.org) will provide complementary interaction data with confidence scores. The Bioplex interactome (bioplex.hms.harvard.edu) offers systematic affinity-purification mass spectrometry data for interaction validation.

*Phosphoproteomics:* PhosphoSitePlus (phosphosite.org) catalogs >400,000 phosphorylation sites with regulatory annotations. We will extract all phosphorylation sites on polarity proteins, associated kinases, and functional consequences. The Kinase Library (kinase-library.org) provides kinase-substrate predictions for sites lacking experimental kinase identification.

*Gene Expression:* Single-cell RNA-seq data from the Human Cell Atlas (humancellatlas.org), Gene Expression Omnibus (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo), and Single Cell Portal (singlecell.broadinstitute.org) will provide cell-type-specific and single-cell resolution expression data. GTEx (gtexportal.org) provides tissue-level expression across human tissues. We will focus on datasets from epithelial cells, migrating cells, and stem cells where polarity is well-characterized.

*Structural Data:* The Protein Data Bank (rcsb.org) contains structures of polarity protein domains and complexes. AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (alphafold.ebi.ac.uk) provides predicted structures for proteins lacking experimental structures. These will inform binding interface predictions and membrane interaction modeling.

**Data Integration and Harmonization**

Integrating heterogeneous data types requires careful harmonization. We will develop a unified data model centered on polarity proteins, with edges representing interactions, modifications, expression levels, and localization patterns. Gene/protein identifiers will be mapped to UniProt accessions using the UniProt ID mapping service. Interaction data will be scored by evidence type and combined across databases using a Bayesian framework that weights experimental evidence. Expression data will be normalized using established pipelines (Scanpy for single-cell, DESeq2 normalization approaches for bulk). Image data will be processed using standardized segmentation and quantification pipelines built on CellProfiler and custom Python tools.

**Computational and Analytical Methods**

*Reaction-Diffusion Modeling:* We will develop partial differential equation (PDE) models of polarity protein dynamics based on established frameworks. Models will incorporate: (1) membrane-cytoplasm exchange with rates parameterized from published FRAP data; (2) protein-protein interactions with affinities from BioGRID and structural predictions; (3) phosphorylation-dependent regulation with kinetics from PhosphoSitePlus annotations. Models will be implemented in Python using FEniCS for finite element solutions and will be systematically varied to identify minimal sufficient networks. Parameter sensitivity analysis will identify critical parameters controlling symmetry breaking.

*Network Analysis:* We will apply graph-theoretic methods to identify network motifs associated with polarity. Motif enrichment analysis will compare polarity networks against randomized networks. Community detection algorithms will identify functional modules. Network controllability analysis will predict which nodes are most critical for polarity establishment.

*Machine Learning:* We will develop predictive models linking molecular features to polarity outcomes. Random forests and gradient boosting will provide interpretable predictions with feature importance. Graph neural networks will learn directly from interaction network structure. Convolutional neural networks will extract features from localization images. All models will be trained with cross-validation and evaluated on held-out test sets.

*Image Analysis:* Automated pipelines will quantify polarity from imaging data. We will measure: polarity index (asymmetry of protein distribution), domain size, boundary sharpness, and establishment dynamics from time-lapse data. Deep learning segmentation (using pre-trained models from cellpose) will identify cell boundaries. Custom algorithms will quantify membrane versus cytoplasmic localization.

**Synthesis Approach**

The key innovation is integrating these heterogeneous data types to test mechanistic hypotheses about emergent polarity. Our synthesis workflow proceeds as follows: (1) Construct comprehensive polarity protein interaction networks from BioGRID/IntAct/STRING; (2) Annotate networks with phosphoregulation from PhosphoSitePlus; (3) Parameterize reaction-diffusion models using interaction and kinetic data; (4) Validate model predictions against localization patterns from HPA and dynamics from time-lapse imaging; (5) Incorporate expression variability from single-cell RNA-seq to predict cell-to-cell differences; (6) Train machine learning models on integrated features to predict polarity outcomes; (7) Compare across cell types to identify conserved versus specialized mechanisms.

**Validation Strategy**

All validation uses existing data: (1) Cross-validation between data types (e.g., predicted interactions validated against co-localization); (2) Known positive controls (models must predict established polarity phenotypes); (3) Literature benchmarking (predictions compared against published experimental results); (4) Held-out test sets for machine learning.

**Timeline and Milestones**

*Year 1:* Data acquisition and harmonization (months 1-4); Initial network construction and annotation (months 3-6); Reaction-diffusion model development (months 4-9); Image analysis pipeline development (months 6-12); First working group meeting at NCEMS (month 6).

*Year 2:* Model parameterization and validation (months 13-18); Machine learning model development (months 15-20); Cross-cell-type comparative analysis (months 18-24); Second working group meeting (month 18); Preprint of initial findings (month 24).

*Year 3:* Model refinement and integration (months 25-30); Comprehensive synthesis and interpretation (months 28-33); Tool and database release (months 30-36); Final publications and dissemination (months 33-36); Training workshop (month 34).

**Team Composition**

This project requires expertise spanning: (1) Cell polarity biology—understanding of PAR proteins, Rho GTPases, and polarity mechanisms; (2) Mathematical modeling—reaction-diffusion systems, dynamical systems theory; (3) Computational image analysis—segmentation, feature extraction, deep learning for microscopy; (4) Systems biology and network analysis—graph theory, network inference; (5) Machine learning—predictive modeling, feature engineering; (6) Data science—large-scale data integration, database management. No single laboratory possesses all these capabilities, necessitating the transdisciplinary collaboration that NCEMS enables.

Expected Outcomes: **Specific Deliverables**

This synthesis project will produce multiple tangible outcomes that advance understanding of emergent polarity and provide resources for the broader research community:

*Integrated Polarity Database:* We will create a comprehensive, publicly accessible database integrating polarity protein interactions, phosphoregulation, localization patterns, and expression data. This resource will include: curated interaction networks for >600 polarity-associated proteins; annotated phosphorylation sites with regulatory consequences; standardized localization classifications across cell types; links to primary imaging data and expression datasets. The database will be hosted with long-term sustainability through established repositories (e.g., EMBL-EBI) and will include programmatic access via REST APIs.

*Quantitative Reaction-Diffusion Models:* We will deliver parameterized mathematical models of polarity establishment for multiple cell types. Models will be provided as: documented Python code with clear parameter definitions; interactive Jupyter notebooks allowing parameter exploration; pre-computed simulation results for common scenarios; model files compatible with standard simulation tools (COPASI, VCell). These models will enable researchers to test hypotheses about polarity mechanisms computationally before experimental validation.

*Minimal Network Motifs:* Through systematic model reduction and network analysis, we will identify the minimal sufficient network architectures for symmetry breaking. This will include: ranked lists of essential versus dispensable interactions; quantitative thresholds for feedback strength and antagonism balance; design principles for engineering polarized systems. These findings will be presented as both detailed technical reports and accessible summaries for non-specialists.

*Machine Learning Predictive Tools:* We will release trained models that predict polarity outcomes from molecular features. Tools will include: web-accessible prediction interfaces; downloadable model weights and code; documentation for applying models to new datasets; benchmarking results against known polarity phenotypes. These tools will enable researchers to predict polarity behavior in unstudied cell types or conditions.

*Image Analysis Pipelines:* Automated pipelines for quantifying polarity from microscopy images will be released as: CellProfiler pipelines for standard analyses; Python packages for custom quantification; pre-trained deep learning models for polarity feature extraction; tutorials and example datasets for pipeline validation.

**Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena**

This project directly addresses NCEMS's focus on emergent properties at the mesoscale. Cell polarity exemplifies how molecular-scale interactions (nanometer binding events, phosphorylation) generate micrometer-scale spatial organization through nonlinear amplification and self-organization. Our synthesis will reveal:

*Principles of Biological Symmetry Breaking:* By identifying minimal network motifs sufficient for polarity, we will establish general principles for how biological systems break symmetry. These principles—positive feedback, mutual antagonism, scaffolding—likely apply beyond polarity to other self-organizing systems including cytoskeletal organization, signaling gradients, and phase separation.

*Quantitative Understanding of Emergence:* Current understanding of polarity is largely qualitative. Our parameterized models will provide quantitative predictions: how much feedback is needed? What antagonism strength maintains stable boundaries? How does expression noise affect robustness? This quantitative framework transforms emergence from a descriptive concept to a predictive science.

*Scale-Bridging Insights:* By connecting molecular interactions to cellular-scale organization, we address the fundamental challenge of understanding how properties at one scale give rise to behaviors at larger scales. Our multi-scale modeling approach—from binding affinities to domain sizes—provides a template for studying emergence in other biological contexts.

**Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology**

Beyond polarity specifically, this project will impact the broader field:

*Methodological Advances:* Our data integration frameworks, combining imaging, interaction, and expression data, will be applicable to other cellular processes. The synthesis approaches we develop will serve as templates for future NCEMS projects addressing different emergent phenomena.

*Disease Understanding:* Polarity disruption contributes to cancer progression, with loss of PAR and Scribble function promoting invasion and metastasis. Our models will help identify which network perturbations most strongly disrupt polarity, potentially revealing therapeutic targets. Understanding polarity variability may explain why some cells are more susceptible to transformation.

*Tissue Engineering:* Creating functional tissues requires establishing proper polarity. Our design principles for minimal polarity networks will guide efforts to engineer polarized organoids and synthetic tissues. Predictive models will help optimize culture conditions for polarity establishment.

*Developmental Biology:* Asymmetric cell division, axis formation, and tissue morphogenesis all depend on polarity. Our comparative analysis across cell types will reveal how polarity mechanisms are adapted for different developmental contexts.

**Enabling Future Research**

This synthesis project will catalyze future investigations by:

*Generating Testable Predictions:* Our models will make specific, quantitative predictions that can be tested experimentally by other laboratories. We will explicitly document key predictions and the experiments needed to test them, enabling the broader community to validate and extend our findings.

*Identifying Knowledge Gaps:* Systematic data integration will reveal where existing data are insufficient, guiding future data generation efforts. We will document these gaps in our publications and database annotations.

*Providing Computational Infrastructure:* Our tools and pipelines will lower barriers for other researchers to study polarity computationally. Training materials will enable adoption by laboratories without extensive computational expertise.

**Dissemination Plans**

*Publications:* We anticipate 4-6 peer-reviewed publications: (1) comprehensive polarity interaction network analysis; (2) reaction-diffusion modeling of symmetry breaking; (3) machine learning prediction of polarity outcomes; (4) comparative analysis across cell types; (5) methods paper on data integration approaches; (6) review synthesizing emergent polarity principles.
