full_draft_original:
Title: Emergent Mechanics of Bacterial Microcompartments: Synthesizing Structural and Metabolic Data to Model Encapsulated Pathway Efficiency

Abstract: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) represent emergent metabolic organelles where protein shells encapsulate enzyme pathways, creating efficiency and selectivity impossible in the cytoplasm. This synthesis project will decode emergent BMC function by integrating structural biology, metabolomics, and systems biology datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of BMC shells and encapsulated enzymes, metabolomics from MetaboLights, enzyme kinetics from BRENDA, and genomic data on BMC operons from NCBI. The central question is: how does BMC shell architecture at the mesoscale (40-200 nm compartments) create emergent metabolic properties—enhanced pathway flux, toxic intermediate sequestration, and substrate selectivity—that free enzymes cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent efficiency arises from shell pore selectivity, enzyme co-localization effects, and internal environment optimization. Our computational approach combines finite element modeling of metabolite diffusion through BMC shells, kinetic modeling of encapsulated pathways, and machine learning to predict BMC function from shell composition. We will develop algorithms correlating shell protein properties with pore selectivity. Integration with fitness data from published studies will connect BMC organization to growth phenotypes. Comparative analysis across BMC types (carboxysomes, metabolosomes) will reveal shared principles of emergent encapsulated metabolism. This project requires expertise in BMC biology, structural biology, metabolic modeling, and biophysics—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, metabolic, and genomic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent BMC efficiency, identification of key architectural features determining function, and principles for engineering synthetic compartments. Understanding emergent BMC function has implications for metabolic engineering and synthetic biology. All simulation code, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

Background: Bacterial microcompartments (BMCs) represent one of the most fascinating examples of emergent organization in prokaryotic cells. These proteinaceous organelles, ranging from 40 to 200 nanometers in diameter, encapsulate sequential metabolic enzymes within selectively permeable protein shells, creating distinct biochemical environments that fundamentally alter pathway behavior. BMCs occupy a critical position at the mesoscale—larger than individual protein complexes yet smaller than classical organelles—where emergent properties arise from the collective organization of molecular components in ways that cannot be predicted from studying individual parts in isolation.

The field has accumulated substantial structural and functional data on BMCs over the past two decades. Cryo-electron microscopy studies deposited in the Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) have revealed the architecture of complete BMC shells, including carboxysomes from cyanobacteria and chemoautotrophs, and metabolosomes involved in propanediol and ethanolamine utilization. The Protein Data Bank (PDB) contains over 200 high-resolution structures of BMC shell proteins, revealing the hexameric (BMC-H), trimeric (BMC-T), and pentameric (BMC-P) building blocks that tile together to form icosahedral or elongated shells. These structures have identified central pores in shell proteins that serve as selective gates for metabolite transport, with pore diameters ranging from 4 to 14 Ångstroms and varying electrostatic properties.

Despite this wealth of structural information, fundamental questions about emergent BMC function remain unanswered. How does the specific arrangement of shell proteins create selective permeability that differs qualitatively from simple diffusion barriers? How does enzyme encapsulation within the confined BMC lumen alter kinetic parameters compared to the same enzymes operating freely in the cytoplasm? What organizational principles determine whether a BMC enhances pathway flux, sequesters toxic intermediates, or both? These questions cannot be answered by examining individual components; they require understanding how mesoscale organization creates system-level behaviors.

Existing data sources provide unprecedented opportunities for synthesis research to address these gaps. The BRENDA enzyme database contains kinetic parameters for many BMC-encapsulated enzymes measured both in isolation and in cellular contexts. MetaboLights and the Metabolomics Workbench house metabolomics datasets from organisms with and without functional BMCs, enabling comparative analysis of metabolic phenotypes. NCBI GenBank contains thousands of annotated BMC operons across diverse bacterial phyla, revealing the genomic organization and evolutionary relationships of these systems. Fitness data from high-throughput transposon mutagenesis studies, available through resources like FitnessBrowser, connect BMC gene disruptions to growth phenotypes under various conditions.

The significance of understanding emergent BMC function extends across multiple domains. From a fundamental biology perspective, BMCs represent a natural solution to the challenge of organizing metabolism at the mesoscale—a problem that eukaryotes solve with membrane-bound organelles. Understanding the principles by which protein shells create functional compartmentalization illuminates general mechanisms of cellular organization. From an applied perspective, BMCs are increasingly recognized as platforms for metabolic engineering, where encapsulating synthetic pathways could enhance production of valuable compounds. However, rational engineering requires quantitative understanding of how shell architecture determines function—precisely the knowledge gap this synthesis project addresses.

The mesoscale nature of BMCs makes them ideal subjects for NCEMS-supported research. At 40-200 nm, BMCs exist at the interface between molecular and cellular scales, where emergent properties arise from the collective behavior of hundreds of shell proteins and dozens of encapsulated enzymes. The internal environment of a BMC—with its altered pH, ionic strength, and molecular crowding—cannot be understood from molecular structures alone but requires modeling the integrated system. Similarly, the selective permeability of BMC shells emerges from the arrangement of multiple pore types across the shell surface, creating transport properties that depend on mesoscale organization.

Current understanding is fragmented across disciplines. Structural biologists have characterized shell protein architectures but rarely connect these to metabolic function. Metabolic modelers have simulated encapsulated pathways but often use simplified representations of shell permeability. Microbiologists have measured fitness effects of BMC mutations but lack mechanistic explanations linking genotype to phenotype. This synthesis project will bridge these disciplinary silos by integrating structural, metabolic, and genomic data into unified computational models that capture emergent BMC function. The collaborative, transdisciplinary approach required for this integration exemplifies the community-scale synthesis that NCEMS is uniquely positioned to support.

Research Questions: This synthesis project addresses three interconnected research questions about emergent properties of bacterial microcompartments at the mesoscale, each with specific hypotheses that can be tested using existing publicly available data.

**Research Question 1: How does BMC shell architecture create emergent selective permeability?**

BMC shells contain multiple pore types with different sizes and electrostatic properties, yet the collective transport behavior of assembled shells cannot be predicted from individual pore structures. We ask: what principles govern how the spatial arrangement and relative abundance of different pore types create shell-level permeability that selectively admits substrates while retaining intermediates?

*Hypothesis 1a*: Emergent shell selectivity arises from the ratio of different shell protein paralogs (BMC-H variants with different pore properties) rather than from any single pore type. We predict that organisms with BMCs handling charged intermediates will show enrichment of shell proteins with complementary electrostatic pore properties, creating electrostatic filtering at the shell level.

*Hypothesis 1b*: The spatial clustering of specific pore types on the shell surface creates local transport microdomains that enhance selectivity beyond what random pore distribution would achieve. We predict that structural data will reveal non-random arrangements of shell protein variants in assembled shells.

These hypotheses will be tested by synthesizing shell protein structures from PDB with genomic data on shell protein operon organization from NCBI. We will correlate shell protein composition (extracted from comparative genomics of BMC operons across >500 bacterial species) with the chemical properties of encapsulated pathway intermediates (from BRENDA and MetaboLights). Machine learning models will identify sequence features predictive of pore selectivity, validated against experimentally characterized pore properties in the literature.

**Research Question 2: How does enzyme co-localization within BMCs create emergent kinetic advantages?**

Encapsulated enzymes operate in a fundamentally different environment than cytoplasmic enzymes—confined within nanoscale volumes with altered crowding, potentially modified pH, and proximity to pathway partners. We ask: what quantitative kinetic advantages emerge from encapsulation, and which architectural features of BMCs determine the magnitude of these advantages?

*Hypothesis 2a*: Substrate channeling between co-localized enzymes creates emergent pathway flux enhancement that scales with the ratio of enzyme spacing to substrate diffusion length. We predict that BMCs with tightly packed enzymes (as determined from cryo-EM reconstructions) will show greater flux enhancement in kinetic models than those with dispersed enzyme arrangements.

*Hypothesis 2b*: The effective concentration of intermediates within BMC lumens exceeds cytoplasmic concentrations by 10-100 fold due to shell retention, creating emergent kinetic advantages even without direct enzyme-enzyme channeling. We predict that metabolomics data from BMC-disrupted strains will show accumulation of pathway intermediates in the cytoplasm, indicating loss of compartmental concentration.

*Hypothesis 2c*: Toxic intermediate sequestration provides fitness advantages that correlate with intermediate reactivity. We predict that fitness costs of BMC disruption (from transposon mutagenesis data) will correlate with the chemical reactivity of pathway aldehydes or other toxic intermediates.

These hypotheses will be tested by integrating enzyme kinetic parameters from BRENDA with structural data on enzyme arrangements within BMCs from EMDB. Finite element models of metabolite diffusion will simulate pathway flux under different organizational scenarios. Predictions will be validated against metabolomics data comparing wild-type and BMC-deficient strains, and against fitness data from systematic mutagenesis studies.

**Research Question 3: What universal principles govern emergent function across diverse BMC types?**

BMCs have evolved independently multiple times to encapsulate different metabolic pathways, from carbon fixation in carboxysomes to aldehyde-generating catabolic pathways in metabolosomes. We ask: do shared architectural principles underlie emergent function across BMC types, or has evolution found multiple solutions to the compartmentalization problem?

*Hypothesis 3a*: Despite sequence divergence, BMC shells converge on similar pore size distributions optimized for their encapsulated pathways. We predict that carboxysomes (handling CO2/HCO3-) and propanediol utilization compartments (handling propionaldehyde) will show distinct but internally consistent pore architectures matched to their substrates.

*Hypothesis 3b*: The ratio of shell volume to encapsulated enzyme content is optimized across BMC types to balance intermediate concentration against diffusion limitation. We predict a universal scaling relationship between BMC size and enzyme loading across diverse BMC types.

*Hypothesis 3c*: Emergent efficiency gains follow predictable relationships with pathway properties (number of steps, intermediate toxicity, substrate/product size differential) that can be captured in a general quantitative framework.

These hypotheses will be tested through comparative analysis synthesizing data across BMC types. We will compile a comprehensive database of BMC structural parameters, enzyme compositions, and pathway properties from PDB, EMDB, UniProt, BRENDA, and published literature. Statistical and machine learning approaches will identify conserved features and predictive relationships.

**Mechanistic Insights Expected**

By addressing these questions, we expect to develop mechanistic understanding of how mesoscale organization creates emergent metabolic properties. Specifically, we anticipate identifying: (1) quantitative relationships between shell protein composition and transport selectivity; (2) the relative contributions of substrate channeling, intermediate concentration, and toxic sequestration to overall pathway enhancement; (3) design principles that could guide engineering of synthetic compartments. These insights will transform BMCs from descriptively characterized structures to quantitatively understood systems, enabling predictive models of compartmentalized metabolism.

Methods: **Data Sources and Acquisition**

This synthesis project will integrate data from multiple publicly available repositories spanning structural biology, enzymology, metabolomics, and genomics. All data sources are established, well-curated repositories with programmatic access.

*Structural Data*: The Protein Data Bank (PDB; rcsb.org) contains >200 structures of BMC shell proteins, including hexameric BMC-H proteins (e.g., PDB: 3NGK, 5DIH), trimeric BMC-T proteins with gated pores (e.g., PDB: 4QIV), and pentameric vertex proteins (e.g., PDB: 3I96). The Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB; ebi.ac.uk/emdb) houses cryo-EM reconstructions of assembled BMC shells and encapsulated enzyme complexes, including carboxysome structures (e.g., EMD-0624) and metabolosome reconstructions. We will systematically retrieve all BMC-related entries using keyword searches and cross-references to UniProt identifiers.

*Enzyme Kinetics*: BRENDA (brenda-enzymes.org) provides kinetic parameters (Km, kcat, Ki) for enzymes encapsulated in BMCs, including RuBisCO, carbonic anhydrase, propanediol dehydratase, and aldehyde dehydrogenases. We will extract parameters measured under varying conditions (pH, temperature, ionic strength) to model how the BMC internal environment affects enzyme function.

*Metabolomics*: MetaboLights (ebi.ac.uk/metabolights) and the Metabolomics Workbench (metabolomicsworkbench.org) contain metabolomics datasets from bacteria with characterized BMC systems. We will identify studies comparing metabolite profiles in wild-type versus BMC-deficient strains, focusing on pathway intermediates and products.

*Genomics*: NCBI GenBank and RefSeq provide annotated genome sequences containing BMC operons. The IMG/M database (img.jgi.doe.gov) offers comparative genomics tools for analyzing BMC gene neighborhoods across thousands of bacterial genomes. We will extract BMC operon compositions, shell protein paralog distributions, and encapsulated enzyme complements.

*Fitness Data*: FitnessBrowser (fit.genomics.lbl.gov) contains genome-wide fitness data from transposon mutagenesis experiments, including studies in organisms with BMCs (e.g., Salmonella enterica). We will extract fitness scores for BMC genes under conditions where compartmentalized pathways are active.

**Data Integration and Harmonization**

Integrating heterogeneous data types requires careful harmonization. We will develop a unified data model centered on BMC systems, linking shell protein structures to their genomic contexts, encapsulated enzymes to their kinetic parameters, and pathway organization to metabolic phenotypes.

*Identifier Mapping*: We will use UniProt accession numbers as primary identifiers, mapping PDB structures, BRENDA entries, and genomic loci to unified protein identifiers. The UniProt ID mapping service and programmatic APIs will automate this process.

*Structural Standardization*: Shell protein structures will be processed using BioPython and MDAnalysis to extract consistent geometric parameters: pore diameters, electrostatic surface potentials (calculated using APBS), and oligomeric interfaces. Cryo-EM maps will be analyzed using UCSF ChimeraX to measure shell dimensions and enzyme positions.

*Kinetic Parameter Curation*: BRENDA entries will be filtered for data quality, retaining measurements with documented experimental conditions. Where multiple measurements exist, we will apply statistical methods to estimate consensus parameters with uncertainty bounds.

*Phylogenetic Framework*: BMC systems will be organized within a phylogenetic framework using 16S rRNA trees from the SILVA database, enabling evolutionary analysis of shell composition and function.

**Computational and Analytical Methods**

*Finite Element Modeling of Shell Permeability*: We will construct 3D models of BMC shells by tiling shell protein structures according to icosahedral symmetry, using experimentally determined stoichiometries. Metabolite diffusion through shell pores will be simulated using COMSOL Multiphysics or the open-source FEniCS package, solving the Nernst-Planck equations for charged metabolites. Simulations will predict effective permeability coefficients for substrates, products, and intermediates as functions of shell composition.

*Kinetic Modeling of Encapsulated Pathways*: We will implement ordinary differential equation (ODE) models of BMC-encapsulated pathways using COPASI and custom Python code. Models will incorporate enzyme kinetics from BRENDA, metabolite transport rates from finite element simulations, and compartmental volumes from structural data. Sensitivity analysis will identify parameters most critical for emergent pathway properties.

*Machine Learning for Structure-Function Prediction*: We will train machine learning models to predict pore selectivity from shell protein sequences and structures. Features will include amino acid composition of pore-lining residues, electrostatic potential distributions, and pore geometry. Random forest and gradient boosting models will be implemented using scikit-learn; deep learning approaches using graph neural networks (PyTorch Geometric) will capture structural relationships. Models will be validated using cross-validation and held-out test sets of characterized pores.

*Comparative Genomics Analysis*: BMC operon compositions across bacterial genomes will be analyzed using custom Python pipelines. We will identify correlations between shell protein paralog distributions and encapsulated pathway properties using statistical methods (Spearman correlation, phylogenetically independent contrasts).

**Validation Strategies**

All computational predictions will be validated against existing data without generating new experiments.

*Cross-Dataset Validation*: Permeability predictions from structural models will be compared against published experimental measurements of BMC transport (from literature mining). Kinetic model predictions will be validated against metabolomics data showing intermediate accumulation in BMC mutants.

*Positive Controls*: Well-characterized BMC systems (alpha-carboxysomes, Pdu metabolosomes) will serve as positive controls, with model predictions compared against extensive published functional data.

*Phylogenetic Validation*: Predicted structure-function relationships will be tested for consistency across phylogenetically independent BMC origins, ensuring that correlations reflect functional constraints rather than shared ancestry.

**Timeline and Milestones**

*Year 1*:
- Months 1-4: Data acquisition and harmonization; construct unified BMC database
- Months 5-8: Develop finite element models of shell permeability; validate against known systems
- Months 9-12: Implement kinetic models of encapsulated pathways; initial comparative genomics analysis

*Year 2*:
- Months 13-16: Machine learning model development and training
- Months 17-20: Integration of permeability and kinetic models; cross-validation
- Months 21-24: Comparative analysis across BMC types; manuscript preparation

*Year 3*:
- Months 25-28: Model refinement based on community feedback; additional validation
- Months 29-32: Tool development and documentation; training workshops
- Months 33-36: Final publications; data and code release; sustainability planning

**Team Composition and Expertise**

This synthesis project requires expertise spanning multiple disciplines:

1. *BMC Biology* (PI 1): Deep knowledge of BMC systems, operon organization, and biological function
2. *Structural Bioinformatics* (PI 2): Expertise in analyzing protein structures, cryo-EM maps, and molecular modeling
3. *Metabolic Modeling* (PI 3): Experience with kinetic modeling, flux analysis, and systems biology
4. *Machine Learning/Data Science* (PI 4): Skills in predictive modeling, feature engineering, and large-scale data analysis
5. *Postdoctoral Researchers* (2): Dedicated effort for data integration, model development, and analysis
6. *Graduate Students* (2): Training opportunities in synthesis research methods
7. *Research Software Engineer* (1): Development of robust, documented, reproducible code

Expected Outcomes: **Specific Deliverables**

This synthesis project will produce four categories of tangible deliverables that advance understanding of emergent BMC function and enable future research.

*Integrated BMC Database*: We will create a comprehensive, curated database linking BMC structural data, enzyme kinetics, genomic organization, and phenotypic information. This resource will include: (1) standardized structural parameters for >200 shell proteins; (2) curated kinetic parameters for >50 BMC-encapsulated enzymes; (3) annotated BMC operons from >500 bacterial genomes; (4) fitness data for BMC genes under relevant conditions. The database will be hosted on a sustainable platform with programmatic API access, enabling community use and extension.

*Computational Models of BMC Function*: We will deliver validated computational models at multiple scales: (1) Finite element models predicting shell permeability as a function of protein composition, available as parameterized simulation templates; (2) Kinetic models of major BMC-encapsulated pathways (carboxysome carbon fixation, Pdu propanediol utilization, Eut ethanolamine utilization) calibrated against experimental data; (3) Integrated multi-scale models connecting shell architecture to pathway flux and fitness. All models will be documented and released with example workflows.

*Machine Learning Tools*: We will develop and release trained machine learning models for: (1) predicting pore selectivity from shell protein sequences; (2) classifying BMC types from operon composition; (3) estimating pathway enhancement from BMC architectural features. These tools will be packaged as Python libraries with clear documentation and tutorials.

*Quantitative Principles of Emergent BMC Function*: Beyond tools and data, we will articulate general principles governing how mesoscale organization creates emergent metabolic properties. These principles will be formalized as quantitative relationships (e.g., scaling laws relating shell composition to selectivity) and qualitative design rules (e.g., conditions favoring channeling versus concentration mechanisms).

**Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena**

This project directly addresses NCEMS's scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale. BMCs exemplify how organization at scales between molecules and organelles creates system-level behaviors unpredictable from component properties. Our synthesis will reveal:

*Emergent Selectivity*: How the collective arrangement of multiple pore types creates transport selectivity exceeding that of individual pores—a mesoscale property arising from spatial organization.

*Emergent Kinetic Enhancement*: How enzyme co-localization within confined volumes creates pathway flux and efficiency gains through mechanisms (channeling, concentration, sequestration) that require mesoscale organization.

*Emergent Robustness*: How BMC architecture buffers pathway function against perturbations, creating system-level robustness from component-level variability.

These insights will establish BMCs as a model system for mesoscale emergence, with lessons applicable to other compartmentalized biological systems including phase-separated condensates, viral capsids, and engineered protein cages.

**Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology**

Understanding emergent BMC function has implications extending beyond bacterial cell biology:

*Metabolic Engineering*: Quantitative models of BMC function will enable rational design of synthetic compartments for biotechnology applications. Our principles will guide selection of shell proteins, enzyme arrangements, and pathway designs for engineered BMCs producing valuable compounds.

*Evolutionary Biology*: Comparative analysis across BMC types will illuminate how evolution discovers solutions to the compartmentalization problem, revealing constraints and opportunities in the evolution of cellular organization.

*Synthetic Biology*: Design rules for emergent compartment function will inform broader efforts to engineer cellular organization, including protein-based organelles and membrane-less compartments.

*Education*: BMCs provide accessible examples of emergence for teaching systems biology concepts, and our curated resources will support educational use.

**Enabling Future Research**

Our synthesis will create foundations for future investigations:

*Hypothesis Generation*: Quantitative models will generate testable predictions about BMC function that can guide future experimental studies (by other groups generating new data).

*Comparative Framework*: The integrated database will enable systematic comparison of BMC systems, supporting discovery of novel BMC types and functions.

*Method Development*: Our computational approaches for modeling compartmentalized metabolism will be applicable to other systems, including eukaryotic organelles and synthetic compartments.

*Community Building*: By bringing together researchers from structural biology, metabolic modeling, and microbiology, this project will catalyze a community focused on quantitative understanding of bacterial compartmentalization.

**Dissemination Plans**

*Publications*: We anticipate 4-6 peer-reviewed publications: (1) database and resource paper; (2) finite element modeling of shell permeability; (3) kinetic modeling of encapsulated pathways; (4) machine learning for BMC function prediction; (5) comparative analysis and design principles; (6) review/perspective on emergent compartment function.

*Workshops*: We will organize two workshops during the project: (1) a methods workshop training researchers in BMC modeling approaches; (2) a synthesis workshop bringing together the BMC community to discuss findings and future directions.

*Conference Presentations*: Results will be presented at relevant meetings including the ASM Microbe meeting, Biophysical Society Annual Meeting, and ISCB conferences.

*Online Resources*: All tools, data, and documentation will be accessible through a project website with tutorials, example analyses, and community forums.

**Long-term Sustainability**

We will ensure lasting impact through:

*Repository Deposition*: Curated data will be deposited in established repositories (Zenodo for datasets, PyPI for Python packages) with persistent identifiers.

*Community Governance*: We will establish a community steering committee to guide database maintenance and extension beyond the funding period.

*Integration with Existing Resources*: Where possible, curated data will be contributed back to source databases (e.g., annotations to UniProt) ensuring long-term preservation.

*Documentation*: Comprehensive documentation will enable community members to maintain and extend tools independently.

Budget and Resources: **Personnel (Total: $720,000 over 3 years)**

*Postdoctoral Researchers (2 positions, $180,000/year total including benefits)*: Two postdocs will provide dedicated effort for data integration, model development, and analysis. Postdoc 1 will focus on structural analysis and finite element modeling, requiring expertise in structural bioinformatics and computational physics. Postdoc 2 will lead kinetic modeling and machine learning efforts, requiring expertise in systems biology and data science. Postdocs are essential for the intensive computational work required for synthesis across heterogeneous data types. Total: $540,000.

*Graduate Student Support (2 students, partial support, $60,000/year total)*: Two graduate students will participate in the project, gaining training in synthesis research methods. Students will contribute to specific analysis modules under postdoc mentorship, with thesis chapters derived from project work. This investment in training aligns with NCEMS's workforce development mission. Total: $180,000.

**Research Software Engineer ($150,000 over 3 years)**

A part-time research software engineer (0.5 FTE) will ensure code quality, documentation, and sustainability. The RSE will implement continuous integration, develop user interfaces, and maintain computational infrastructure. This investment is critical for producing tools that the community can actually use and maintain. Professional software engineering expertise is essential for open science goals.

**Computing Resources ($90,000 over 3 years)**

*Cloud Computing (AWS/Google Cloud, $50,000)*: Finite element simulations and machine learning training require substantial computational resources beyond typical lab allocations. Cloud computing provides flexible, scalable resources for computationally intensive analyses. Costs include GPU instances for deep learning and high-memory instances for large simulations.

*High-Performance Computing Allocation ($20,000)*: Supplementary HPC allocations through XSEDE/ACCESS will support large-scale parameter sweeps and ensemble simulations. Budget covers allocation purchase and data storage.

*Data Storage and Hosting ($20,000)*: Long-term storage for curated databases and simulation outputs, including Zenodo fees for large datasets and web hosting for project resources.

**Travel ($60,000 over 3 years)**

*Team Meetings ($30,000)*: Annual in-person meetings of the full working group are essential for synthesis research requiring deep collaboration across disciplines. Budget supports travel for 8-10 participants to two-day meetings at rotating locations.

*Conference Presentations ($20,000)*: Dissemination of results at scientific meetings (ASM Microbe, Biophysical Society, ISCB) ensures community engagement and feedback. Budget supports 4-6 conference trips per year across team members.

*Collaboration Visits ($10,000)*: Short visits between labs enable intensive collaborative work on specific project components.

**Workshops and Training ($40,000 over 3 years)**

*Methods Workshop (Year 2, $20,000)*: A two-day workshop training 20-30 researchers in BMC modeling approaches. Budget covers venue, participant support, and materials.

*Synthesis Workshop (Year 3, $20,000)*: A capstone workshop bringing together the BMC research community to discuss findings and future directions. Budget covers venue and participant support.

*Repository and Hosting Fees ($5,000)*: Costs for GitHub organization, Docker Hub, and web hosting beyond free tiers.

*Documentation Tools ($5,000)*: Licenses and hosting for documentation platforms, tutorial hosting, and community forums.

*Publication Fees ($5,000)*: Open access publication fees for project papers, ensuring unrestricted access to findings.

**Supplies and Materials ($10,000 over 3 years)**

Miscellaneous supplies including computing peripherals, reference materials, and workshop supplies.

**Total Budget: $1,085,000 over 3 years**

**Budget Justification Summary**

This budget reflects the community-scale nature of the proposed synthesis. Personnel costs dominate because synthesis research is fundamentally a human intellectual endeavor requiring sustained effort to integrate heterogeneous data and develop sophisticated models. Computing costs are substantial but necessary for the finite element simulations and machine learning that enable quantitative modeling of emergent BMC function. Travel and workshop costs support the collaborative, transdisciplinary approach essential for synthesis research that no single lab could accomplish. Open science infrastructure costs ensure that project outputs are accessible, documented, and sustainable. This investment will produce lasting resources—databases, tools, and trained researchers—that benefit the molecular and cellular biology community far beyond the funding period.

full_draft_original:
Title: Emergent DNA Repair Pathway Choice: Synthesizing Damage Proteomics and Chromatin Data to Model Repair Mechanism Selection

Abstract: DNA repair pathway choice represents emergent decision-making where chromatin context, cell cycle stage, and damage characteristics collectively determine repair mechanism—a mesoscale phenomenon integrating multiple inputs into discrete outcomes. This synthesis project will decode emergent pathway choice by integrating damage proteomics, chromatin biology, and cell biology datasets. We will synthesize DNA damage proteomics from PRIDE and published studies, ChIP-seq of repair factors from ENCODE, chromatin accessibility from ATAC-seq datasets, and cell cycle proteomics from published studies. The central question is: how do repair protein assemblies at damage sites (mesoscale foci of 100-1000 nm) create emergent pathway selection that individual protein-DNA interactions cannot explain? We hypothesize that emergent pathway choice arises from competitive recruitment kinetics, chromatin-mediated accessibility, and feedback loops that amplify initial pathway commitment. Our computational approach combines kinetic modeling of repair protein recruitment, machine learning to predict pathway choice from chromatin and damage features, and network analysis of repair factor interactions. We will develop algorithms integrating damage site proteomics with chromatin context to model pathway selection. Integration with mutation signature data from COSMIC will connect pathway choice to genomic outcomes. Comparative analysis across cell types will reveal how emergent repair decisions adapt to different genomic contexts. This project requires expertise in DNA repair, chromatin biology, proteomics, and computational modeling—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of damage, chromatin, and proteomic data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include predictive models of emergent pathway choice, identification of key features determining repair selection, and principles for modulating repair outcomes. Understanding emergent repair decisions has implications for cancer therapy and genome editing. All models, analysis pipelines, and curated datasets will be openly released.

Background: DNA double-strand breaks (DSBs) represent one of the most dangerous forms of genomic damage, capable of triggering cell death, chromosomal rearrangements, and cancer when improperly repaired. Cells have evolved multiple repair pathways to address DSBs, including homologous recombination (HR), non-homologous end joining (NHEJ), alternative end joining (alt-EJ), and single-strand annealing (SSA). The selection among these pathways is not random but represents a sophisticated decision-making process that integrates multiple cellular inputs to produce discrete repair outcomes. This pathway choice phenomenon exemplifies emergent behavior at the mesoscale—the spatial and organizational level between individual biomolecules and organelles—where collective properties arise that cannot be predicted from individual molecular interactions alone.

At the molecular level, individual repair proteins have well-characterized biochemical activities: Ku70/80 binds DNA ends, BRCA1 promotes end resection, 53BP1 inhibits resection, and RAD51 catalyzes strand invasion. However, at DNA damage sites, these proteins assemble into mesoscale structures called repair foci, spanning 100-1000 nanometers and containing hundreds to thousands of protein molecules. Within these foci, emergent properties arise from the collective behavior of repair factors: competitive binding dynamics, phase separation phenomena, chromatin reorganization, and feedback amplification loops. The pathway choice that emerges from these foci cannot be explained by summing individual protein-DNA interactions; rather, it represents a higher-order property of the assembled repair machinery.

Substantial publicly available data now exists to address this emergent phenomenon through synthesis research. The PRIDE proteomics repository contains over 50 datasets examining DNA damage-induced protein recruitment, phosphorylation, and ubiquitination. ENCODE and 4D Nucleome projects have generated extensive ChIP-seq data for repair factors including 53BP1, BRCA1, γH2AX, and RAD51 across multiple cell types. ATAC-seq datasets from the ENCODE consortium and GEO repository provide chromatin accessibility maps that influence repair factor access. Cell cycle proteomics studies deposited in PRIDE and ProteomeXchange characterize the temporal dynamics of repair protein expression and modification. The COSMIC database contains mutation signatures that serve as genomic footprints of repair pathway activity. Despite this wealth of data, no systematic integration has been performed to model how mesoscale repair foci generate emergent pathway choice.

Critical gaps exist in our understanding that synthesis research can uniquely address. First, while individual datasets characterize specific aspects of repair (proteomics, chromatin state, or genomic outcomes), no integrated framework connects these scales. Second, the kinetic parameters governing competitive recruitment at damage sites remain poorly quantified across cellular contexts. Third, the chromatin features that bias pathway choice are incompletely catalogued and their predictive power untested. Fourth, how pathway choice varies across cell types and genomic locations—and whether universal principles exist—remains unknown.

Understanding emergent repair pathway choice has profound implications. In cancer therapy, many treatments induce DNA damage, and tumor cells often exhibit altered repair pathway usage. Predicting pathway choice could enable rational therapeutic combinations. In genome editing, CRISPR-induced breaks are repaired by cellular machinery, and controlling pathway choice is essential for precise editing outcomes. More fundamentally, DNA repair pathway choice represents a tractable model system for understanding how mesoscale biological assemblies generate emergent decision-making—a question central to NCEMS's scientific vision.

The synthesis approach proposed here is essential because the relevant data span multiple disciplines (proteomics, chromatin biology, genomics, cell biology) and exist in disparate repositories with different formats and standards. No single laboratory possesses the expertise to integrate damage proteomics, chromatin biology, and computational modeling required for this project. By bringing together specialists across these fields, we can achieve insights impossible for individual research groups, exemplifying the community-scale synthesis that NCEMS seeks to catalyze.

Research Questions: This synthesis project addresses three interconnected research questions that probe the emergent nature of DNA repair pathway choice at the mesoscale:

**Research Question 1: How do competitive recruitment kinetics at mesoscale repair foci generate emergent pathway commitment?**

At DNA damage sites, multiple repair pathways compete for access to broken DNA ends. The proteins 53BP1 and BRCA1 represent antagonistic factors promoting NHEJ and HR, respectively. However, the dynamics of their recruitment, accumulation, and displacement within mesoscale foci remain poorly understood. We hypothesize that pathway choice emerges from kinetic competition governed by three parameters: (1) initial recruitment rates determined by damage-induced chromatin modifications, (2) cooperative binding that amplifies initial pathway bias, and (3) feedback loops where early-arriving factors modify the chromatin environment to favor continued recruitment of pathway-specific proteins.

*Measurable Predictions:* By synthesizing time-resolved proteomics data from PRIDE with ChIP-seq binding profiles from ENCODE, we predict that the ratio of 53BP1 to BRCA1 recruitment within the first 30 minutes post-damage will predict ultimate pathway choice with >80% accuracy. We further predict that cooperative binding coefficients extracted from dose-response proteomics data will correlate with the sharpness of pathway commitment (switch-like versus graded responses).

*Validation Approach:* We will test these predictions by comparing our kinetic models against independent datasets not used in model training, and by examining whether predicted pathway choices match mutation signatures in COSMIC for the corresponding cell types and genomic contexts.

**Research Question 2: What chromatin features create emergent accessibility landscapes that bias pathway selection?**

Chromatin state profoundly influences repair pathway choice, with heterochromatin and euchromatin showing different repair pathway preferences. However, the specific chromatin features that determine pathway bias—and how they combine to create emergent accessibility landscapes—remain incompletely characterized. We hypothesize that pathway choice is determined by a chromatin accessibility code integrating histone modifications, nucleosome positioning, chromatin compaction, and three-dimensional genome organization. This code operates at the mesoscale, where the collective chromatin environment surrounding a break (spanning kilobases) matters more than local sequence features.

*Measurable Predictions:* By integrating ENCODE ChIP-seq for histone modifications, ATAC-seq for accessibility, and Hi-C data for 3D organization, we predict that a machine learning model incorporating features within 10 kb of damage sites will predict pathway choice with significantly higher accuracy than models using only local (<1 kb) features. We predict that specific chromatin feature combinations (e.g., H3K36me3 + high accessibility + A compartment) will show >90% HR usage, while alternative combinations (H3K9me3 + low accessibility + B compartment) will show >90% NHEJ usage.

*Validation Approach:* Predictions will be validated against mutation signature distributions across chromatin states in COSMIC, and against published repair pathway reporter assays mapped to genomic locations with known chromatin features.

**Research Question 3: How do cell type-specific contexts modulate emergent pathway choice rules?**

Different cell types show dramatically different repair pathway preferences—stem cells favor HR while differentiated cells often prefer NHEJ. We hypothesize that cell type-specific pathway choice emerges from the integration of three factors: (1) baseline expression levels of repair factors (setting the competitive landscape), (2) cell cycle distribution (determining HR competence), and (3) cell type-specific chromatin organization (creating distinct accessibility landscapes). Importantly, we hypothesize that universal pathway choice rules exist but are parameterized differently across cell types.

*Measurable Predictions:* By synthesizing cell type-specific proteomics from ProteomeXchange, cell cycle data from published studies, and chromatin profiles from ENCODE across multiple cell types, we predict that a unified pathway choice model with cell type-specific parameters will outperform cell type-specific models, indicating conserved underlying mechanisms. We predict that the ratio of 53BP1 to BRCA1 protein levels, combined with cell cycle phase distribution, will explain >60% of variance in pathway choice across cell types.

*Validation Approach:* We will perform leave-one-cell-type-out cross-validation, training models on data from multiple cell types and testing predictions on held-out cell types. Successful prediction of pathway choice in unseen cell types will validate the existence of universal rules.

**Mechanistic Insights Expected:**

Through addressing these questions, we expect to elucidate several mechanistic principles of mesoscale organization. First, we will quantify how competitive kinetics at repair foci create bistable pathway commitment—a hallmark of emergent decision-making systems. Second, we will identify the minimal set of chromatin features sufficient to predict pathway choice, revealing the information content of the chromatin accessibility code. Third, we will determine whether pathway choice represents a continuous spectrum or discrete states, informing whether repair foci function as analog sensors or digital switches. Fourth, we will map the parameter space of pathway choice, identifying conditions where small perturbations cause large outcome changes (sensitivity analysis) versus robust regions where pathway choice is buffered against variation. These insights will establish DNA repair pathway choice as a paradigm for understanding emergent decision-making at the mesoscale.

Methods: **Data Sources and Acquisition Strategy**

This synthesis project will integrate data from multiple publicly available repositories spanning proteomics, chromatin biology, genomics, and cell biology:

*Proteomics Data:* We will obtain DNA damage proteomics datasets from PRIDE (PRoteomics IDEntifications database) and ProteomeXchange, focusing on studies examining protein recruitment to damage sites, damage-induced post-translational modifications (phosphorylation, ubiquitination, SUMOylation), and temporal dynamics of repair factor accumulation. Specific datasets include: PXD004787 (quantitative proteomics of DNA damage response), PXD012345 (phosphoproteomics following ionizing radiation), PXD008934 (ubiquitin-modified proteome after DSB induction), and approximately 40 additional datasets identified through systematic repository searches. Cell cycle proteomics will be obtained from PXD006476 and related studies characterizing protein abundance across cell cycle phases.

*Chromatin Data:* ChIP-seq data for repair factors (53BP1, BRCA1, γH2AX, RAD51, Ku70, DNA-PKcs, MDC1) will be obtained from ENCODE (approximately 200 datasets across cell types), 4D Nucleome, and GEO. ATAC-seq data for chromatin accessibility will be sourced from ENCODE (>500 datasets) and published studies in GEO. Histone modification ChIP-seq (H3K4me3, H3K27me3, H3K36me3, H3K9me3, H3K27ac, H2AK119ub) will be obtained from ENCODE and Roadmap Epigenomics. Hi-C data for 3D genome organization will be sourced from 4D Nucleome and published studies.

*Genomic Outcome Data:* Mutation signatures will be obtained from COSMIC (Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer), which contains >40,000 whole-genome sequenced tumors with characterized mutation signatures. Signatures SBS3 (HR deficiency), ID6 and ID8 (NHEJ signatures), and others provide genomic footprints of repair pathway activity.

*Cell Type and Context Data:* Cell type-specific expression data will be obtained from the Human Protein Atlas, GTEx, and CCLE (Cancer Cell Line Encyclopedia). Cell cycle phase markers and distributions will be extracted from published flow cytometry and single-cell studies deposited in GEO.

**Data Integration and Harmonization Strategy**

Integrating heterogeneous datasets requires systematic harmonization across multiple dimensions:

*Genomic Coordinate Harmonization:* All datasets will be mapped to GRCh38/hg38 coordinates using liftOver where necessary. ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq peaks will be processed through uniform pipelines (ENCODE standards) to ensure comparable peak calling and signal quantification.

*Protein Identifier Mapping:* Proteomics data use various identifier systems (UniProt, gene symbols, RefSeq). We will create a unified protein identifier mapping using UniProt ID mapping service, ensuring consistent protein identification across datasets.

*Cell Type Ontology:* Cell types will be mapped to Cell Ontology (CL) terms to enable systematic comparison across studies using different nomenclature.

*Batch Effect Correction:* For proteomics data, we will apply ComBat and related methods to correct batch effects while preserving biological variation. For ChIP-seq data, we will use quantile normalization and spike-in controls where available.

*Quality Control:* Each dataset will undergo quality assessment including: replicate correlation analysis, comparison to expected positive controls (e.g., γH2AX enrichment at known fragile sites), and outlier detection.

**Computational and Analytical Methods**

*Kinetic Modeling of Repair Protein Recruitment:* We will develop ordinary differential equation (ODE) models describing competitive recruitment of repair factors to damage sites. Models will incorporate: (1) damage-induced chromatin modifications as initial signals, (2) protein-protein interactions enabling cooperative binding, (3) enzymatic activities that modify the chromatin environment, and (4) feedback loops where early factors influence subsequent recruitment. Parameters will be estimated from time-resolved proteomics data using Bayesian inference (PyMC3/Stan). Model selection will use information criteria (AIC/BIC) to identify minimal models capturing observed dynamics.

*Machine Learning for Pathway Choice Prediction:* We will train gradient boosting models (XGBoost, LightGBM) and neural networks to predict pathway choice from chromatin and damage features. Input features will include: local chromatin accessibility (ATAC-seq signal), histone modifications (ChIP-seq signals for multiple marks), 3D genome compartment (A/B from Hi-C), replication timing, gene density, and sequence features (GC content, repetitive elements). Pathway choice labels will be derived from mutation signature enrichment in COSMIC. We will use nested cross-validation to prevent overfitting and SHAP values for feature importance interpretation.

*Network Analysis of Repair Factor Interactions:* Protein-protein interaction networks will be constructed from BioGRID and STRING databases, filtered for DNA repair-relevant interactions. We will apply network propagation algorithms to identify modules of co-recruited factors and community detection to identify pathway-specific subcomplexes. Dynamic network analysis will examine how interaction networks rewire across cell cycle phases.

*Integration Algorithm Development:* We will develop a novel Bayesian integration framework that combines: (1) prior probabilities from chromatin features, (2) likelihood functions from proteomics recruitment data, and (3) posterior pathway choice probabilities. This framework will explicitly model uncertainty from each data source and propagate it to final predictions.

**Validation Strategies**

*Cross-Dataset Validation:* Models trained on one set of cell types/conditions will be tested on held-out datasets. Successful generalization validates model robustness.

*Known Positive Controls:* We will verify that models correctly predict: (1) HR preference in S/G2 phases, (2) NHEJ preference in G1, (3) HR deficiency signatures in BRCA1/2-mutant samples from COSMIC, (4) increased NHEJ in heterochromatin.

*Mutation Signature Validation:* Predicted pathway choices will be compared against mutation signature distributions in COSMIC, providing independent validation from genomic outcomes.

**Timeline and Milestones**

*Year 1:*
- Months 1-4: Data acquisition, quality control, and harmonization
- Months 5-8: Kinetic model development and parameter estimation
- Months 9-12: Initial machine learning model training and validation

*Year 2:*
- Months 13-16: Integration framework development
- Months 17-20: Cross-cell type analysis and universal rule identification
- Months 21-24: Model refinement and comprehensive validation

*Year 3:*
- Months 25-28: Final model integration and testing
- Months 29-32: Tool development and documentation
- Months 33-36: Dissemination, publication, and community engagement

**Team Composition and Expertise Required**

*DNA Repair Biology:* Expert in repair pathway mechanisms, factor functions, and pathway choice regulation
*Chromatin Biology:* Specialist in chromatin modifications, accessibility, and 3D genome organization
*Proteomics/Mass Spectrometry:* Expert in proteomics data analysis, post-translational modifications
*Computational Biology/Machine Learning:* Specialist in predictive modeling, data integration, algorithm development
*Systems Biology/Mathematical Modeling:* Expert in kinetic modeling, dynamical systems, parameter estimation

This transdisciplinary team structure ensures that domain expertise guides data interpretation while computational specialists develop rigorous analytical frameworks.

Expected Outcomes: **Specific Deliverables**

This synthesis project will produce five major categories of deliverables that advance understanding of emergent DNA repair pathway choice:

*1. Integrated Multi-Omic Database of DNA Repair Pathway Choice (RepairChoiceDB):* We will create a comprehensive, harmonized database integrating damage proteomics, chromatin features, and pathway outcomes across cell types and conditions. This database will include: (a) curated proteomics data from >50 DNA damage studies with standardized protein identifiers and quantification, (b) processed ChIP-seq and ATAC-seq data for repair factors and chromatin marks mapped to uniform coordinates, (c) cell type-specific pathway choice annotations derived from mutation signatures, and (d) metadata enabling filtering by cell type, damage type, and experimental conditions. RepairChoiceDB will be deposited in Zenodo with DOI assignment and maintained through a dedicated web interface.

*2. Kinetic Models of Competitive Repair Factor Recruitment:* We will deliver parameterized ODE models describing the dynamics of repair factor recruitment to damage sites. These models will include: (a) rate constants for initial recruitment of key factors (53BP1, BRCA1, Ku70/80, RAD51), (b) cooperativity coefficients quantifying positive feedback, (c) inhibition parameters describing antagonistic interactions, and (d) cell cycle-dependent parameter variations. Models will be implemented in Python (using scipy and PyMC3) and SBML format for compatibility with standard systems biology tools.

*3. Machine Learning Pathway Choice Predictor (PathwayPredict):* We will develop and release a trained machine learning model that predicts repair pathway choice from chromatin and damage features. The model will: (a) accept genomic coordinates and return predicted pathway probabilities (HR, NHEJ, alt-EJ), (b) provide confidence intervals on predictions, (c) output feature importance scores explaining predictions, and (d) include pre-computed predictions for the entire human genome at 1 kb resolution. PathwayPredict will be released as a Python package with command-line and API interfaces.

*4. Chromatin Feature Atlas for Pathway Choice:* We will produce a comprehensive atlas mapping chromatin features to pathway choice across the human genome. This atlas will include: (a) genome-wide maps of predicted pathway preference, (b) identification of genomic regions with strong pathway bias, (c) characterization of chromatin feature combinations associated with each pathway, and (d) cell type-specific pathway choice landscapes. The atlas will be available as genome browser tracks and downloadable files.

*5. Analysis Pipelines and Reproducible Workflows:* All computational methods will be released as documented, containerized pipelines including: (a) data harmonization workflows, (b) kinetic model fitting procedures, (c) machine learning training and evaluation scripts, and (d) visualization tools for exploring results.

**Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena**

This project will establish DNA repair pathway choice as a paradigm for mesoscale emergence in molecular and cellular biology. Our work will demonstrate how collective behavior of repair proteins within mesoscale foci (100-1000 nm) generates pathway selection that cannot be predicted from individual protein properties. Specifically, we will:

*Quantify Emergent Decision-Making:* By parameterizing kinetic models, we will measure how competitive dynamics create bistable pathway commitment—a hallmark of emergent systems where collective behavior produces discrete outcomes from continuous inputs.

*Identify Information Integration Principles:* Our machine learning analysis will reveal how multiple chromatin features combine to determine pathway choice, establishing principles for how mesoscale assemblies integrate diverse inputs.

*Characterize Robustness and Sensitivity:* Parameter sensitivity analysis will identify conditions where pathway choice is robust versus sensitive to perturbation, informing how emergent systems maintain reliable function despite molecular noise.

*Establish Universal versus Context-Specific Rules:* Cross-cell type analysis will determine whether pathway choice follows universal principles with context-specific parameters, or whether fundamentally different mechanisms operate in different cellular contexts.

**Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology**

Beyond DNA repair, this project will impact multiple areas:

*Cancer Biology:* Understanding pathway choice has direct implications for cancer therapy. Many chemotherapeutics and radiation therapy induce DNA damage, and tumor cells often show altered repair pathway usage. Our predictive models could inform therapeutic strategies by identifying tumors likely to respond to specific treatments based on their pathway choice landscape.

*Genome Editing:* CRISPR-Cas9 and related technologies induce targeted DNA breaks that are repaired by cellular machinery. Controlling whether breaks are repaired by HR (enabling precise editing) or NHEJ (causing insertions/deletions) is a major challenge. Our chromatin-based pathway choice predictions could guide editing strategies and target site selection.

*Aging and Neurodegeneration:* DNA damage accumulation contributes to aging and neurodegenerative diseases. Understanding how pathway choice changes with age and in post-mitotic neurons could inform interventions to maintain genomic integrity.

*Methodology Transfer:* The computational frameworks we develop—integrating proteomics, chromatin data, and genomic outcomes to model emergent phenomena—will be applicable to other mesoscale processes including transcription factor hub formation, signaling complex assembly, and phase separation.

**Enabling Future Research**

Our deliverables will enable multiple future research directions:

*Hypothesis Generation:* PathwayPredict will identify genomic regions with unexpected pathway preferences, generating hypotheses for mechanistic investigation.

*Therapeutic Target Identification:* Kinetic models will identify rate-limiting steps in pathway choice that could be targeted pharmacologically.

*Synthetic Biology:* Understanding pathway choice rules could enable engineering of cells with desired repair properties.

**Dissemination Plans**

*Publications:* We anticipate 4-6 peer-reviewed publications including: (1) a flagship paper describing the integrated framework and major findings, (2) a methods paper detailing computational approaches, (3) a database/resource paper for RepairChoiceDB, and (4) focused papers on specific aspects (kinetic modeling, chromatin features, cell type variation).

*Workshops:* We will organize two workshops: (1) a methods workshop training researchers to use our tools, and (2) a scientific workshop bringing together DNA repair and chromatin communities to discuss implications.

*Conference Presentations:* Results will be presented at major meetings including ASBMB, ASCB, and specialized DNA repair conferences.

**Long-Term Sustainability**

RepairChoiceDB will be deposited in Zenodo ensuring long-term preservation with DOI assignment. Software tools will be maintained on GitHub with clear documentation enabling community contributions. We will establish partnerships with existing databases (COSMIC, ENCODE) to ensure continued accessibility and potential integration.

This position will lead algorithm development, machine learning model training, and integration framework implementation. Justification: The computational complexity of integrating heterogeneous datasets and developing novel predictive models requires dedicated full-time effort from a PhD-level researcher with expertise in computational biology and machine learning.

*Postdoctoral Researcher - DNA Repair/Chromatin Biology (50% effort, 3 years):* $XXX,XXX including salary and benefits. title_norm: integrative multi-omics synthesis to identify shared molecular mechanisms of mammalian hibernation
title: Integrative Multi-Omics Synthesis to Identify Shared Molecular Mechanisms of Mammalian Hibernation
author: Human
abstract_original: Hibernation is a complex physiological strategy that allows certain mammals to withstand prolonged periods of resource scarcity and low temperatures by dramatically suppressing metabolism, while maintaining organ integrity and preserving muscle and bone mass. Despite decades of study, the shared molecular and cellular regulatory mechanisms that drive and sustain hibernation remain largely unresolved. This project aims to unify existing omics-scale datasets, mostly transcriptomic, from numerous hibernating mammals to identify conserved pathways and molecular signatures underlying this extreme phenotype. Our project will leverage publicly available datasets and apply cutting-edge computational tools that are developed in the context of this project to analyze transcriptional variation underlying hibernation in a phylogenetic context.
full_draft_original: 4. Introduction and Goals Hibernation is a physiological strategy that allows animals to endure extended periods of limited resources and low temperatures. Within mammals, hibernation is observed in a subset of rodent, bat, lemur, and bear species. Across these diverse species, hallmarks of hibernation include profound reductions in metabolic rate, reductions in body temperature, reduced feeding or complete fasting, and inactivity (1). Still, interspecific nuance in hibernation physiology is rampant across mammalian hibernators. For example, hibernating ground squirrels reduce body temperatures to near environmental levels and experience intermittent “arousal” periods in which metabolic rate and body temperatures temporarily rebound to normal levels (2). In contrast, bears experience less extreme decreases in body temperature and metabolic rate, yet sustain this suppressed state for the duration of hibernation without physiological arousals. Our understanding of hibernation physiology across mammals thus argues for both the presence of a shared suite of hibernation mechanisms, with additional species-specific variation. Identifying genes and signaling pathways underlying hibernation phenotypes in many or all hibernators will highlight mechanisms of fundamental importance for metabolic modulation in mammals. Numerous studies have investigated hibernation mechanisms in specific species and tissues to date, providing insight into the genes, signaling pathways, and biological processes driving hibernation phenotypes in specific lineages (3-11). However, few studies have used a comparative approach to test whether hibernation across mammals is driven by shared versus lineage-specific transcriptional mechanisms (but see 12,13). Moreover, neither of those approaches have considered the phylogenetic context in which the species are placed, thereby giving equal weight to more closely or distantly related species and not accurately capturing the evolution of transcriptional change while analyzing hibernation-related transcriptional differences and similarities. By integrating decades of existing datasets on hibernation gene expression spanning multiple tissues from diverse mammalian hibernators using a phylogenetic framework, we will identify shared and unique molecular mechanisms underlying hibernation. While identifying shared 1 mechanisms is the ultimate goal of this proposal, identifying lineage-specific mechanisms will reveal unique solutions to the same evolutionary problem of seasonal resource availability. Both findings will advance our understanding of the diversity of molecular mechanisms driving hibernation, thus providing context for understanding how these lineages can achieve metabolic feats beyond the physiological capacity of humans. Collectively, this aim will address the following questions: How do diverse mammals converge on similar physiological outcomes during hibernation through distinct yet overlapping molecular mechanisms? By comprehensively integrating existing datasets across taxa—including bears, ground squirrels, bats, and lemurs—this synthesis will address the central question: What conserved molecular processes enable reversible metabolic suppression and tissue protection across hibernators? And test the following hypothesis: hibernating mammals share a set of genes that are differentially regulated during hibernation and thus represent “core” genes underlying hibernation phenotypes. One of the challenges is that the datasets are sparse and are not necessarily taken from the same tissue among species. Therefore, approaches are needed that analyze changes in a phylogenetic framework and account for missing data. We propose to develop the necessary tools to address our central question. 5. Proposed Activities Existing RNA-sequencing (RNA-seq) datasets comparing hibernation to active-state gene expression in a variety of hibernating mammals are publicly available (Datasets Table #1-12, 14-16, 20). These data are comprised of RNA-seq from numerous tissues (adipose, liver, muscle, bone, intestine, brain, kidney, and blood) collected from species from major hibernating mammal groups (squirrels, hamsters, bears, bats, and lemurs). We will also include an additional 17 non-hibernating species from (14) (Datasets Table #13, 17-19, 21) and add other datasets if additional RNA-seq datasets from multiple tissues become publicly available during the project. We will also leverage existing high quality reference genomes (Datasets Table #22) and whole- genome alignments (Datasets Table #23) for the proposed analysis. To identify shared and lineage-specific gene expression shifts during hibernation, raw RNA-seq reads will be downloaded from the NCBI Short Read Archive and quality-checked with FastQC (15); low quality reads will be removed before proceeding. For each species, RNA-seq reads will be mapped to the corresponding reference genome (Datasets Table #22) using STAR (16) and raw read counts will be quantified using featureCounts (17). Using these existing data, we will investigate the evolution of hibernation using two complementary approaches: First, we will use a phylogenetically informed approach to test for convergent shifts in gene expression in hibernating species while focusing exclusively on expression in active (i.e., non- hibernating) physiological states. This will test the hypothesis that there are baseline differences in “normal” state expression patterns between hibernating and non-hibernating species. This analysis will reveal previously undetected nuances in active season physiology and gene expression in hibernating species and provide a better baseline understanding for the degree of similarity between active hibernators and non-hibernators, while accounting for tissue. There are several developed methods that can be used for this analysis, including EVE (18) and CAGEE (19). These models often treat gene expression evolution as an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck (OU) process, which is typically described as modeling a trait evolving under stabilizing selection toward some optimum value (20). By allowing for a shift in the optimum trait value along the 2 phylogeny, these OU models can be used to model directional selection. Note that the OU model is generally found to be an adequate model of gene expression evolution (21). While these analyses are running, we will develop novel approaches to investigate longitudinal shifts (i.e., active versus hibernation) in gene expression in hibernators using a phylogenetic context. We will implement a bivariate model of trait evolution that simultaneously considers the evolution of gene expression in both the hibernating and active states. Two versions of the model will be fit: 1) the optimum is constrained to be the same for a gene in both states (no differential expression), and 2) the optimum of a gene is allowed to vary (differential expression). For non- hibernating species, we will treat gene expression evolution as a univariate trait mapping to the active state. We will identify the better model fit via AICc, as is standard in phylogenetic comparative methods. By utilizing data across many species, this model is intended to identify convergent shifts in gene expression between the active and hibernating states. We expect that the multi-optimum bivariate OU model will perform better than the single-optimum bivariate OU model only when there are convergent shifts in gene expression between states across the hibernators. This framework will also provide other parameters of interest, such as the strength of natural selection on gene expression. Model performance will be determined via simulation tests. For each approach, lists of convergently expressed genes will be compared between species using ortholog information generated using OrthoFinder (22). We will also use existing (Data Table #23) and generate genome alignments for all focal study species (Data Table #22) using Cactus (23) for further evaluation of gene orthology and as a valuable resource for future hibernation research. Shared and lineage-specific differentially expressed genes will then be characterized via Gene Ontology and KEGG pathway overrepresentation analyses using clusterProfiler in R (24). Ultimately, the interpretation of the genes will rely on a mix of database integration and the expertise of our working group team. Figure 1. Hibernation capacity is distributed across the mammalian phylogeny. Species in red exhibit hibernation adaptations and have publicly available RNA-seq data comparing active and hibernating states. A selection of non- hibernating mammals are shown in black. RNA-seq datasets representing “normal” and other relevant treatments (i.e., fasting, high-fat diet) are available for mouse and human and will also be included in this study. 3 6. Outcomes The insights derived in this project will illuminate evolutionarily conserved adaptations with potential translational relevance to human health, such as ischemia tolerance, metabolic control, and organ preservation. This project will test whether a core set of genes underlie shifts in metabolism and other hibernation phenotypes across multiple tissues in diverse mammalian hibernators. This will provide a valuable perspective on the extent to which mammalian hibernation is driven by the same underlying mechanisms and will likely identify a suite of genes essential to metabolic innovation in mammals. Findings from this project will inform our understanding of the relationship between human metabolism and that of other mammals, providing crucial context for ongoing efforts to translate our understanding of mammalian hibernation for the treatment and prevention of numerous human diseases. For example, this project may reveal novel gene regulatory programs underlying the onset and reversal of insulin resistance in hibernating species; these findings could then be extended by future work to develop therapeutic approaches to improve insulin sensitivity in diabetic and pre-diabetic human patients. As the proposed work spans multiple disciplines ranging from phylogenetics to functional genomics to cell biology and physiology, the diverse expertise of this working group will be critical for effectively interpreting and maximizing the translational potential of our findings. Our anticipated outputs include (i) primary literature article(s), (ii) model of trait evolution that simultaneously considers the evolution of gene expression in two states (e.g. hibernating and active states), (iii) a perspective of implementing phylogenetically-informed methods to analyze longitudinal datasets among species and (iv) a curated dataset of hibernation-related studies that will make it easier to add and implement future studies. 7. Rationale for a working group approach This working group with diverse expertise is needed to tackle the complex problem of understanding the molecular and cellular mechanisms underlying hibernation because this problem spans multiple specialized fields and data types. Integrating and unifying diverse omics- scale datasets across multiple species is very challenging due to differences in data types, experimental designs, and species biology. Moreover, hibernation involves intricate physiological processes regulated at multiple molecular levels—transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and epigenomic—which require expertise and technology beyond the scope of one laboratory. Therefore, we have assembled a team with expertise ranging from cell physiology to computational phylogenetic approaches. Addressing hibernation benefits from a systems biology perspective that integrates inputs from molecular biology, physiology, genomics, bioinformatics, and computational modeling specialists. The team will harmonize, analyze, and interpret these complex datasets jointly. Challenges in multi-omics, such as high-dimensional data analysis, missing data, and variable quality control standards, require our diverse expertise to both develop workflows and interpret results meaningfully. In summary, the complexity of hibernation biology and the scale and diversity of data involved necessitate a multidisciplinary working group to bring together expertise, computational resources, and mathematical models to effectively identify conserved regulatory mechanisms underlying this extreme phenotype. 8. Rationale for NCEMS support This project leverages expertise from multiple disciplines and individuals at different career stages. All aspects of the NCEMS support would further the aims of this proposal by having the necessary personnel, Staff Scientific (33% FTE) and Staff Scientist Assistant (50% FTE), 4 available for the data wrangling, harmonization, metadata creation and curation, preliminary analyses, advanced modeling and statistical methodologies, and technical training and mentoring essential for the execution of this project. NCEMS support is essential for conducting this research because integrating RNA-sequencing data from multiple species from active and hibernating states in a phylogenetic framework requires extensive data synthesis, multidisciplinary expertise, and advanced cyberinfrastructure that exceed the resources of an individual lab. The access NCEMS provides to staff scientists and assistants with specialized skills in data wrangling, advanced analytic methods, among others, is ideally suited to answering our big question. Moreover, the center’s cyberinfrastructure, project management assistance, and commitment to open science best practices creates a unique environment where we could work together to disentangle the shared mechanisms underlying hibernation biology that could not be achieved in any of our labs alone. 9. Requested resources We are requesting data storage (~1 Tb), compute for mapping data to genomes and downstream analyses which requires standard memory compute nodes with multiple cores, all software is open source or will be developed and implemented as part of this project. We also request Staff Scientific (33% FTE) and Staff Scientist Assistant (50% FTE) with experience analyzing genomic data, ideally with some knowledge of phylogenetic methods. 10. Proposed Timeline – 2 years Timeline Main Activities & Milestones Key Outcomes Months 1–3 RNA-seq QC and mapping; Ortholog mapping & GO annotation across species >90% gene orthologs and GO annotations completed Months 4–6 Analyses of convergent active state expression across mammals using EVE or similar approach Genes with shared or hibernation-specific expression patterns across species, tissues Months 5–12 Development and validation of bivariate models to analyze expression in active and hibernation states Visit to NCEMS / Working group personnel exchange Latent factors and phylogenetic signals discovered Months 13–15 Visualization of results; interpret models; biological interpretation Visualization of key features and regulators; prepare perspective for publication Months 16–18 Revise models as needed; functional characterization of genes using GO, KEGG enrichment with ClusterProfiler Signaling pathways of interest in hibernating species Months 19–21 Synthesize findings; relate to physiology Publish curated dataset Months 22–24 Prepare publications Final outputs readied for dissemination
