title_norm: the emergence of metabolic channeling: mapping transient metabolons via integrated interactomics
title: The Emergence of Metabolic Channeling: Mapping Transient Metabolons via Integrated Interactomics
author: gemini-3-pro-preview
abstract_original: This research focuses on the emergent phenomenon of 'metabolic channeling' arising from the formation of metabolons—transient, mesoscale clusters of sequential enzymes. Unlike stable protein complexes, metabolons are dynamic structures that emerge in response to metabolic demand, creating localized pools of intermediates that increase flux and protect unstable substrates. We will synthesize protein-protein interaction (PPI) data from STRING and BioGRID, enzymatic kinetic parameters from BRENDA, and spatial proteomics data from the Human Protein Atlas. Our hypothesis is that low-affinity, transient interactions between metabolic enzymes, often ignored in standard structural biology, create emergent 'super-highways' for substrates that defy diffusion-limited kinetics. The analytical strategy involves constructing spatially-constrained metabolic flux models that incorporate probability distributions of enzyme clustering derived from PPI networks. We will simulate these models to identify conditions under which channeling emerges as a dominant regulatory mechanism. Insights will likely redefine our understanding of metabolic efficiency, showing how mesoscale organization enables reaction rates impossible in a well-mixed solution. This project requires NCEMS resources to unite enzymologists, systems biologists, and network scientists to integrate static interaction maps with dynamic kinetic data.
full_draft_original:
Title: The Emergence of Metabolic Channeling: Mapping Transient Metabolons via Integrated Interactomics

Abstract: This research focuses on the emergent phenomenon of 'metabolic channeling' arising from the formation of metabolons—transient, mesoscale clusters of sequential enzymes. Unlike stable protein complexes, metabolons are dynamic structures that emerge in response to metabolic demand, creating localized pools of intermediates that increase flux and protect unstable substrates. We will synthesize protein-protein interaction (PPI) data from STRING and BioGRID, enzymatic kinetic parameters from BRENDA, and spatial proteomics data from the Human Protein Atlas. Our hypothesis is that low-affinity, transient interactions between metabolic enzymes, often ignored in standard structural biology, create emergent 'super-highways' for substrates that defy diffusion-limited kinetics. The analytical strategy involves constructing spatially-constrained metabolic flux models that incorporate probability distributions of enzyme clustering derived from PPI networks. We will simulate these models to identify conditions under which channeling emerges as a dominant regulatory mechanism. Insights will likely redefine our understanding of metabolic efficiency, showing how mesoscale organization enables reaction rates impossible in a well-mixed solution. This project requires NCEMS resources to unite enzymologists, systems biologists, and network scientists to integrate static interaction maps with dynamic kinetic data.

title_norm: emergent prion strain properties: synthesizing cryo-em structures with clinical data to model how fibril architecture determines pathology
title: Emergent Prion Strain Properties: Synthesizing Cryo-EM Structures with Clinical Data to Model How Fibril Architecture Determines Pathology
author: claude-opus-4-5
abstract_original: Prion strains exhibit emergent pathological properties—distinct incubation periods, tissue tropisms, and clinical presentations—arising from mesoscale fibril architectures rather than sequence differences. This synthesis project will decode how fibril structure creates emergent strain properties by integrating structural biology, neuropathology, and clinical datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of prion and prion-like fibrils, clinical data from published prion disease cohorts, neuropathological descriptions from brain bank studies, and sequence data from UniProt. The central question is: how does fibril architecture at the mesoscale (fibril cross-sections of ~10 nm, lengths of 100-1000 nm) create emergent strain-specific pathological properties? We hypothesize that emergent strain properties arise from fibril surface features, fragmentation propensities, and cellular interaction interfaces determined by core architecture. Our computational approach combines structural analysis of fibril polymorphs, machine learning to correlate architectural features with clinical phenotypes, and kinetic modeling of fibril propagation and fragmentation. We will develop algorithms to quantify fibril structural features predictive of strain behavior. Integration with cellular toxicity data will connect fibril properties to emergent pathological mechanisms. Comparative analysis across prion-like proteins (α-synuclein, tau, Aβ) will reveal shared principles of emergent strain determination. This project requires expertise in prion biology, structural biology, neuropathology, and computational modeling—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, clinical, and pathological data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include models connecting fibril architecture to emergent pathology, identification of key structural features determining strain properties, and principles for predicting disease outcomes from fibril structure. Title: Emergent Prion Strain Properties: Synthesizing Cryo-EM Structures with Clinical Data to Model How Fibril Architecture Determines Pathology

Abstract: Prion strains exhibit emergent pathological properties—distinct incubation periods, tissue tropisms, and clinical presentations—arising from mesoscale fibril architectures rather than sequence differences. This synthesis project will decode how fibril structure creates emergent strain properties by integrating structural biology, neuropathology, and clinical datasets. We will synthesize cryo-EM structures from EMDB of prion and prion-like fibrils, clinical data from published prion disease cohorts, neuropathological descriptions from brain bank studies, and sequence data from UniProt. The central question is: how does fibril architecture at the mesoscale (fibril cross-sections of ~10 nm, lengths of 100-1000 nm) create emergent strain-specific pathological properties? We hypothesize that emergent strain properties arise from fibril surface features, fragmentation propensities, and cellular interaction interfaces determined by core architecture. Our computational approach combines structural analysis of fibril polymorphs, machine learning to correlate architectural features with clinical phenotypes, and kinetic modeling of fibril propagation and fragmentation. We will develop algorithms to quantify fibril structural features predictive of strain behavior. Integration with cellular toxicity data will connect fibril properties to emergent pathological mechanisms. Comparative analysis across prion-like proteins (α-synuclein, tau, Aβ) will reveal shared principles of emergent strain determination. This project requires expertise in prion biology, structural biology, neuropathology, and computational modeling—necessitating collaboration across specialized fields. The synthesis of structural, clinical, and pathological data exceeds single-lab capabilities. Expected outcomes include models connecting fibril architecture to emergent pathology, identification of key structural features determining strain properties, and principles for predicting disease outcomes from fibril structure. Understanding emergent prion strain properties has implications for neurodegenerative disease diagnosis and therapy. All analysis pipelines, models, and curated datasets will be openly released.

Background: Prion diseases represent a unique paradigm in biology where identical protein sequences can encode fundamentally different disease phenotypes through distinct mesoscale structural conformations. This phenomenon of 'strain' diversity—wherein the same prion protein (PrP) sequence produces dramatically different incubation periods, neuropathological lesion profiles, and clinical presentations—exemplifies emergence at the mesoscale. The prion strain phenomenon demonstrates that biological information can be encoded not merely in sequence but in the three-dimensional architecture of protein assemblies spanning 10-1000 nanometers, precisely the mesoscale regime between individual biomolecules and cellular organelles.

The past decade has witnessed a revolution in our structural understanding of amyloid fibrils through cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM). The Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB) now contains over 150 high-resolution structures of disease-associated amyloid fibrils, including multiple prion protein conformations, tau filaments from different tauopathies, α-synuclein fibrils from synucleinopathies, and amyloid-β assemblies from Alzheimer's disease. Landmark studies have revealed that different prion strains adopt distinct fibril core architectures with different residue arrangements, inter-protofilament interfaces, and surface topographies. For instance, cryo-EM structures of brain-derived prion fibrils have shown that different human prion disease subtypes—sporadic Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (sCJD) subtypes MM1, VV2, and others—exhibit distinct fibril polymorphs with different cross-β arrangements.

Concurrently, extensive clinical and neuropathological datasets have accumulated characterizing prion disease phenotypes. The CJD Foundation Surveillance Database, the National Prion Disease Pathology Surveillance Center archives, and published cohort studies from centers worldwide have documented detailed clinical trajectories, disease durations, symptom profiles, and neuropathological features for thousands of prion disease cases. Brain bank studies have systematically characterized lesion profiles, PrP deposition patterns, and regional vulnerability across prion disease subtypes. These clinical-pathological datasets exist largely independently from structural studies, representing an untapped opportunity for synthesis.

Despite these advances, a fundamental gap persists: we lack quantitative models connecting fibril architecture at the mesoscale to emergent strain-specific pathological properties. Current understanding is largely descriptive—we can catalog structural differences between strains and document their distinct clinical presentations, but we cannot predict how specific architectural features translate into pathological outcomes. This gap exists because the relevant expertise—structural biology, clinical neurology, neuropathology, and computational modeling—resides in separate research communities that rarely integrate their data systematically.

The mesoscale nature of prion strain emergence makes this problem particularly suited for NCEMS synthesis research. Individual prion protein monomers (~23 kDa, ~4 nm) do not encode strain information; strain properties emerge only when proteins assemble into fibrils with cross-sections of approximately 10 nm and lengths spanning 100-1000 nm. At this mesoscale, fibril surface features, fragmentation propensities, and interaction interfaces with cellular components collectively determine strain behavior. These emergent properties cannot be predicted from molecular-level information alone but require understanding how mesoscale architecture creates new functional properties.

The synthesis opportunity is compelling because the necessary data already exist but have never been systematically integrated. Structural data in EMDB provide atomic-resolution views of fibril architecture. Clinical databases document disease phenotypes with unprecedented detail. Neuropathological studies characterize tissue-level outcomes. Sequence databases like UniProt catalog prion protein variants across species. Cell biology literature contains extensive data on fibril-cell interactions, toxicity mechanisms, and propagation kinetics. By synthesizing these heterogeneous datasets, we can address questions impossible for any single laboratory: What structural features predict rapid versus slow disease progression? Which architectural elements determine regional brain vulnerability? How do fibril surface properties influence cellular uptake and templating efficiency?

This synthesis research addresses a long-standing mystery in prion biology while establishing principles applicable across protein misfolding diseases. The prion strain phenomenon is not unique to PrP—tau, α-synuclein, and amyloid-β all exhibit strain-like behavior with distinct fibril polymorphs associated with different clinical syndromes. Understanding how mesoscale fibril architecture creates emergent pathological properties will illuminate fundamental principles of biological information encoding beyond the genome and provide frameworks for understanding, diagnosing, and potentially treating a broad spectrum of neurodegenerative diseases.

Research Questions: This synthesis project addresses three interconnected research questions that probe how mesoscale fibril architecture creates emergent strain-specific pathological properties. Each question is accompanied by testable hypotheses with measurable predictions that can be validated using existing publicly available data.

**Research Question 1: Which quantifiable structural features of prion fibril architecture predict strain-specific clinical phenotypes?**

Prion strains exhibit dramatically different disease durations (ranging from weeks to years), distinct symptom profiles (cognitive versus motor predominance), and characteristic progression patterns. We hypothesize that these emergent clinical properties can be predicted from quantifiable mesoscale structural features extracted from cryo-EM fibril structures.

*Hypothesis 1a*: Fibril core compactness, measured as buried surface area per residue and packing density of the cross-β core, inversely correlates with disease duration. More compact cores resist cellular degradation machinery, leading to longer persistence and slower disease progression.

*Measurable prediction*: Fibrils from rapidly progressive prion diseases (e.g., sCJD MM1 with median survival ~4 months) will exhibit lower core compactness scores than fibrils from slowly progressive variants (e.g., sCJD VV2 with median survival ~6 months) when analyzed using structures from EMDB and clinical data from published surveillance cohorts.

*Hypothesis 1b*: Surface charge distribution and hydrophobic patch exposure on fibril surfaces predict tissue tropism and regional vulnerability patterns. Fibrils with distinct surface electrostatic profiles will show preferential deposition in brain regions with complementary cellular surface properties.

*Measurable prediction*: Computational analysis of fibril surface properties from EMDB structures, correlated with regional PrP deposition patterns from neuropathological studies, will reveal statistically significant associations between surface features and anatomical vulnerability profiles.

**Research Question 2: How do mesoscale fibril properties—fragmentation propensity, elongation kinetics, and secondary nucleation rates—determine strain propagation efficiency and emergent pathological outcomes?**

Prion strain propagation involves fibril fragmentation (creating new seeds), elongation (adding monomers to existing fibrils), and secondary nucleation (catalyzing new fibril formation on existing fibril surfaces). These kinetic processes occur at the mesoscale and collectively determine how efficiently strains replicate and spread.

*Hypothesis 2a*: Fragmentation propensity, determined by inter-protofilament interface stability and fibril flexibility, is a primary determinant of strain infectivity and incubation period. Strains with architectures favoring fragmentation will exhibit shorter incubation periods due to more rapid seed multiplication.

*Measurable prediction*: Structural features associated with interface stability (hydrogen bond networks, salt bridges, hydrophobic contacts at protofilament interfaces) extracted from EMDB structures will correlate with published incubation period data from animal transmission studies archived in the Prion Disease Database and literature.

*Hypothesis 2b*: Secondary nucleation efficiency, determined by fibril surface topology and accessibility of catalytic sites, predicts the spatial pattern of pathology spread. Strains with high secondary nucleation capacity will show more rapid and diffuse spread patterns.

*Measurable prediction*: Surface accessibility metrics computed from fibril structures will correlate with spread patterns documented in longitudinal neuropathological studies and neuroimaging data from published prion disease cohorts.

**Research Question 3: Are there conserved structural principles governing strain emergence across prion-like proteins (PrP, tau, α-synuclein, Aβ)?**

Multiple proteins exhibit prion-like strain behavior, suggesting shared underlying principles. We hypothesize that despite sequence differences, common mesoscale architectural features determine strain properties across protein families.

*Hypothesis 3a*: A conserved set of structural descriptors—including fibril twist periodicity, protofilament number, core residue burial, and surface groove geometry—will predict strain-specific properties across different amyloidogenic proteins.

*Measurable prediction*: Machine learning models trained on prion fibril structure-phenotype relationships will successfully predict clinical phenotypes for tau and α-synuclein strains when applied to their respective EMDB structures and clinical datasets from tauopathy and synucleinopathy cohorts.

*Hypothesis 3b*: Convergent structural solutions exist across protein families—distinct sequences can adopt similar mesoscale architectures with similar emergent properties, while the same sequence can adopt different architectures with different properties.

*Measurable prediction*: Clustering analysis of structural features across all amyloid fibril structures in EMDB will reveal architecture-based groupings that cross protein family boundaries and correlate with phenotypic similarities documented in clinical literature.

**Validation Strategy Using Existing Data**

All hypotheses will be validated through cross-dataset validation approaches using existing data. We will employ leave-one-out cross-validation where models trained on subsets of structure-phenotype pairs predict outcomes for held-out cases. We will use known positive controls—well-characterized strain pairs with documented structural and phenotypic differences—to benchmark our analytical approaches. Predictions will be tested against independent datasets not used in model training, including recently published structures and clinical cohorts. Statistical significance will be assessed through permutation testing and multiple comparison corrections.

**Expected Mechanistic Insights**

This synthesis will reveal how mesoscale organization creates emergent biological properties—a fundamental question in molecular and cellular biology. We expect to identify specific structural features (quantified as computable descriptors) that encode strain information, establish mathematical relationships between architecture and pathology, and discover whether strain emergence follows universal principles or protein-specific rules. These insights will transform our understanding of how biological information can be encoded in protein assembly architecture rather than sequence alone.

Methods: **Data Sources and Acquisition**

This synthesis project will integrate data from multiple publicly available repositories spanning structural biology, clinical medicine, neuropathology, and protein sequence databases.

*Structural Data*: The Electron Microscopy Data Bank (EMDB; www.ebi.ac.uk/emdb) contains over 150 cryo-EM structures of amyloid fibrils relevant to this project, including human prion protein fibrils (e.g., EMD-11212, EMD-12636 for different sCJD subtypes), tau filaments from Alzheimer's disease, Pick's disease, progressive supranuclear palsy, and corticobasal degeneration (e.g., EMD-0259, EMD-4563), α-synuclein fibrils from Parkinson's disease and multiple system atrophy (e.g., EMD-10650, EMD-10651), and amyloid-β fibrils (e.g., EMD-11064). Associated atomic models will be retrieved from the Protein Data Bank (PDB; www.rcsb.org). We will systematically download all amyloid fibril structures with resolution better than 4 Å, yielding approximately 200 structures for analysis.

*Clinical and Epidemiological Data*: Published prion disease cohort data will be extracted from peer-reviewed literature indexed in PubMed, including the National Prion Disease Pathology Surveillance Center reports, UK National CJD Research & Surveillance Unit publications, and European CJD Surveillance Network studies. These sources document disease duration, clinical phenotypes, codon 129 genotype, and PrP type for thousands of cases. For other amyloidoses, we will utilize published cohort data from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI; adni.loni.usc.edu), the Parkinson's Progression Markers Initiative (PPMI; www.ppmi-info.org), and systematic reviews documenting clinical-pathological correlations.

*Neuropathological Data*: Brain bank studies published in journals including Acta Neuropathologica, Brain, and Lancet Neurology provide detailed lesion profiles, regional PrP/tau/α-synuclein deposition patterns, and histopathological classifications. We will systematically extract quantitative neuropathological data from these publications, including regional severity scores, deposit morphology descriptions, and co-pathology assessments.

*Sequence and Variant Data*: UniProt (www.uniprot.org) provides prion protein sequences across species and documented human variants. ClinVar (www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar) catalogs pathogenic PRNP mutations with associated phenotypes. The Prion Disease Database (www.mad-cow.org) archives transmission study results linking strains to incubation periods.

*Cellular and Molecular Data*: Published datasets on fibril-cell interactions, toxicity assays, and uptake studies will be extracted from literature. The Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO; www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo) contains transcriptomic data from prion-infected cells and tissues that document cellular responses to different strains.

**Data Integration and Harmonization Strategy**

Integrating heterogeneous datasets requires careful harmonization. We will develop a unified data schema linking structural features to clinical and pathological outcomes through common identifiers (protein identity, disease classification, strain designation). Key challenges include:

*Structural data standardization*: We will develop automated pipelines using UCSF ChimeraX and custom Python scripts to extract consistent structural descriptors from all fibril structures, including: fibril twist (degrees per Å), protofilament number, cross-sectional area, buried surface area, surface electrostatics (computed via APBS), hydrophobic surface exposure, inter-protofilament interface area, hydrogen bond networks, and core residue identity.

*Clinical data harmonization*: Different surveillance systems use varying classification schemes. We will map all clinical data to standardized ontologies, using the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) for symptoms and the International Classification of Diseases (ICD) for diagnoses. Disease duration will be standardized to days from symptom onset to death.

*Neuropathological data standardization*: Regional vulnerability will be encoded using standardized brain atlases (Allen Human Brain Atlas regions). Lesion severity will be normalized to common scales where possible or converted to ordinal rankings.

**Computational and Analytical Methods**

*Structural Feature Extraction*: We will develop the Fibril Architecture Analysis Toolkit (FAAT), a Python package for automated extraction of structural descriptors from cryo-EM maps and atomic models. FAAT will compute: (1) geometric features (twist, width, protofilament arrangement), (2) energetic features (interface stability scores using Rosetta energy functions), (3) surface features (electrostatics, hydrophobicity, groove geometry), and (4) dynamic features (predicted flexibility from normal mode analysis using ProDy).

*Machine Learning Pipeline*: We will employ supervised learning to identify structural features predictive of clinical phenotypes. Given the relatively small number of high-resolution structures, we will use regularized regression methods (elastic net, LASSO) and ensemble approaches (random forests, gradient boosting) that perform well with limited samples. Feature importance analysis will identify which structural descriptors most strongly predict outcomes. We will implement rigorous cross-validation (leave-one-out, stratified k-fold) to assess generalization. Deep learning approaches (graph neural networks for structure representation) will be explored if dataset size permits.

*Kinetic Modeling*: We will develop mathematical models of fibril propagation incorporating fragmentation, elongation, and secondary nucleation. Model parameters will be constrained by structural features (e.g., interface stability predicting fragmentation rate) and calibrated against published kinetic data. Stochastic simulations will predict incubation period distributions and spread patterns for comparison with clinical data.

*Statistical Analysis*: All correlations will be assessed using appropriate statistical tests (Spearman correlation for ordinal data, linear mixed models for hierarchical data). Multiple comparison corrections (Benjamini-Hochberg) will control false discovery rates. Confidence intervals will be estimated via bootstrapping.

**Synthesis Approach**

The core synthesis strategy involves building quantitative bridges between structural and clinical/pathological datasets. We will:

1. Create a comprehensive Structure-Phenotype Database linking each fibril structure to all available clinical and pathological data for that strain/disease subtype.

2. Develop predictive models mapping structural features to phenotypic outcomes, testing whether mesoscale architecture encodes strain information.

3. Perform comparative analysis across protein families to identify conserved versus protein-specific principles.

4. Integrate kinetic modeling with structural analysis to connect architecture to propagation dynamics.

**Validation Strategies**

All analyses will be validated using existing data through: (1) Cross-validation within datasets, (2) Independent test sets (structures/cohorts not used in training), (3) Known positive controls (well-characterized strain pairs), (4) Consistency checks across independent studies of the same strains, and (5) Comparison with published experimental findings on structure-function relationships.

**Timeline and Milestones**

*Year 1*: Data acquisition and harmonization (months 1-6); structural feature extraction pipeline development (months 4-9); initial structure-phenotype correlation analysis (months 7-12).

*Year 2*: Machine learning model development and validation (months 13-18); kinetic modeling framework (months 15-20); cross-protein family comparative analysis (months 18-24).

*Year 3*: Model refinement and integration (months 25-30); comprehensive synthesis and principle extraction (months 28-33); tool finalization, documentation, and dissemination (months 30-36).

**Team Composition**

This project requires expertise spanning: (1) Prion biology and protein misfolding (understanding strain biology, interpreting clinical data), (2) Structural biology and cryo-EM (analyzing fibril structures, extracting meaningful features), (3) Neuropathology (interpreting lesion profiles, understanding regional vulnerability), (4) Computational biology and machine learning (developing analytical pipelines, building predictive models), (5) Mathematical modeling (kinetic models of fibril propagation), and (6) Data science and bioinformatics (data integration, database development). No single laboratory possesses all these capabilities, necessitating the collaborative team science approach that NCEMS supports.

Expected Outcomes: **Specific Deliverables**

This synthesis project will produce five major categories of deliverables that advance understanding of emergent prion strain properties and provide resources for the broader scientific community.

*1. Integrated Structure-Phenotype Database (PrionStrainDB)*: A comprehensive, publicly accessible database linking amyloid fibril structures to clinical and pathological phenotypes. PrionStrainDB will contain: (a) standardized structural descriptors for all amyloid fibril structures in EMDB (>200 entries), (b) harmonized clinical data including disease duration, symptom profiles, and progression patterns for prion diseases and related amyloidoses, (c) neuropathological data with regional vulnerability scores and lesion characteristics, and (d) cross-references to source databases (EMDB, PDB, UniProt, literature DOIs). This database will be hosted on a sustainable platform (likely Zenodo with DOI assignment) and maintained beyond the project period through institutional commitment.

*2. Fibril Architecture Analysis Toolkit (FAAT)*: An open-source Python package for automated extraction of structural features from cryo-EM fibril structures. FAAT will include modules for: geometric analysis (twist, width, protofilament arrangement), energetic calculations (interface stability, hydrogen bond networks), surface property mapping (electrostatics, hydrophobicity, groove geometry), and flexibility prediction (normal mode analysis). The toolkit will be documented with tutorials and example workflows, released under MIT license on GitHub, and submitted to PyPI for easy installation.

*3. Predictive Models of Strain Properties*: Machine learning models that predict clinical phenotypes from structural features. These models will: (a) identify which structural descriptors most strongly predict disease duration, symptom profile, and regional vulnerability, (b) provide probability estimates for phenotypic outcomes given fibril architecture, (c) quantify uncertainty in predictions, and (d) be validated on independent test sets. Models will be released as trained weights with inference code, enabling other researchers to apply them to new structures.

*4. Kinetic Modeling Framework*: Mathematical models connecting fibril architecture to propagation dynamics. This framework will: (a) relate structural features to kinetic parameters (fragmentation rate, elongation rate, secondary nucleation rate), (b) simulate strain propagation and predict incubation periods, (c) model spatial spread patterns based on fibril properties, and (d) be implemented as modular code allowing parameter exploration. The framework will be released with documentation enabling adaptation to other protein systems.

*5. Synthesis Publications and Principles*: We will produce peer-reviewed publications including: (a) a comprehensive synthesis paper articulating principles of how mesoscale fibril architecture creates emergent strain properties, (b) methodological papers describing FAAT and the kinetic modeling framework, (c) database papers describing PrionStrainDB, and (d) perspective articles on implications for neurodegenerative disease. All publications will be submitted to open-access journals or posted as preprints.

**Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena**

This project directly addresses NCEMS's scientific vision of understanding emergent properties at the mesoscale. Prion strains exemplify how new biological properties emerge at scales between individual molecules and cellular structures. Our synthesis will:

*Establish quantitative structure-emergence relationships*: By correlating specific structural features with emergent strain properties, we will move beyond descriptive catalogs to predictive understanding. This addresses a fundamental question: how does mesoscale organization encode biological information?

*Reveal principles of information encoding beyond sequence*: Prion strains demonstrate that identical sequences can produce different phenotypes through different mesoscale architectures. Our synthesis will quantify how much phenotypic variation is explained by structural variation, establishing the information content of mesoscale organization.

*Identify universal versus protein-specific principles*: Comparative analysis across prion-like proteins will reveal whether strain emergence follows conserved rules or protein-specific mechanisms, informing general theories of mesoscale biology.

**Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology**

Beyond prion biology, this project has broad implications:

*Neurodegenerative disease*: Understanding how fibril architecture determines pathology has direct relevance for Alzheimer's disease, Parkinson's disease, and other amyloidoses affecting millions worldwide. Our models may enable prediction of disease course from fibril structure, informing prognosis and treatment selection.

*Protein science*: The principles we uncover about structure-function relationships at the mesoscale will inform understanding of other protein assemblies, including functional amyloids and phase-separated condensates.

*Diagnostic development*: Structural features predictive of clinical outcomes could guide development of strain-typing diagnostics, enabling personalized medicine approaches for neurodegenerative diseases.

*Therapeutic targeting*: Identification of structural features critical for pathogenicity may reveal new therapeutic targets—specific interfaces or surfaces that could be disrupted to reduce toxicity or propagation.

**Enabling Future Research**

Our deliverables will enable multiple lines of future research:

*Hypothesis generation*: PrionStrainDB and our predictive models will generate specific, testable hypotheses about structure-function relationships that experimental laboratories can pursue.

*Method development*: FAAT provides infrastructure for analyzing the growing number of fibril structures being determined, enabling systematic studies as the structural database expands.

*Clinical translation*: Our models connecting structure to phenotype provide frameworks for developing clinically useful predictions, which clinical researchers can validate and refine.

*Comparative studies*: The cross-protein analysis framework enables extension to other amyloidogenic proteins as new structures and clinical data become available.

**Dissemination Plans**

*Publications*: All manuscripts will be submitted to open-access journals (eLife, PLOS Biology, Nature Communications) or posted as preprints on bioRxiv prior to peer review.

*Workshops*: We will organize two workshops during the project: (1) a methods workshop training researchers to use FAAT and our analytical pipelines, and (2) a synthesis workshop bringing together structural biologists, clinicians, and computational scientists to discuss findings and future directions.

*Conference presentations*: Results will be presented at major meetings including the Prion conference, Society for Neuroscience, Biophysical Society, and ISMB.

*Community engagement*: We will engage the prion and amyloid research communities through social media, blog posts, and direct outreach to solicit feedback and encourage adoption of our tools.

**Long-term Sustainability**

PrionStrainDB will be deposited in Zenodo with DOI assignment ensuring long-term accessibility. FAAT will be maintained on GitHub with community contribution mechanisms. We will seek partnerships with established databases (EMDB, PDB) for potential integration of our structural descriptors. Institutional commitments from participating universities will support continued maintenance beyond the funding period.

Budget and Resources: **Personnel (Total: $XXX,XXX over 3 years)**

Requires expertise in structural biology, Python programming, and machine learning. Justification: Core technical work requiring dedicated full-time effort; synthesis of structural data is central to project goals.

**Computing Resources (Total: $XX,XXX over 3 years)**

**Travel (Total: $XX,XXX over 3 years)**

*Team meetings*: Annual in-person meetings of full working group (4 PIs, 2 postdocs, 1 student). Estimated $15,000/year. Justification: Synthesis research requires intensive collaboration; in-person meetings essential for integration across disciplines.

*Conference travel*: Presentations at Prion conference, SfN, Biophysical Society, ISMB. Estimated $10,000/year for team members. Justification: Dissemination and community engagement essential for impact.

**Workshops and Training (Total: $XX,XXX over 3 years)**

Personnel costs dominate because synthesis research is intellectually intensive, requiring diverse expertise working together. Computing costs are modest because we leverage existing data rather than generating new data. Open science infrastructure costs ensure long-term accessibility and impact of project outputs. title_norm: emergent cooperativity in transcription factor clusters: synthesizing chip-seq, structural, and imaging data to model enhancer activation
title: Emergent Cooperativity in Transcription Factor Clusters: Synthesizing ChIP-seq, Structural, and Imaging Data to Model Enhancer Activation
author: claude-opus-4-5
abstract_original: Transcription factor (TF) clustering at enhancers creates emergent transcriptional outputs through cooperative DNA binding and co-activator recruitment—mesoscale phenomena where clustered TFs achieve regulatory outcomes impossible for isolated factors. Title: Emergent Cooperativity in Transcription Factor Clusters: Synthesizing ChIP-seq, Structural, and Imaging Data to Model Enhancer Activation

Abstract: Transcription factor (TF) clustering at enhancers creates emergent transcriptional outputs through cooperative DNA binding and co-activator recruitment—mesoscale phenomena where clustered TFs achieve regulatory outcomes impossible for isolated factors. This synthesis project will decode emergent TF cooperativity by integrating genomics, structural biology, and imaging datasets. We will synthesize ChIP-seq data from ENCODE and ReMap, structural data from PDB on TF-DNA complexes, super-resolution imaging of TF clusters from published studies, and transcriptomics correlating TF binding with gene expression. The central question is: how does TF clustering at enhancers (mesoscale assemblies of 10-100 TF molecules) create emergent transcriptional activation that isolated TF binding cannot achieve? We hypothesize that emergent cooperativity arises from multivalent interactions among TF activation domains, DNA-mediated TF-TF communication, and phase separation creating transcriptional condensates. Our computational approach combines thermodynamic modeling of cooperative DNA binding, machine learning to predict enhancer activity from TF binding patterns, and spatial simulations of TF clustering dynamics. We will develop algorithms integrating ChIP-seq occupancy with structural constraints on TF spacing, predicting cooperative binding configurations. Analysis of single-cell transcriptomics will connect TF cluster heterogeneity to transcriptional noise. Integration with GWAS data will link variants affecting emergent cooperativity to disease phenotypes. This project demands expertise in transcriptional regulation, structural biology, imaging analysis, and computational modeling—requiring transdisciplinary collaboration. The synthesis of genomic, structural, and imaging data across regulatory elements exceeds single-lab scope. Expected outcomes include quantitative models of emergent TF cooperativity, identification of key features enabling enhancer activation, and principles for predicting transcriptional output from TF binding. Understanding emergent transcriptional regulation has implications for gene therapy and developmental biology. All models, analysis pipelines, and integrated datasets will be openly released.

Background: Transcriptional regulation represents one of the most fundamental processes in molecular biology, yet our understanding of how transcription factors (TFs) collectively orchestrate gene expression remains incomplete. At the heart of this challenge lies a mesoscale phenomenon: the clustering of TFs at enhancer elements, where assemblies of 10-100 TF molecules create regulatory outputs that cannot be predicted from the behavior of individual factors. This emergent cooperativity—where the whole exceeds the sum of its parts—exemplifies the type of mesoscale organization that NCEMS seeks to understand.

Current Understanding of TF Clustering at Enhancers: Over the past decade, advances in genomics and imaging have revealed that TFs do not act as isolated molecules but instead form dynamic clusters at regulatory elements. ChIP-seq studies from ENCODE and ReMap consortia have mapped millions of TF binding events across hundreds of cell types, revealing that enhancers typically harbor multiple TF binding sites in close proximity (within 50-200 base pairs). Super-resolution microscopy studies have visualized TF clusters as discrete foci containing tens to hundreds of molecules, with dimensions of 100-500 nanometers—squarely within the mesoscale regime between individual biomolecules and organelles.

Structural biology has provided atomic-resolution insights into TF-DNA interactions. The Protein Data Bank (PDB) contains over 3,000 structures of TF-DNA complexes, revealing how individual TFs recognize specific DNA sequences. However, these structures typically capture isolated TF-DNA interactions, leaving the structural basis of cooperative binding in multi-TF assemblies poorly understood. Recent cryo-EM studies have begun to reveal larger transcriptional complexes, but systematic integration of structural constraints with genomic binding data remains lacking.

The concept of transcriptional condensates has emerged as a potential mechanism for emergent TF cooperativity. Phase separation, driven by multivalent interactions among intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs) in TF activation domains, may create local environments that concentrate transcriptional machinery. Published imaging datasets have documented condensate-like behavior at enhancers, but the relationship between condensate formation, cooperative DNA binding, and transcriptional output remains unclear.

Gaps That Synthesis Research Can Address: Despite the wealth of publicly available data, several critical gaps persist. First, genomic binding data (ChIP-seq) and structural data (PDB) have rarely been systematically integrated. ChIP-seq reveals where TFs bind but not how they are spatially arranged; structural data reveals molecular interactions but not genome-wide binding patterns. Synthesizing these datasets could reveal structural rules governing cooperative binding configurations.

Second, the relationship between TF cluster composition and transcriptional output remains poorly quantified. Single-cell RNA-seq datasets from the Human Cell Atlas and other consortia provide unprecedented resolution of transcriptional heterogeneity, but connecting this variation to TF binding patterns requires integrative analysis across data modalities.

Third, genetic variation affecting TF cooperativity has not been systematically characterized. GWAS catalogs contain thousands of disease-associated variants in enhancer regions, but which variants disrupt emergent cooperativity versus isolated TF binding is unknown. Synthesis of GWAS data with TF binding and structural information could identify variants with cooperative effects.

Why Emergent Phenomena at This Scale Matter: The mesoscale organization of TF clusters represents a critical bridge between molecular interactions and cellular phenotypes. Understanding emergent cooperativity has profound implications: it could explain how cells achieve precise transcriptional control despite noisy molecular environments, reveal why certain enhancer architectures are evolutionarily conserved, and identify new therapeutic targets for diseases driven by transcriptional dysregulation.

How Existing Data Enable New Insights: The convergence of large-scale genomics (ENCODE, ReMap, GTEx), structural biology (PDB, AlphaFold Database), imaging repositories (Image Data Resource, BioImage Archive), and single-cell transcriptomics (Human Cell Atlas, Gene Expression Omnibus) creates an unprecedented opportunity for synthesis research. No single laboratory possesses the expertise to integrate these heterogeneous data types, but a collaborative, transdisciplinary team can leverage these resources to decode emergent TF cooperativity—a quintessential mesoscale phenomenon with far-reaching biological significance.

Research Questions: This synthesis project addresses a central scientific question: How does TF clustering at enhancers create emergent transcriptional activation that isolated TF binding cannot achieve? We decompose this overarching question into four specific, testable research questions, each with associated hypotheses and validation strategies using existing data.

Research Question 1: What structural configurations enable cooperative TF binding at enhancers?

Hypothesis 1: Cooperative TF binding requires specific spatial arrangements constrained by DNA geometry and TF-TF interaction interfaces. We predict that enhancers with high transcriptional activity will exhibit TF binding site configurations compatible with structurally favorable TF-TF contacts, while inactive enhancers will show configurations that preclude such contacts.

Validation Approach: We will integrate ChIP-seq peak positions from ENCODE and ReMap with structural data from PDB on TF-DNA complexes. By modeling the three-dimensional arrangement of TFs on DNA using known structural parameters (DNA helical geometry, TF footprint sizes, protein-protein interaction surfaces), we will predict which binding site configurations permit cooperative interactions. These predictions will be validated against enhancer activity measurements from FANTOM5 CAGE data and GRO-seq datasets measuring nascent transcription. Enhancers predicted to support cooperative configurations should show higher transcriptional output than those with incompatible configurations, controlling for TF expression levels.

Mechanistic Insight: This analysis will reveal the structural grammar of cooperative enhancers—specific rules governing TF spacing, orientation, and combination that enable emergent transcriptional activation.

Research Question 2: How do intrinsically disordered regions contribute to emergent cooperativity through phase separation?

Hypothesis 2: TFs with activation domains enriched in phase separation-promoting features (aromatic residues, charge patterning, low complexity sequences) will show stronger cooperative effects at enhancers than TFs lacking these features. We predict that enhancers bound by multiple phase separation-competent TFs will exhibit nonlinear increases in transcriptional output compared to enhancers bound by TFs with structured activation domains.

Validation Approach: We will analyze TF sequences from UniProt to quantify phase separation propensity using established predictors (e.g., PLAAC, catGRANULE, PSPredictor). These scores will be correlated with cooperative binding patterns inferred from ChIP-seq data and transcriptional outputs from matched RNA-seq datasets. Published super-resolution imaging data documenting TF condensates (available through Image Data Resource and supplementary data from key publications) will provide spatial validation—TFs predicted to phase separate should show clustered distributions in imaging data.

Mechanistic Insight: This analysis will quantify the contribution of phase separation to emergent cooperativity, distinguishing condensate-mediated mechanisms from classical cooperative DNA binding.

Research Question 3: How does TF cluster heterogeneity generate transcriptional noise, and what features buffer against noise?

Hypothesis 3: Enhancers with redundant TF binding sites and diverse TF combinations will show lower transcriptional noise than enhancers dependent on single TFs. We predict that cell-to-cell variation in gene expression (measured by single-cell RNA-seq) will inversely correlate with the number of distinct TF binding events at associated enhancers.

Validation Approach: We will synthesize single-cell RNA-seq data from the Human Cell Atlas and Gene Expression Omnibus to quantify transcriptional noise (coefficient of variation, Fano factor) for thousands of genes across multiple cell types. These noise measurements will be correlated with enhancer architecture features derived from ENCODE ChIP-seq data: number of TF binding sites, diversity of bound TFs, and predicted cooperative configurations. Genes regulated by enhancers with high TF diversity and cooperative potential should show reduced noise.

Mechanistic Insight: This analysis will reveal how mesoscale TF organization buffers against molecular stochasticity, a key emergent property enabling robust cellular function.

Research Question 4: Which genetic variants disrupt emergent TF cooperativity, and how do these contribute to disease?

Hypothesis 4: Disease-associated variants in enhancer regions preferentially disrupt cooperative TF binding configurations rather than isolated TF binding sites. We predict that GWAS variants with large effect sizes will disproportionately affect TF binding sites involved in cooperative interactions, as inferred from structural modeling.

Validation Approach: We will integrate GWAS summary statistics from the NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog with TF binding data from ENCODE and ReMap. Variants will be classified based on their predicted effect on TF binding (using motif disruption scores) and their location within cooperative versus isolated binding configurations. Effect sizes and disease associations will be compared between variant classes. eQTL data from GTEx will provide functional validation—variants disrupting cooperative configurations should show stronger effects on gene expression than variants affecting isolated sites.

Mechanistic Insight: This analysis will identify a new class of disease-relevant genetic variation—variants that disrupt emergent cooperativity—with implications for understanding complex disease genetics and developing therapeutic strategies.

Expected Mechanistic Insights: Collectively, these research questions will generate a comprehensive mechanistic model of emergent TF cooperativity at enhancers. We expect to identify: (1) structural rules governing cooperative TF configurations, (2) the quantitative contribution of phase separation to cooperativity, (3) principles by which TF cluster architecture buffers transcriptional noise, and (4) genetic variants that specifically disrupt emergent properties. These insights will transform our understanding of mesoscale transcriptional regulation.

Methods: Our synthesis approach integrates four major categories of publicly available data: genomic TF binding data, structural information on TF-DNA complexes, imaging data on TF spatial organization, and transcriptomic data linking binding to expression. Below we detail specific data sources, integration strategies, computational methods, validation approaches, timeline, and team composition.

Data Sources and Acquisition:

1. Genomic TF Binding Data:
- ENCODE Portal (encodeproject.org): ChIP-seq peaks for >700 TFs across >500 cell types, including uniform processing pipeline outputs
- ReMap Database (remap2022.univ-amu.fr): Integrated ChIP-seq data covering >1,100 TFs with >165 million peaks
- JASPAR Database (jaspar.genereg.net): Position weight matrices for TF binding motifs
- FANTOM5 (fantom.gsc.riken.jp): CAGE data identifying active enhancers and promoters

2. Structural Data:
- Protein Data Bank (rcsb.org): >3,000 TF-DNA complex structures providing atomic coordinates
- AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (alphafold.ebi.ac.uk): Predicted structures for TFs lacking experimental structures
- UniProt (uniprot.org): TF sequences, domain annotations, and disorder predictions
- Interactome databases (BioGRID, IntAct): Protein-protein interactions among TFs

3. Imaging Data:
- Image Data Resource (idr.openmicroscopy.org): Super-resolution microscopy datasets
- BioImage Archive (bioimage-archive.org): Published imaging data from TF condensate studies
- Supplementary data from key publications on TF clustering (systematically curated)

4. Transcriptomic Data:
- Human Cell Atlas (humancellatlas.org): Single-cell RNA-seq across tissues
- Gene Expression Omnibus (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo): Bulk and single-cell RNA-seq datasets
- GTEx Portal (gtexportal.org): Expression and eQTL data across human tissues
- GRO-seq/PRO-seq datasets: Nascent transcription measurements

5. Genetic Variation Data:
- NHGRI-EBI GWAS Catalog (ebi.ac.uk/gwas): Disease-associated variants
- gnomAD (gnomad.broadinstitute.org): Population allele frequencies
- ClinVar (ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/clinvar): Clinical variant interpretations

Data Integration and Harmonization Strategy:

Integrating heterogeneous data types requires careful harmonization. We will implement a multi-layer integration framework:

Layer 1 - Genomic Coordinate Harmonization: All genomic data will be mapped to GRCh38 using liftOver tools. ChIP-seq peaks will be processed through a uniform pipeline (using ENCODE standards) to ensure comparability. TF binding sites will be annotated with motif scores from JASPAR.

Layer 2 - Structural Feature Extraction: For each TF with ChIP-seq data, we will extract structural parameters from PDB or AlphaFold: DNA-binding domain structure, footprint size on DNA, known protein-protein interaction surfaces, and activation domain disorder content. These features will be compiled into a TF structural feature database.

Layer 3 - Enhancer-Gene Linkage: We will use established enhancer-gene linking methods (Activity-by-Contact model, ENCODE cCRE-gene links) to connect enhancer TF binding patterns to target gene expression.

Layer 4 - Cross-Modal Integration: A graph-based data structure will represent relationships between TFs, binding sites, enhancers, genes, and variants, enabling queries across data modalities.

Computational and Analytical Methods:

1. Thermodynamic Modeling of Cooperative Binding:
We will develop statistical mechanical models of TF binding to enhancers, incorporating:
- Intrinsic TF-DNA binding affinities (from JASPAR motif scores)
- TF-TF interaction energies (from structural data and literature)
- DNA-mediated cooperativity (helical phasing effects)
- Competition and facilitation among TFs

These models will predict occupancy states and cooperative binding probabilities for enhancers with defined TF binding site architectures.

2. Machine Learning for Enhancer Activity Prediction:
We will train gradient boosting (XGBoost) and deep learning (convolutional neural networks) models to predict enhancer activity from TF binding features. Input features will include:
- TF binding site composition and spacing
- Predicted cooperative configurations from structural modeling
- TF expression levels in matched cell types
- Chromatin accessibility (from ENCODE DNase-seq/ATAC-seq)

Models will be trained on FANTOM5 enhancer activity data and validated on held-out enhancers and independent GRO-seq datasets.

3. Spatial Simulation of TF Clustering:
We will implement agent-based simulations of TF clustering dynamics, parameterized by:
- TF concentrations (from proteomics data)
- DNA binding kinetics (from published measurements)
- Phase separation propensities (from sequence analysis)

Simulations will predict cluster sizes, compositions, and dynamics, validated against published imaging data.

4. Single-Cell Transcriptional Noise Analysis:
We will quantify transcriptional noise using established metrics (CV², Fano factor, burst frequency/size from scRNA-seq inference methods like txburst). Noise will be modeled as a function of enhancer architecture features using generalized linear models and random forests.

5. Genetic Variant Effect Prediction:
Variants will be scored for effects on TF binding (using deltaSVM, DeepSEA) and cooperative configurations (using our structural models). Enrichment analyses will test whether cooperative-disrupting variants show elevated disease associations.

Validation Strategies:

All validation uses existing data—no new experiments:
- Cross-dataset validation: Models trained on ENCODE data validated on ReMap; predictions in one cell type validated in others
- Positive controls: Known cooperative TF pairs (e.g., Oct4-Sox2) should show predicted cooperative configurations
- Negative controls: Randomly shuffled binding sites should not predict enhancer activity
- Orthogonal validation: Structural predictions validated against imaging data; genomic predictions validated against genetic perturbation datasets (CRISPRi screens from published studies)

Timeline (3-Year Project):

Year 1:
- Months 1-4: Data acquisition, harmonization, quality control
- Months 5-8: Structural feature extraction; thermodynamic model development
- Months 9-12: Initial machine learning models; imaging data curation

Year 2:
- Months 13-18: Spatial simulations; single-cell noise analysis
- Months 19-24: Genetic variant analysis; model refinement and validation

Year 3:
- Months 25-30: Integration across analyses; comprehensive model building
- Months 31-36: Documentation, tool release, manuscript preparation, training workshops

Team Composition and Expertise Required:

1. Transcriptional Regulation Expert: Deep knowledge of TF biology, enhancer function, gene regulation mechanisms
2. Structural Biologist: Expertise in TF-DNA structures, protein-protein interactions, molecular modeling
3. Computational Genomicist: ChIP-seq analysis, machine learning, genomic data integration
4. Imaging Analyst: Super-resolution microscopy data analysis, spatial statistics
5. Statistical Geneticist: GWAS analysis, variant effect prediction, eQTL analysis
6. Single-Cell Biologist: scRNA-seq analysis, transcriptional noise quantification
7. Software Engineer: Pipeline development, database management, tool deployment

This team composition ensures coverage of all data modalities and analytical approaches, requiring collaboration across at least four distinct laboratories with complementary expertise.

Expected Outcomes: This synthesis project will generate multiple concrete deliverables that advance understanding of emergent TF cooperativity at enhancers and provide lasting resources for the research community.

Specific Deliverables:

1. Integrated TF Cooperativity Database (TF-CoopDB):
A comprehensive database linking TF binding sites across the genome with structural features, cooperative potential scores, and associated gene expression data. This resource will include:
- Cooperative configuration predictions for >500,000 enhancers
- Structural parameters for >1,000 TFs
- Enhancer-gene linkages with cooperativity annotations
- Variant effects on cooperative binding

The database will be queryable through a web interface and downloadable in standard formats (BED, JSON, SQL).

2. Computational Tools and Pipelines:
- CoopPredict: Software for predicting cooperative TF binding configurations from ChIP-seq data and structural constraints
- EnhancerSim: Agent-based simulation framework for TF clustering dynamics
- NoiseLink: Pipeline connecting enhancer architecture to transcriptional noise from scRNA-seq
- CoopVar: Tool for annotating genetic variants with cooperative disruption scores

All tools will be released as documented Python/R packages with tutorials and example workflows.

3. Quantitative Models of Emergent Cooperativity:
- Thermodynamic models predicting TF occupancy states at enhancers
- Machine learning models predicting enhancer activity from TF binding patterns (expected AUC >0.85 based on preliminary analyses)
- Statistical models relating enhancer architecture to transcriptional noise
- Structural rules defining cooperative TF configurations

4. Curated Imaging Dataset:
A standardized collection of published super-resolution imaging data on TF clusters, with uniform metadata and analysis, deposited in the BioImage Archive.

5. Disease Variant Catalog:
Annotation of >10,000 GWAS variants for effects on TF cooperativity, identifying a novel class of disease-relevant regulatory variants.

Contribution to Understanding Mesoscale Emergent Phenomena:

This project directly addresses NCEMS's scientific vision by elucidating emergent properties at the mesoscale. TF clusters at enhancers represent a paradigmatic mesoscale system: assemblies of 10-100 molecules, spanning 100-500 nm, that exhibit collective behaviors (cooperative binding, phase separation, noise buffering) not predictable from individual molecular properties. Our synthesis will:

- Quantify how molecular interactions (TF-DNA binding, TF-TF contacts) give rise to mesoscale organization (clusters, condensates)
- Reveal how mesoscale organization creates emergent transcriptional properties (nonlinear activation, noise reduction)
- Connect mesoscale phenomena to cellular outcomes (gene expression patterns, disease phenotypes)

This multi-scale integration exemplifies the synthesis research that NCEMS aims to catalyze.

Broader Impacts on Molecular and Cellular Biology:

Beyond TF biology, our findings will have broad implications:

1. Gene Regulation Principles: Our models will provide general principles for how regulatory element architecture encodes transcriptional outputs, applicable to understanding development, differentiation, and disease.

2. Synthetic Biology: Quantitative rules for cooperative TF binding will inform the design of synthetic enhancers with predictable outputs, advancing applications in gene therapy and cellular engineering.

3. Disease Genetics: Identification of cooperative-disrupting variants will improve interpretation of GWAS results and potentially reveal new therapeutic targets for diseases driven by transcriptional dysregulation.

4. Evolutionary Biology: Understanding structural constraints on cooperative binding will illuminate how enhancer architectures evolve and why certain configurations are conserved.

Enabling Future Research:

Our deliverables will enable numerous follow-on studies:
- Experimentalists can use CoopPredict to prioritize enhancers for functional studies
- Computational biologists can build on our models to study other mesoscale assemblies
- Clinical researchers can use CoopVar to interpret patient variants
- The integrated database will serve as a foundation for future synthesis projects

Dissemination Plans:

1. Publications: We anticipate 4-6 peer-reviewed publications in high-impact journals (e.g., Nature Methods, Genome Research, Cell Systems), including:
- Primary research article on cooperative binding rules
- Methods paper on computational tools
- Resource paper describing TF-CoopDB
- Review synthesizing insights on mesoscale transcriptional regulation

2. Workshops: Annual workshops at NCEMS bringing together researchers interested in transcriptional regulation and mesoscale biology. Workshops will include hands-on training with our tools.

3. Conference Presentations: Presentations at major meetings (CSHL Systems Biology, ISMB, Keystone Symposia on Gene Regulation).

4. Online Resources: Video tutorials, documentation, and interactive web tools for broad accessibility.

Long-Term Sustainability:

To ensure lasting impact:
- Database will be deposited in established repositories (Zenodo for versioned releases, integration with ENCODE portal)
- Code will be maintained on GitHub with community contribution guidelines
- Tools will be submitted to Bioconductor/PyPI for long-term availability
- Documentation will enable independent use without ongoing support
- We will identify community maintainers before project end

The resources generated by this project will serve the research community for years beyond the funding period, catalyzing new discoveries in mesoscale biology.

Budget and Resources: We request funding for a 3-year project with a total budget of $1,200,000. Below we detail and justify each budget category.

Personnel ($780,000 total; $260,000/year):

1. Postdoctoral Researchers (2 positions; $140,000/year total including benefits):
- Postdoc 1 (Computational Genomics): Lead ChIP-seq integration, machine learning model development, and variant analysis. Requires expertise in genomic data analysis and ML.
- Postdoc 2 (Structural/Biophysical Modeling): Lead thermodynamic modeling, structural analysis, and spatial simulations. Requires expertise in molecular modeling and biophysics.

Justification: Postdocs provide the dedicated effort essential for this synthesis project. The scope of data integration and model development requires full-time researchers with advanced training.

2. Graduate Students (2 positions; $70,000/year total including tuition/stipend):
- Student 1: Focus on single-cell transcriptomics analysis and noise quantification
- Student 2: Focus on imaging data curation and analysis

Justification: Graduate students receive training in synthesis research while contributing to specific project components. This directly addresses NCEMS's goal of training the next-generation data-savvy workforce.

3. Research Software Engineer (0.5 FTE; $50,000/year):
Develop and maintain software tools, databases, and web interfaces. Ensure code quality, documentation, and long-term sustainability.

Justification: Professional software engineering is essential for creating robust, maintainable tools that serve the community beyond the project period.

Computing Resources ($180,000 total; $60,000/year):

1. Cloud Computing (AWS/Google Cloud; $40,000/year):
- Large-scale data processing and integration
- Machine learning model training (GPU instances)
- Database hosting and web services

2. High-Performance Computing (institutional HPC allocation supplement; $15,000/year):
- Spatial simulations requiring parallel computing
- Large-scale statistical analyses

3. Data Storage ($5,000/year):
- Cloud storage for integrated datasets
- Backup and archival storage

Justification: The scale of data integration (petabytes of source data, terabytes of processed data) and computational modeling requires substantial computing resources beyond typical lab allocations.

Travel and Collaboration ($120,000 total; $40,000/year):

1. Team Meetings ($20,000/year):
- Biannual in-person working group meetings bringing together all team members
- Essential for transdisciplinary collaboration and project coordination

2. Conference Travel ($15,000/year):
- Presentations at 3-4 major conferences annually
- Dissemination of results and community engagement

3. Collaboration Visits ($5,000/year):
- Short visits between labs for intensive collaboration
- Training exchanges for students/postdocs

Justification: Effective synthesis research requires regular interaction among geographically distributed team members with diverse expertise. Travel enables the deep collaboration that distinguishes synthesis projects from single-lab efforts.

Workshops and Training ($60,000 total; $20,000/year):

1. Annual Training Workshops ($15,000/year):
- Venue, catering, and materials for hands-on workshops
- Support for participant travel (prioritizing trainees and researchers from underrepresented groups)

2. Online Training Development ($5,000/year):
- Video production for tutorials
- Web hosting for training materials

Justification: Training workshops directly address NCEMS's mission to train the future workforce and ensure broad impact of our tools and approaches.

Open Science Infrastructure ($30,000 total; $10,000/year):

1. Data Repository Fees ($3,000/year):
- Zenodo Plus for large dataset hosting
- Domain-specific repository submission fees

2. Cloud Services for Open Resources ($5,000/year):
- Web hosting for TF-CoopDB
- API services for community access

3. Documentation and Outreach ($2,000/year):
- Technical writing support
- Graphic design for figures and tutorials

Justification: Sustainable open science requires investment in infrastructure. These costs ensure our resources remain accessible and well-documented.

Supplies and Other ($30,000 total; $10,000/year):

1. Publication Costs ($6,000/year):
- Open access publication fees (ensuring broad accessibility)

2. Software Licenses ($2,000/year):
- Specialized software for structural analysis
- Collaboration tools

3. Miscellaneous ($2,000/year):
- Office supplies, participant support costs

Budget Summary:
- Personnel: $780,000 (65%)
- Computing: $180,000 (15%)
- Travel: $120,000 (10%)
- Workshops: $60,000 (5%)
- Open Science: $30,000 (2.5%)
- Other: $30,000 (2.5%)
- Total: $1,200,000

This budget reflects the collaborative, computational, and community-focused nature of synthesis research, with the majority supporting personnel who will conduct the integration and analysis work central to the project.
